MADRID, July 30-Spain and
Portugal were linked today by new
pact calling for immediate consulta-
ton if either should be threatened
with attack.


1t was stated the agreement would
not affect existing alliances or
treaties the countries have with
other nations.


Portugal long has been friendly
with Great Britain, while Nationalist
Spain leans toward the axis powers,
which helped Generalissimo Fran
cisco Frances forces win the Span
ish Civil War;


The new agreement, signed yes
terday as a protocol to the Spanish
Portuguese non-aggression treaty
concluded March 18, 1899, is effective
Immediately.


The protocol provides that either
of the Iberian peninsular neighbors
may take the initiative in such con-
sultation whenever events may be
foreseen or take place which by their
nature may threaten the inviolabil.
ity Of their respective metropolitan
territories or constitute a danger fol-
their safety or independence"

BRUSSELS, March 1.-TWO Bel
gian army planes were shot down
over their homeland today in a
clash with German bomber which
the government quickly protested to
Berlin as grave violation of Bel
gian neutrality and an act OF
aggression.


One Belgian pilot was killed and
another wounded in the clash.


The incident, announced In . COM
munique. was followed swiftly by a
series OF unrelated accidents in
which four other Belgian planes
Grained AND one pilot WAS killed,
making the day the worst In the
nations aviation history.


Within q short time after the
issuance of the communique, Ger
man Ambassador Vicco Karl Won
Buelow-Schwante, obviously dis
turbed, hastened to the Belgian
Foreign ONCE.


With Spaak 10 Minutes.


He was kept waiting As minutes
before he was admitted to Foreign
Minister Paul Henri Spaak. He was
with Spaak for about 10 minutes,
and after his departure the govern
ment announced a vigorous" pro-
test had been registered.


The official Belgian version said
three Belgian planes were involved
in the encounter with the German
plane, a large Dornier bomber, over
Saint Hubert in Belgium's Luxem-
bourg province.


The Belgians surrounded the craft,
which then opened fire upon them,
it was said.


The leader Of the Belgian squad
ron, Sub-Lt. Hernard. was killed
when he was struck by a burst of
fire and his plane crashed near
the village Of Hemroulle.


A few minutes later, another of
the Belgian planes was forced down
at Achene with bullet holes in the
gas tank, but the pilot was unin-
jured. The pilot Of the third place
was wounded.


Planes Collide Near Antwerp.


Another flyer was killed SUBJ
sequently when two Belgian army
planes collided near Antwerp. Two
other Belgian military planes were
reported to have cracked up near
Antwerp and at Bierzet, but the
flyers escaped injury.


The clash of the Belgian planes
and the German Dornier was the
first such incident since the start
Of the European war, although
Belgian patrols frequently have
gone aloft to drive off belligerent
craft flying over their territory.
Belgian anti-aircraft batteries also
have fired sat belligerent planes,
driving them across the border, but
no hits have been reported.


The Belgian government has re-
peatedly warned belligerent ma
tions against violation of her, neu-
trality. She has sent ct least II
protests to Berlin concerning the
reported appearance Of German
aircraft over Belgian territory, and
has sent at least four such pro-
tests to London.

OTTAWA, May 16.-A broad plan
for a reyamped confederation setup
and simplified financial system, de-
signed to remove causes of friction
and financial difficulties, was pro-
posed today in historic report of
the Royal Commission of Dominion
Provincial Relations.


The commissions report, result
ing from survey started in Novem-
ber, 1887, records Canada's progress
to nationhood and has for its goal
full realization of the objectives
laid down in 1867 by the fathers of
the confederation.


The commissions long-range plan
In general would shuttle the finan-
cial powers and responsibilities of
Canadas various governments for
the attainment of real autonomy"
for the provinces in local matters
and give effective federal control in
fields where national interest is
paramount.


Would Cost $4,000, 900.


The financial plan, crux of the
report, would cost the Dominion
government an estimated $4,000, 900
year under present conditions.


It calls for Dominion assumption
of entire responsibility for relief of
unemployed employables, and also
provides for the federal govern
ment taking over all existing provin-
cial debt, involving service charges
of about $60,OOO0O0 year.


To compensate the Dominion, the
provincial governments would be
asked to withdraw from the income,
corporation and inheritance tax
fields, which could be expected to
yield around s65 5000 900 a year.
They would also give up their
present right to subsidies from the
Dominion, which average around
100000 annually.


Since the Dominion assumes re-
sponsibility for unemployment relief,
kindred phases of the same problem.
such as unemployment insurance.
a national employment service and
right to establish basic minimum
wages and maximum hours, would
also be placed under Dominion
jurisdiction.


All other welfare services, the
commission asserted. should remain
the responsibility of the provinces.


Would Aid Government.


The report claimed that the finan-
cial scheme would improve the
position of every provincial govern
ment, although in varying degree.


The present inefficient and waste
full tax structure, the commission
reported. "sabotages" efforts to in
crease the national income and
even depresses that income While
the proposed plan would not reduce
the absolute tax level, the commits
sion said, it should permit substan-
tial increases in the national income
which would make the taxload rela-
lively lighter.


The commission suggested that
the added revenue required to carry
out the fiscal plan might be obtained
by broadening the income tax base
in the lower and middle brackets and
increasing succession taxes. Progress
sive elimination of the sales tax
was recommended.


sThe commission stated that 'the
tendency in most federal states
has been toward centralization at
the expense Of the provinces or
states"

On July 10, 1885, a destitute colored
man gambled his life against the
swirling currents of the Anacostia
River to save two white children
and failed.


With the two children, Sterling
Calhoun was drowned of Buzzards
Point, leaving behind him grief
stricken young wife and three small
children.


Because of his courage, because
he plunged into the current without
thought of his own feebleness as
swimmer, voluntary contributions
for his impoverished family and to
save him from pauper's grave
started pouring into The Star.


Stirred by an act of self-sacrifice
in world where unquestioning
selflessness is rare, Washingtonians
sent more than sl,500 to The Star
for the 25-year-old widow and the
youngsters who lost their father.


Today the Salvation Army, which
handled the payment OF monthly
installments from The Star fund
to the young widow, gave Mrs. CAL
noun her last check.

By the Associated Press.


MONTEVIDEO, Jan. 5.-The con-
centration of four British cruisers
off Montevideo caused speculation
among marine authorities today on
whether hunt was on for another
German raider like the scuttled
pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spec.


After the cruiser Ajax put out to
sea from this harbor this morning
port observer sighted two other
Warships. which he tentatively iden-
titled as the Cumberland and Shrop-
sire, about two hours sailing off,
shore.


The cruiser Achilles left Buenos
Aires early this morning, apparently
to join the squadron.
The Achilles and Ajax, together
with the cruiser Exeter, were re-
sponsible for the defeat of the Graf
Spec.


The Cumberland later joined the
Ajax and Achilles to lie in wait
while the Graf Spec was in the
harbor here before she was sailed
out into the channel and Scuttled
by her crew.


Twenty armed Uruguayan ma
rlnes boarded the interned German
freighter Tacoma to guard against
any further flights of German sea-
men.


Five members of the Admiral Graf
specs crew who were aboard the
Tacoma sought to escape to Buenos
Aires by launch two nights ago,
police said, but were caught. They
remained today at the headquar-
tiers of the maritime police.


Six Chinese laundrymen who were
on the Admiral Graf Spec and had
been detained Professionally will be
sent back to their native land by
way of Genou.

The honey bee chooses flowers
more carefully than do humans, for
she refuses to mix her favors, says
the National Geographic society.
When she starts slipping from one
variety of blossom, she will fly for
miles if necessary seeking others of
the same variety, so that the honey
will be pure. This strict selective-
ness of insect diet gives the world
some distinctive honey, such as the
Greek honey of Mount Hymettus and
the American brands favored with
star thistle or purple alfalfa or tulip
tree blossoms.


The bee that has acres of blooms
which she prefers within easy reach
naturally fattens the honeycomb
more quickly than the insect with
only an area of assorted wildfowers
available. Clover is the principal
raw material for the honey makers
in the United States.


California, where the American
honey tide rises highest, encourages
the bee with fragrant orange and
sage blossoms. Michigan and Ohio,
however (the states next in honey
production) have miles and miles of
clover for their bees to drink. Iowa
and New York are also chiefly clo-
yer states, but their hives produce
such variations as raspberry and
buckwheat honey. Texas turns it's
bees out to feast on cotton bios
SONS and mesquite, with results that
place the state among the half a
dozen largest honey producers.


The bee is a tidy little European
immigrant that has made good in
the United States. Her secret for
mula for making sugar from flowers
is ages older than mans way of ex-
tracing it from cane or beets.
Egyptians are supposed to have do
mesticated the insect. During Old
Testament times the bee was well
established in the business of max
ing honey.

MEMPHIS, Tenn. Feb. 3-Chief
ice menace in the Mississippi River
shifted to a gorge near Helena,
Ark, tonight after released waters
cut a channel through 13-mile
winter-made dam near Caruthers-
vile, Mo.


Forecasts of warmer weather
brought expectations that the Hell
ena gorge would go out over the
week end and if the breakup is
swift several boats along the water
front will be imperilled.


Although the cutting Of the Ca
ruthersville barrier left the Helena
gorge as the only major danger
point along the river, surface packs
still remained at Buffers Landing,
Ark, where the river is blocked, and
at Oldtown Bend, Ark, where
channel was cut through yesterday.
All major craft in both these areas
were believed safe and the jams
were expected to melt soon.


Danger also was believed past for
the huge towboat Illinois, which was
1ammed near Charlottesville until
last night, when the gorge started
breaking and tore loose Of her 10
barges.


The steel-hulled Illinois floated
with the ice for three miles, moored
the three barges that remained tied
to her and started out today under
her own steam for the first time In
IS days. Six barges were sighted
aground Immediately and the sew
enth was found lodged against ice
three miles further down. The
Illinois will reassemble this tow and
pull into q safe spot until the ice
danger passes.


How great a volume of water had
been damned up was shown by
depth measurements at Caruthers-
vile, below the pack. When only
the lower part gave way, the gauge
showed a 3-foot rise in 80 min
utes last night. In 10 hours the
rise had amounted to 78 feet.


From Missouri all the way to
Plaquemine, La, floating ice cakes
threatened light craft and there was
virtually no traffic.


Although many chunks weigh tons
Army engineers expressed no con-
cern for the lower Mississippi's seven
bridges.


On the Ohio River, navigation was
suspended and much new ice formed
today, including a new gorge far
upstream at Ashland, KY.

BUCHAREST. Oct. 26.-The axis
powers, Soviet Russia and Rumania
prepared tonight to take over control
of the mouth of the Danube River
from the old international commits
sion on which Britain and France
were represented.


Preliminary conversations are
scheduled for tomorrow. A formal
meeting will be held Monday

decide whether to extend the new
commissions authority to the upper
reaches of the river where Bulgaria,
Yugoslavia and Hungary now share
control.

rests in the old commission and that

ROME, May 28.--The surrender Of
the Belgian Army was expected In
foreign circles here today to hasten
Italy's entrance into the war to help
Germany finish of the Allies and
win share Of the victor's gains.


Omcial Italian comment on the
new disaster for the Allies, however,
was not Immediately available.

zens attempting to leave Italy had
been stopped because they had no
exit visas.


Allied sources said that the re-

that thus far it had been invoked
only against Frenchmen.


The government announced that

1ealy when their own countries re-
quired such visas. The regulation

British and Egyptians.


These residents of Italy would first
have to obtain italian permission

zerland.

SALEM, Greg, Nov. 5.-Senator
McNary concluded his vice presi-
Dental campaign last night with
the charge the New Deal is taking
deeper and deeper refuge in pater-
nalism and statism."


The Senator, in an address broad
cast from his native city. said:


The New Deal, which assumed
power when our forces had been
demoralized by a world economic
crisis, organized retreat. The fault
I charge now is that the New Deal
continued to retreat from our ira
ditions, taking deeper and deeper
refuge in paternalism and statism.


Tomorrow we must decide
whether this retreat shall go on. We
must guard against rout in the
next four years; rout, in which
might be lost our personal liberties,
our substance and our power to
make future decisions"


The Nation cannot exist, he said,
half prosperous, half depressed.


THE call to advance has been
sounded with notable clarity and
candor. Wendell Willkie, with un-
believable energy, courage and sin
cerity, has carried the call into
every corner of the land. = have
contended against the fearful doc
trine that self government and free
enterprise have run their course;
that we must rely increasingly upon
the Government for instruction,
guidance and support"


The Senator said the Nation must
"equate the price the farmer re-
ceives with the price he pays for
what he purchases from those who
live in the cities"

aid of refugee craftsmen are pre-
pared to offer duplicate lines of equal
quality, design and price.

of the war.

duction of chintzes, damasks and
antique stripes, Of quality and design
equal to that formerly imported

HAIFA. Palestine, Nov. 26.-PlaneS
droned overhead and tugs piled the
litter scattered waters of Haifa Har-
Dor today for bodies and survivors
among 1,77l wandering, homeless
Jewish refugees hurled overheard
yesterday when the 11,885-ton
steamer Patria exploded and cap
sized.


Most of those aboard managed to
swim ashore following the unex-
planned blast, but authorities feared
the loss of life was heavy. The refu-
gees, who had sought Illegally to
settle in Palestine, had been placed
aboard the Patria for transportation
to some other British colony for the
wars duration.


Waiting Safe Passage.


They had been packed into the
ship, waiting to begin their voyage
as soon as authorities felt conditions
in the Mediterranean to be reason
ably safe.


The refugees, mostly from Austria,
Slovakia, Bohemia, Hungary and
Rumania, had been here since No
vember 81, when they arrived aboard
two ships identified as the Pacific
and the Milos from Black Sea port.


British authorities were reported
to have found these ships unSea-
worthy and had arranged for their
transfer to another place, since
Jewish immigration to Palestine has
been forbidden since June, 1889,
when the British Colonial Secretary
reported an organized attempt to
thwart the usual immigration quota.


This was the second tragedy to
overtake refugees seeking to enter
Palestine. In August, 1889, the 1000
ton ship Parita, with 870 Jews aboard
and manned by an all-Jewish crew,
ran aground at nearby Tel Aviv after
futile efforts to enter various Med
iterranean ports. The Parita's pas
sengers were interned.

One of the most interesting by
products of the triple axis pact is
the way it's members are vying with
one another in declaring their warm
friendship for Soviet Russia. For
German spokesmen this is nothing
new, since Nazi editors got their cue
q year ago, when the Russo German
accord was concluded. However,
until the momentous Berlin pact was
signed, a few days ago, neither Japan
nor Italy had followed suit. only
yesterday" as Frederick Allen might
put it, japanese writers were warm
ing against Red Russia as the ulti-
mate enemy and Moscow as the seat
of dangerous thoughts" In Fascist
Italy, the Bear Jared no better. A
backward glance through press files
will turn up blistering editorials dur
ing the Spanish and Finnish wars,
when Virginio Gayda and his COL
leagues excoriated Joseph Stain and
all his works in the journalistic
billingSgate for which the Fascist
press is so justly famous.


Today, how the tune has changed!
In Toxic, editorial comment unitedly
stresses the idea that good relations
with Russia are both desirable and
practical, and that "moldy queS-
tions" belonging to the past should
not be revived. In Rome, Virginio
Gayda sets the tone with long his
torical summary purporting to show
that Fascist Italy has always been
friendly to the Soviet regime. "Ital-
ian policy during the Fascist era"
he writes, has never shown any
wavering and, even less, any hostility
toward Soviet Russia. 1t has been
inspired by calm Mussolinian real
ism" After pointing out many SIM
ilaritieS between the two systems,
Signor Gayda concludes: Italy has
always been attentive to the phe-
nomena of humanity, and the nation
has been following with great inter-
est for a long time the internal evo-
lutions of Russian concepts and her
political system"


Since neither Japanese nor Italian
spokesmen would thus suddenly
change their tune except by official
order, 1t is plain that the three axis
governments have adopted a vigor-
Gus RuSSophile line. Soviet Russia
seems, indeed, to have many friends
these days. Has not Britains Labor
ite Ambassador, Sir Stafford CrippS,
been tireleSsly promoting good rela-
tions despite many rebuffS? And
does not the government Of Free
China, dependent upon Russia as it's
sole avenue to the outer world, seek
to propitiate Moscow in every way?
With so variegated throng knock
Ing at his door, canny Joseph Stain
doubtless smokes his famous pipe,
perhaps concealing beneath his
dropping muStache the quirk of
cynics smile.


The one outstanding exception to
the current trend appears to be the
Roman Pontiff. A Vatican City dis
patch reports that Pope Plus XII is
preparing an encyclical warning
Catholics throughout the world to
be on guard against "Communistic
influences resulting from the inter-
national struggle to win Russia's
support. The Vatican, according to
this dispatch, is about to take a
decisive stand in face of what it con-
siders the ruinouS expansion of Bol-
shevik philosophy and influence
throughout the world.


With the war, now well into it's
second year, becoming more terrible
with the approach of winter and
threatening to engulf the whole
world in its scope, all these maneu-
vers centering about Soviet Russia
have deep interest. Their full sig
nificance may become startlingly
evident in the months to come.

been kept secret.

campaign in Northern Finland,
where they said one of, historys
most notable displays of tactical
skill had thrown back the Russian
invaders.

1t was agreed generally that May
would bring the ultimate turning
point. 1t is then that the SHOWS
melt and the ground becomes firm
enough for best use of the Soviet
mechanical equipment.
Military observers in Finland have
said that major Russian smash at
the Karelian Isthmus defenses
might come in March or April. Bit
ter cold ordinarily continues through
March, however.

adequate arms, ammunition, planes
and the designated fresh fighting
force, the Firms might hold out even
through a May crisis because the
rugged, lake-strewn terrain of
their countryside is a defensive
asset.

LONDON, Feb. 22.-Two German
warplanes were shot down by British
fighters today, the air ministry an
nounced, as Nazi airmen raided

which they attempted to attack.


The fire from the trawlers gave
concrete form to the warning last
week by Winston Churchill, first lord
Of the admiralty, that all British
vessels plying the war-tossed North
Sea waters henceforth would be
armed for protection against Ger
man bombing and machine cunning
from the air.

ASTORIA, Greg, Dec. THE
four survivors of the Inflated tug
Tyee, which wrecked yesterday in a
stormy sea off Tillamook Bar, lay in
a hospital here today, bruised and
exhausted, but not seriously injured.


Close watch was kept on Oregons
rugged coast for the bodies Of two
of the tugs crew who persisted three
hours before the Coast Guard cut
ter Onondaga came to the rescue.


The survivors are Capt. Hillary
Hubble, Chief Engineer Neil Logue,
Assistant Engineer George Thorburg
and Mate Evan Campbell, all of
Hoquiam. Wash.


The survivors told the Coast
Guard that Deckhand John Hender-
son and Cook Julius Long, also of
Hoquiam, became exhausted after
nearly three hours and drowned.


The men were picked up by the
Onondaga as they drifted helplessly
in 15-foot work boat about 6 miles
north OF the spot where the Tyee
went down. The small boat was
awash when sighted by the cutter.


The four survivors said the small
boat was capsized several times by
towering breakers. The boat was
kept afloat by its air tanks.


The Onondaga left Astoria at 9:15
am. and sighted the four men at
2:15 pm. after proceeding under
forced draft to the Tillamook area.


When the Onondaga sped to the
rescue little hope had been held
that any of the crew would be found
alive as the vessels two nfeboats
and a full complement of life pre-
servers had been washed ashore,
along with the Tyees superstruc-
ture.

OTTAWA. Sept. 26.-The Cana
dian armed merchant cruiser Prince
Robert has captured the German ex-
press cargo ship Weser off Manza-
Milo. Mexico. Navy Minister Angus
Macdonald announced today.


The Weser, a 9,l79-ton ship which
piled as a passenger liner on the
North German Lloyd's Bremen-Pa-
cific service. took refuge in Punta
Arenas, Costa Rica, shortly after
the war began. She moved thence to
Manzanillo, arriving late in July.


Mr.. Macdonald said the Weser
left Manzanillo yesterday and was
seized last night.


The captain and most of the crew
of the Weser have been transferred
to the Prince Robert and the prize
ship is being escorted to Esquimalt,
British Columbia, the Navy Minister
said.


Mexican west coast waters, in
which the capture apparently was
made, are included in the American
neutrality zone.


In July there was an unconfirmed
report that the Weser was being
equipped as a raider, with paint
taken aboard to camouf1age her.
This word came from Costa Rica
after she had moved to Manzanillo.


British have suspected the Weser
of supplying fuel to German subma-
rines. She took aboard more than
100000 gallons Of Diesel oil while at
Punta Arenas, Costa Rica.

At present about 100 children and

domo, adjutants, officials on hight

The shelter is being expanded

In Berlin they are saying the shell

ital's safest lying-in hospital" !"
Physicians and nurses are in at

children living in the poorer quar-
tiers of the city, where air raid shell
ters are inadequate, are brought to
the chancellery In emnibuses.

LONDON, Sept. 26.-Long- range
German guns flung shells across
the Channel into Dover this after
noon while the Nazi assault on
London was renewed by two waves
of bombers.


The shells bursting in Dover killed
a man and woman. For over an
hour the bombardment continued


The warplanes which flew against
London did not penetrate to the
center of the city, but veered OIL
about the time they reached the de-
fense ring. British authorities said
the attackers were driven off.


The British Air Ministry de-
clared that in heavy attacks against
Berlin and seven German-occupied
ports on the continent last night
the Royal Air Force came off with
out the loss of plane.


Berlin objectives hit were the great
Templehof airport, power stations
and rail communications. the min
istry said.


Bomb Near Scharnhorst.


During last nights attack on the
German naval dockyard at Kiel the
flash of one big explosion was seen
very close" to the 26,000-ton Ger
man battleship Scharnhorst, the Air
Ministry news service said.


Early in the evening German
planes again were reported over
Wales and Southwest England.


British submarines have torpedoed
three German supply ships. the Ad-
miralty announced, but the COM
munique did not specify the date or
place of the engagement.


1t said that the submarine H-49
attacked a convoy of eight supply
vessels, scoring torpedo hits on two,
and that the submarine Tuna re-
ported the destruction of large
supply ship which was screened by
two destroyers.


A number of persons were killed
and wounded in northeast coast
town where German raider drop
ped bombs during the morning
Houses, stores, garage and NOV
ing picture theater were damaged.


Aerial Duel at Peak.


The German-British aerial duel
reached new peaks with Berlin's
longest raid alarm of the war, the
heaviest bombardment of the Ger
man-held invasion coast" and the
18th consecutive night of bombing
for London.


British bombs raked Berlin's 300,-
000-kilowatt Klingenberg power sta
ton, fountainhead of much of the
city's industrial power, and other
vital objectives last night in the
R. A. F.'s greatest assault on the
Reich capital, the Air Ministry said


The power station, in the heart
of the factory section to the east
of Berlin, was straddled by "sticks"
of heavy-caliber bombs in four sep
arate attacks within an hour, the
ministry communique said. and
bombs bursting on and around the
station were followed by fire.


Opening their bombardment
shortly after 10 pm. and continu-
ing into the early morning hours,
the r. A. F. nighthawks also plunged
explosives onto the capitals west
power station, the Schoenberg rail-
way yard, railway station near the
Charlottenburg district and nearby
railway sidings, the ministry said.

BONCOURT, On the Franco-Swiss
Frontier, June 10 LP)-Of all the
strange stories Of refugees in Europe,
where millions have marched in the
last year. one of the strangest was
the story Of 1000 Spaniards and TOO
Poles who came to the Swiss border
last night.


The Swiss. playing their tradi-
tional neutral part in this war as
host and as Red Cross sanctuary
for the wounded and refugees, ad-
mitted tens of thousands of French
non-combatants.


Their crack citizen soldiers first
disarmed and then admitted under
guard thousands of French and
Belgian soldiers. Their volunteer
Red Cross nurses and doctors at
tended to hundreds of French
wounded who had suffered the shock
of long days and nights of travelling
seeking rest before the swiftly
changing backgrounds.


Sitting by Fires, Waiting.


Across on the French side of this
frontier last night 1000 Spaniards
sit by camp fires in the Jura Noun
tains singing Republican Spanish
songs, and wondering about their
strange fate.


Two years ago these men were
sitting around campfires in the
Pyrenees Mountains, singing the
same songs. Then they were wait
ing for French troops patrolling the
border with rifles and machine guns
!. to let them in. Last night they were
waiting for Swiss troops patrolling
the border with rifles and machine
guns to let them in.


Then they were fleeing Gen.
Frances armies and the German
Army's Candor legions. Last night
they were fleeing the Germans.
Then they were soldiers of the de-
feated Republican army. Now they
are munitions workers without a
country who fled unarmed from the
French Peugeot works between Bel
fort and Hericourt.


The Poles Reconsider.
Just before sundown TOO Polish
artillerymen dashed up to the Swiss
frontier with four batteries of 75s
and several large truckloads of am
munition.


The excited Polish officer COM
manding them rushed up to calm the
Swiss frontier commander, and
learned that they must abandon all
artillery and ammunition if they
were to cross the frontier.
/ The Poles then engaged in a dis
cussion ending in streams of explo-
sive Polish exclamations. Others
rushed back and turned the whole
outfit-guns, ammunition and trucks
around again while the command
ing colonel explained to the Swiss {:


I'VE are going back to give the
Germans the rest of oul ammunition.
See you again when it's gone"


They vanished back into France
along the refugee road

Special Correspondent OF The Star.


TRENTON, N. j.. Oct. 5.-Resent-
ment OF other Democratic leaders
around New Jersey against the tac-
tics Of Mayor Frank Hague's Hudson
County machine has helped the Re-
publican cause considerably within
the last week.


Mayor Hague's organization pro-
vided a fresh sensation that kept
the fight for the governorship In
the foreground and the presidential
election In second place. The Hague
organization admitted In Supreme
Court that the poll books for the
1887 gubernatorial election, sought
by the Republicans for three years,
had been burned last January.


The Democrats justified the burn
ing on the basis the law required the
municipal clerks to keep the records
for only two years. Lieutenants Of
Senator Robert C. Hendrickson, Re-
publican candidate for Governor,
contended the law required preser-
vation for five.

ing, Democratic leaders In other

declared privately that the destruc-
ton has hurt the entire Democratic
cause and will make it more diff
ficult to elect their local candidates
and to get out the vote for Presi-
dent Roosevelt.


Republicans we're jubilant. They
see a tailor made issue for Wendell
L. Willkie when he makes his first
campaign appearance here.

turning point of the campaign for

organization and the Willkie sup
porters. The Democratic machine

Republican controlled Legislature

election day. In addition, there Is

thousands of commuters in the

The positive value of the agree
ments is even more striking than
their negative merit Samuel Crow
ther, pleading the cause of protec-
tive-tariff New England before the
House Ways and Means Committee,
gave the impression that American
trading under the agreements was
sentimental, at sorry variance with
the old idea of hard-headed Yankee

partment shows in its review of

through November, 1899, that our
exports to the Heterogeneous

fell by eight per cent. Mr.. Crow
Their protested that the program
was nothing more than a low-tariff
system in disguise. But the facts
disprove him. It is true that the
American tariff wall has been let.
down thirty-nine per cent since 1884
by the trade agreements. It is true
also that foreign barriers against
sixty per cent of our trade have been
lowered. Congressional tariff max
Ing brings no direct benefit to our
sales abroad. The reciprocal trade
agreements open markets overseas.

Hungry men and women are FORM
ing night-long queues stretching
several blocks before Moscow food
stores, Mrs. Spencer Williams,
resident there for nine years, said
today.


Mrs. Williams. wife of the rep
resentative to the American Rus
sian Chamber of Commerce who has
returned to London, said she left
Moscow February because she
could not get butter and eggs for
her daughter Tamara, 7. The
child was taken to Moscow when
months old and had been away
only for short vacations.


Mrs. Williams said Tamara
gorged herself with rolls at her
first American meal and then asked:
Are rolls just for pleasure, or are
they food, too?"


Since 1881 we went through diff
ferent periods of semi famine" said
Mrs. Williams at the Cairo Hotel,
but there were never the famine
conditions as now. Queues form at
II o'clock at night and wait for the
stores to open at 9 o'clock the next
morning, hoping therell be bread
for sale.


pathetic Sight"


"On New Year Eve we left party
at the American Embassy about S
o'clock in the morning and passed
line four or five blocks long watt
ing through a snowfall and tenn
perature of IS degrees below zero.
They were covered with snow and
bundled In rags. 1t was the most
pathetic sight ever saw


Frequently Mrs. William and her
sister, Miss Joan Graf, 10, of At
lanta, who went to Moscow last
July, paused to consider the ad-
visibility of permitting their re-
marks to be quoted. And just as
frequently they told each other:
"They can't hurt you now"


Il guess we haven't got over the
fear psychology" explained Mrs.
Williams.


Censorship has become so severe
recently, she added, that nothing
really comes through about true
conditions in Russia" Correspond
ents have been forbidden to quote
Russian newspapers in their dis
patches, Mrs. Williams declared.


Finnish War Unpopular.


Numerous "pitiful letters came
from the Finnish front, and Soviet
soldiers begged that relatives send
food and warm clothing. They
warned their relatives to do every
thing they could against being sent
to the 'front.'"


The war was "very unpopular" )"
and signing treaty with Germany
was equally unpopular, she said.


The people were completely be-
wildered. For 10 years they had
been told the Germans were dirty
dogs, and they found it hard to
understand Stalin's actions"


Mrs. Williams visited the State
Department yesterday but declined
to reveal what was discussed. She
expects to 60 soon to London, where
her husband has become a news
paper correspondent.


Miss Graf said she came home
particularly to see "Gone With the
Wind"

The music history of Count Basic,
who brings his famous swing orches-
ira to Roseland State Ballroom on
April 2, really begins when the great
colored pianist joined the Gozale
White show in 1926. The White "cir-
Gus" folded few months after and
Count Basic found himself in Kansas
City, Mo-, looking for job. He
joined "Walter Pages Blue Devils,
incidentally Walter now works for
Basic playing bass fiddle in the orch
estra) doing the piano and arrange
ment assignments. He toured Texas,
Oklahoma, Missouri and Kansas with
Page, and left to join Bonnie Moten's
band at the Reno Club in Kansas City.


In 1885 Bonnie Motion died, and
Basic formed his own orchestra,
1rawing on the best talent of the
Moten outfit, as well as on the finest
tanners all over the country. He
remained at the Reno Club for almost
two years and it was during his en-
gagement from this spot that Benny
Goodman heard one of his broadcasts
and became his staunchest booster.
Soon afterward he was booked into
Chicago's Grand Terrace and this en-
gagement was followed by his first
venture into New York to play at the
Roseland Ballroom.


From the Roseland, Basic went on
to Pittsburgh's William Penn Hotel,
hen to the Savoy in New York and
the Ritz Carlton in Boston. Last
spring Basic was booked into the
Famous Door in New York, followed
this with a record smashing turn at
Chicago's Hotel Sherman and then
returned to the Famous Door before
hiking out to California and host of
one-nighters.


The Count comes to Roseland State
Ballroom, Tuesday evening, April 2,
and, with his famous orchestra, fea-
turing James Rushing and Helen
Humes, will play for the Dining Car
Employees Union, Local $40.

TORONTO, June Ontario.
where the paddle and the quill
wrote early North American his
tory through a sweeping wilderness
of interlocking water trails, will
again this summer have its water
empire rediscovered from steamer
decks, yachts, sailboats, motor
launches and canoes.


The vacationist can view Ontario
through the eyes Of mariner, with
his diary a logbook recording the
sweeping romance of magnificent
lakes, rivers, straits and indented
bays, as the Great Lakes bounda-
ries with the st. Lawrence and
Ottawa Rivers make the province
virtually an island with a water
area greater than the size of the
British Isles. Added to its kingdom
of waterways are the canals from
which the Great Lakes go to the sea.
creating the quaint canal towns
with an atmosphere akin to old
time coaching days, and the water
gate" and water street" crowds ever
remindful of here comes the mules"
and here comes the news" before
the age of steam.


Old Field Stone Houses.


In rural Ontario are the quaint
old field-stone houses, recalling the
spirit of pioneer days when the
province was Canadas real West.
Atmosphere and story seem to radi-
ate from the windows where within
are the hand-loomed woven carpets,
piece-patterned bedquilts and old
English and Colonial furniture. En-
tering Canada from the Niagara
Falls district, which is one of the
"a bridge or ferry links between
Ontario and the United States, are
the shorelined bays of the Niagara
Peninsula washed by Lake Ontario
and Lake Erie.


A short distance north of Toronto,
famed as the clear sky region" by
its elevation of 1000 feet, are the
300 lakes and 400 islands of the
Muskoka lakes, known as the Eng
nsh lake district of Canada" bv
its beauty and boating activities
fine hotels and resorts. Numerous
rivers feed the lake chain with
steamer transportation linking the
Lakes of Muskoka, Joseph and Ros-
seau. Directly northeast is the Lake
of Bays, famed for its canoeing on
its many miles of tributary streams
through Fairy Lake north to Lake
Vernon. The many Kawartha lakes
are divided into an eastern and
western group, with steamer service
through both the falls and island
sections.


Land of $4,000 Islands.


Continuing north, yet barely so
miles from Toronto, is beautiful
Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching
district, with the MagnetaWan River
containing Grand Manitoulin, one
of the largest fresh-water islands in
the world. To the north are the
south shore towns of the 200 miles
of blue water country, the 10000
island archipelago of the Georgia
Bay. Summer steamers criss-cross
the broad waters and parallel a
shoreline where literally $4,000
islands have been counted from the
North Channel to Georgian Bay
Island National Park. Further north
is Pickerel River, the French River
and Lake Nipissing. the latter as
sociated with the Port of Callander,
home of the famous quintuplets.


Entering Canada through the
Thousand Islands to Kingston,
where first the Indians, then the
French, then the British gave the
historic town its three steps in his
tory, tradition and development, the
trails lead north to the Halliburton
Highlands, the scene of the Trent
Waterways, with the famed Rideau
Lakes, which are part of the great
Canal system, connecting Ottawa
with Kingston, to the mouth of the
st. Lawrence River.


Large bodies of water for yachting
and canoeing with the enchanting
beauty of sparkling big lakes, are to
be found in the Timagami Provincial
Park of 1900 islands. Here beauti-
full Lake Timagami of 100 miles area
is monarch to a gorgeous cluster
of lakes and rivers vying in water
beauty with the 2,720 water-ribbed
square miles of Algonquin Park and
its fairyland of waterways. Follow

The Plymouth Rock routine goes
somewhat as follows:


/. Partners facing each other in
normal dancing position. Man taps
heel of left foot forward and toe OF
left foot back, in one count each
Girl duplicates his movements, but
uses right foot.


2. Partners execute forward two
step, starting from last position in
movement one imam with left foot,
girl with right and ending up
prepared to execute heel and toe
tapping again, this time with op-
posite feet from movement one.


3. Partners facing. man taps heel
of right foot forward, toe of right
foot back in one count each. Girl
duplicates, using left foot.


4. Partners again execute for
ward two-step, starting from last
position in movement three.


5. At end of movement four,
partners work Immediately into
rock step. -Four rock steps are
executed, two on each foot. Man
starts with left foot. girl with right.
Each extends arms parallel with
floor and swing left and right legs
alternately to the side.


6. At end of fourth count, part
ners end up with feet together. and
girl whirls around once under the
outstretched left arm of man. At
end of whirl, partners again facing
each other.


7. Each flexes knees. Then slaps
palms against knees, then against
outstretched palms of partner.


8. Move Immediately into execu-
ton of eight two-steps. and then
into the start of the dance again.

ROME, Aug. II (P.-Italian
troops advancing in British Somali-
land have established contact with
the main British forces defending
the capital and chief port of Ber-
bera, the high command announced
today.


The daily communique merely
announced:


In British Somaliland our troops,
continuing their advance, have
made contact with the main enemy
forces"


1t was presumed the three Ital-
ian columns which previously had
occupied the port of leila, the
towns of Hargeisa and Adueina
and the Karin and Godajere
passes finally had engaged in bat
tie with the troops holding the
main British position.


But the high command did not
issue any word that fighting be-
tween the two forces actually was
in progress.


Authoritative sources said the
capture OF the TWO SOmalland
passes meant that the Italian
forces had safely left the desert
wastes behind and were attacking
the British on the sea side OF the
slopes.


Celebrating on a high command
report of the bombing Of a British
airdrome near Erkovit yesterday,
military authorities said the exist
ence of the airport was discovered

By Staff Correspondent Of The Star.


BOSTON, April 24-The Amer
lean League pennant race scarcely is
. week old, less postponements, and
already the pennant bug is buzzing
In Beantown.


The Red SoX, with a 7-to-2 victory
over the Nationals yesterday, are
pacing the circuit and, at long last,
they proceed in their quest of Bos-
tons first flag since 1918, with evi-
dence that at least one young hurler
may come through.


HIS Is Maurice Mickey Harris.
22-year-old southpaw attempting to
negotiate. in one jump, the gap
between the Eastern League and the
majors. Harris making his big
league debut, turned back the Mats
with seven hits and, as the Yankees
were losing and the Indians were
idle, pitched the Red Sox into
undisputed possession of first place.


Cronir Called the Turn.


This young southpaw, Harris, may
well bear watching. A year ago he
was pitching for Scranton, virtually
unknown and unheralded He won
II, lost only 4, and led the circuit
in strikeouts with 147. Yet, despite
his record, he appeared to be no
important figure in the 1910 Amer
ican League race.


Today, however. Mickey is cock
O the walk in this sector. Ever
since the Red Sox went into spring
training at Sarasota, Fla, the Sox,
particularly Manager Joe Cronin,
have been touting Harris.


1T doesn't add up" Cronin said
one day in Tampa, "but this kid
looks like he's ready to make the
jump. He's got plenty of stuff and
plenty of confidence. He's like Ted
Williams; he knows he's good and
he acts like it,"


Harris Surprise Starter.


Mickey was surprise starter
yesterday. It was Bob Groves turn
to pitch, but the weather was too
bad for old folks. Instead, Cronin
unclaimed Harris and his perform
ance was even better than the box
score shows.


The longest stretch of pitching
done by Mickey prior to yesterday
was five innings. For six rounds
Mickey shut out the Mats. not that
it is any great feat. and gave only
two hits. In the last three innings
he tired, which isn't surprising, and
allowed five hits and both of the
Washington runs. He famed eight,
including Jimmy Wasdell three
times.


The Sox, in the meantime, were
teeing up and going for distance
against Dutch Leonard and Ale
jandro Carrasquel. Boston made
only eight hits but three were home
runs - well-socked blows by Will
liams, Finney and Jimmy Foxx.


Carrasquel took over the pitching
in the fifth, just long enough to
pitch Foxx a home-run ball with
mate on base, and there was the ball
game beyond reach.


Today the Griffmen were to try
to win with Joe Haynes pitching
for the first time. The Red Sox
we're to counter with Grove, who
shut out the Mats on opening day
in Washington with two hits.

announcement today said Greek

The fall of Argirocastro, another

what supplies they could before

from the front indicated a persist

Edda.

italian losses in this area were de-

By the Associated Press.


CAMP BEAUREGARD, La. May
25.-Army officers, fortified with the
lessons gained from this Nations
greatest peace-time war games, went
into a huddle today to study the
United States needs in equipment
in the light of European hostilities.


Umpires also tackled the task Of
deciding just what happened be-
tween the BLUE" defending forces
and the Red" invading contingent
involving approximately 10000 SOL
diers in the Sd Army manuevers.


One need - dive-bombing war
planes - was revealed yesterday
when the Red forces defeated nu-
merically stronger defense force in
the country's first test with q blitz-
krieg ending the three-week games.
The experiment, carried out by pur-
suit planes substituting for dive
bombers, will result in pressure to
re-establish an attack bomber wing
in the Air Corps, military observers
indicated.


Highways leading in all directions
from the "war zone" are expected
to be crowded within the next few
days with hard-bitten doughboys,
mechanical units and infantry
trucks heading homeward.


Officers have worked out to the
minutest detail the route which the
returning forces will take, where
they will bivouac, where one unit
has priority over others on the high
ways, and the day on which they
will reach their home barracks.


Units making the longest jour-
ney home were the Headquarters
Company and Company F, 68th In
fantry, which will require 13 days
to reach Fort Lewis, Wash.


The exodus is expected to be COM
pleted by early June.

BY the Associated Press.


HONOLULU, April 5.-Usually re.
liable sources said today Britain's
swift liner Mauretania would quit
Honolulu at noon to resume her
secrecy wartime voyage,
apparently to New Zealand or Aus
tralia to pick up troops.


The spacious passenger ship was
being made ready here for depar-
ture. A crew of 410 was aboard $50
of them in the culinary service-a
fact which lent credence to the
theory she would enter transport
duty.


One crewman expressed the
opinion the vessel would pick up a
British naval escort on leaving
Hawaii. Protecting craft lowered
on the horizon on the trip from
the Bahama Islands to the Panama
Canal, he said, but none had been
seen between the Canal and Homo
lulu.


Crew members, who were granted
shore leave after the liner made a
surprise docking here yesterday, said
the vessel was operating under
sealed orders. They expressed the
belief, however. the huge vessel, one
of the largest ever to enter Honolulu
Harbor, would sail some time today
after loading fuel and water.

Secretary Hull said today the
United States had proposed arbi-
tration to Mexico to settle the two
year-old dispute over Mexicos
appropriation of American oil prop
critics.


Mr.. Hull said note had been
delivered by the State Department
to the Mexican Ambassador, Cas-
tillo Najera, to this effect.


Beyond saying that the note sug-
gested arbitration, Mr.. Hull said he
could not go into any details con-
nected with it.


The State Department head said
he could not say whether any OBJ
servations had been received from
Mexico on the subject.


The United States and Mexico are
slgnatories of the 1929 inter-Amer-
lcan treaty of conciliation and
arbitration.


The United States proposed the
same method in 1888 to Mexico to
settle the controversy over the ex-
preparation of American agrariap
properties. Mexico replied then by
suggesting instead that Joint
commission evaluate the claims and
fix the compensation. The State De-
partment agreed to this.


The oil controversy has been car
ried on since March, 1888. when
the appropriation decree was put
into effect. The two large American
oil groups interested in Mexico, the
Standard Oil of New jersey and
the Sinclair. carried on direct ne
gotiations with the Mexican govern
ment which thus far have been un-
successful.


Mexico contends that the oil uues-
ton is domestic matter and not
subject to international action. The
Mexican Supreme Court has upheld
the appropriation and ordered evaiu-
alton and compensation for the
properties within 10 years.
Evaluation is now under way by
Mexico alone, the oil companies hav.
ing declined to participate in the
work.

TOXIC. Aug. 10 Via Wireless) -
Mount Mihara. Japans famous sui
eide volcano off the entrance OF
Toxic Bay, erupted spectacularly
early today after II years of COM
parative inactivity, Domei Gapan-
ese news agency reported in a
broadcast.


For more than three hours huge
columns of fame and smoke shot
from the. crater causing fears for
the villages. with total populations
of 5000, around the mountains foot.
However, no casualties or serious
damage we're reported.


Mihara, $500 feet high, on the
Island of Oshima, had not erupted
since 1923, but the spectacular view
into it's crater. with its bubbling,
smoking lava masses, drew thou
sands of sightseers. For a few
months in 1888 it attracted scores
each month who killed themselves
by leaping into the pit. High barbed-
wire barriers then were erected
around the crater and police patrols
were put constantly on duty to end
the suicide wave.

nounced yesterday that the Nazi

press communique which lays fur

mines threatening the vessel on its
contemplated course"

the view that the German govern
ment received sufficient advance
notice = to take every precau-

bv the German combat forces"


The German declaration that the
American Legion was risking "ex-

warning the Nazi government issued
last October when the liner Iroquois

persons aboard.


On that occasion the United
States was informed by Grand
Admiral Raeder that he had been
Informed the Iroquois was to be
sunk-presumably by the British
off the eastern coast of the United
States. Thereafter the liners prog
ress was followed with great anx-
iety, but she reached port without
incident.

BY the Associated Press.


ATHENS, Dec. 11.-Fierce knife
welding men from the wild hills of
Crete, surpassed in toughness only
by Greece's famous mountain troops,
have been thrown into the Greek
front line attack against the retreat
ing Italians, it was disclosed today.


At the same time a govern
ment spokesman reported important
moves are now in full development,
but would give no hint of the new
Greek offensive action beyond saying
advances were continuing on all
fronts.


The British Royal Air Force an
nounced raid on Valona, Italian
supply port in Southwestern Albania,
in which ship, munitions dump
and some buildings were said to have
been hit despite italian fighter op-
position.


Charge Italians With Knives.


The men from Crete, dark, hardy
Mediterraneans, have already en-
gagged the Italians, one dispatch
from the front said. Brandishing
their long, cleaning knives which
they prefer to bayonets in close
fighting, they charged the Italians.

Valona, an ancient coastal town,
is one of the principal ports OF de-

Turkey when called to the colors
are on their way to the front.


The government spokesman said
details of fighting are slow in reach
ing Athens because many local en-
gagements take place in rough, lso-
lated mountains regions.


One dispatch said bad weather

The leader of the R. A. F. bombing

down from heavy clouds to find
Italian planes guarding the city.
The British dumped their bombs
and roared back into the clouds
before the Italians could strike.
One British plane, he said, had a

Italians Falling Back.


Italian troops were reported still
falling back steadily for possible
new stand on the heights around
Chimara-almost half way up the
coast from Porto Edda to Valona.


A Greek spokesman said the 1tal-
ians were withdrawing rapidly along
the coast road and north of fallen
Argirocastro and added that heavy
blows also hastened the Italian re-
treat through the tangle OF snow
covered mountains between Pogra-
detz and Elbasani in mid-Albania.


Although exact Greek advance
positions were not disclosed, they
apparently were almost twice as
deep into Albania at both f1anks
of the battlefront as the maximum
Italian thrusts into Greece before
the Fascist invasion forces were
thrown into reverse.


Offensive Continues.


The Greek high command de-
clared "our offensive activities con-
tinued all over the entire front"
and added:


Strong enemy positions were oc-
cupied at bayonet point. The enemy
suffered heavy losses. Three 100
millimeter guns have fallen into
our hands"


A spokesman said that at some
strong points along the Italian line
of retreat rear-guard forces offered
resistance until they were driven out
by Greek infantry and Evzone
(highland shock troop bayonet
charges.


The Greeks were said to have
captured an Italian officer and a
number of Alpine troopers in the
drive toward Elbasani and found
large quantities Of abandoned war
material at Delvino, wrested from
the Italians between Porto Edda and
Argirocastro.


Drifts of snow and a glaze Of ice
in the mountain passes and seas of
slush and mud in the valleys con-
tinued to hamper operations in the
northern sector where mountain
recruited Greek Evzones opposed
Italian regiments.

store, antique shop and general

BY the Associated Press.


BERLIN, March 27.-The German
naval auxiliary vessel Altmark ar
rived at Kiel, Germany, late this
afternoon after long and adven-
turous war cruise abroad.


The Altmark, raided by the Brit
ish destroyer Cossack in Norwegian
territorial waters on February 16,
when 200 British merchant seamen
prisoners were rescued, reached
German waters safely by slipping
through the British blockade. She
steamed down the Norwegian coast
and through Danish waters.


When the Altmark was attacked
by the Cossack she was backed into
Josingfjord, on the Norwegian coast,
and run aground. Her propeller
was damaged and she remained
there for some time.


The 12,000-ton Altmark comes
home after having been at sea since
before the beginning of the war. She
formerly was freighting in the West
ern Hemisphere.


Outf1tted as an auxiliary naval
vessel, the Altmark was used as a
prison ship for the raiding German
pocket battleship Admiral Graf
Spec. After the Graf Spec was
scuttled last December II the Alt
mark presumably headed home.

NEW ORLEANS, Feb. 6.-Grandpa
and grandma, papa and mamma, all

moved to the streets today for the
annual Mardi Gras celebration.


Hundreds Of thousands Of carefree
people donned weird costumes, fas-
tened on masks and danced and
played In elimination of celebra-
ton which started with the first
carnival ball January 6.


Overhanging clouds failed to
dampen the ardor Of a people ac-
customed for more than century
to observe the day despite inclement
weather.


Rain last night did force the
mythical god of the sea, Proteus, to
cancel his torchlight parade, but
that was because members Of the
organization, principally elderly busi-

The high command reported that

on the strategic northwestern base
town of Ioannina (Janina), both
from the Kalamas River Valley on
the northwest of the town and from
the Pindos (Pindus) heights on the
northeast, which reach elevations
above 1000 feet.


The locations of these columns
we're not stated, but unofficially it
has been said that they have pene-
trated the "Metaxas Line" of light
Notifications which are especially
thick in the Kalamas Valley.


Strikes at Salonika.


From the valley to the quays of
Salonika, Crete, Corfu and Patras
the Italian bombers blasted away
with explosive and incendiary
bombs, ton upon ton of them.


(The Rome radio broadcast
report tonight that 100 Italian
fighter and bomber planes had
attacked the British Mediter-
'ranean Island of Malta during
the afternoon, striking at an
aviation camp and naval base in
''the most important Italian air
action since the outbreak of war;


("Visible destruction" on the
airdrome was claimed and it was
stated that at least one British
fighter plane, and perhaps two,
had been shot down.


The "disperato' or suicide squad
ron, which Count Ciano, the italian
Foreign Minister, led in Ethiopia,
struck at the naval base of Salonika
on the Aegean. The Stefani Agency
said the first raid, yesterday, left
the fortified zone devastated, the
planes smashing and firing barracks,
supply dumps, reservoirs and other
military and naval objectives.


There were rumors that Ciano
himself flew a plane in one of the
two waves, but this was not con-
firmed.


The Ministry of Air did, however,
announce that Ciano had been pro-
NOTED from major to lieutenant
colonel in the air force.


Patras is Bombed.

By the Associated Press.


CLANCY, Swiss-French Frontier,
June 22.-French sources reported
today the French defenders OF
L'Ecluse fort, near Bellegarde, not
only repulsed an attack on the
mountain citadel early this after
noon, but drove the Germans out
of the town of Bellegarde, miles
away.


The guns of the big fort defending
the Rhone River gorges and the
junction of the lower Jura with the
Alpine foothills below the Italian
front were silent in midafternoon for
the first time since early morning.


Bellegarde Recovered.


Refugees said the French regained
possession Of Belgrade.


The French dynamited the rail-
road south of Bellegarde to prevent
an attack north along the Rhone.


Powerful German motorized
forces. backed by artillery and sup
ported by bombers, we're reported to
have captured Bellegarde hours earl
ier, and were attacking Fort LEcluse
called the Gibraltar of the
Rhone."


L'Ecluse Fort is carved out of rock
beside the winding highway be-
tween the Swiss frontier and the
town of Bellegarde. 1t dominates
the Rhone gorges and rises a thou
sand feet above sea level. The French
call it the guardian to the northern
entrance Of the Alpine frontier with
Italy.


Battle Began at 4 AM.


The battle began at 4a.m. From
tier guards on the Swiss side of the
CLANCY Bridge over the Rhone, 10
miles from the town of Bellgarde
and five miles from the LEcluse
Fort, heard artillery fire, air bombs
and other sounds of battle from Bell
garde.


Refugees later reported the Ger
mans stormed and captured Belize
garde. where the Rhone River
vanishes under rock, drops about 80
feet and emerges in narrow gorge.


German troops apparently con-
centrated all possible mechanized
forces, men and planes in Southern
France for the attack. 1t was
launched from Mantua, on the west,
simultaneously with a push from
the Valserine Valley on the north.


Defenders Fall Back.


The city of Bellegarde, which is
600 feet lower than peaks around
it, was occupied within a few hours
while defending troops fell back on
L'Ecluse Fort. Once on this side
OF Bellegarde, German forces pressed
up the steep hill toward the fort.


The French for two years have
been strengthening the fort with
elaborate tunneling. However, most
of the huge guns dominating the
area between Bellegarde and An
necy were aimed toward the south
and east, while the Germans were
attacking from the west and north

Thanks to the toughest job Of ice
breaking that boats using the route
regularly have encountered in 40

Moderate temperatures of the last

major share of the credit must go

vessel of the Norfolk & Washington
Steamboat Co.


Where bigger and younger ships
bucked the Potomac ice for only

Southland slipped downstream past
Hains Point at daylight Thursday

pect of jamming In heavy ice or
having to turn back. No other ship
had been able to fight its way
through the 50-mile stretch Of frozen
Potomac.

land, bound for Alexandria, rammed
its way northward to Morgantown,
rested for . week hoping for better

Baltimore.

NEW YORK, April 27.-The latest
information on the whereabouts of
the British liner Queen Mary comes
from officers of the Javanese
steamer Poelau Tello, who say they
saw the liner at Cape Town, South
Africa, April 2.


The giant liner sailed from New
York March %. presumably for
service as troop transport for an
unannounced destination.


DR.. Bernard Van Mort, ships
surgeon of the Poelau Tello, said
Cape Town citizens had been ex-
pecting the Queen Mary, as they
understood she was on her way
to Australia.


The Poelau Tello arrived in New
York yesterday. Passengers and
officers said the Queen Mary was
conveyed by three destroyers and
apparently was taking on fuel and
supplies at the South African port.


Another OF the worlds great

York Harbor


Since yesterday, huge barges

pier itself many trucks have been
seen unloading provisions.


At about the time the Queen
Mary slipped away, the British
owned Mauretania, also painted
drab gray as protection against
enemy craft, left the harbor and
disappeared in the open sea. Later

BY the Associated Press.


CHICAGO, May 20.-A gun fight
in which three men were shot and
two milk trucks damaged introduced
Chicago's milk strike to Northern
Illinois early today.


The fighting broke out near Volo,
ILL.,, where State Policeman Paul
Sans said 500 pickets had gathered
to halt milk shipped from Wisconsin.


About 100 pickets stopped two
Meadowmoor Dairy trucks, Police
man Sans reported, dumped the
milk, shot holes in the windows Of
the cabs, ripped out ignition wires,
smashed carburetors and poured
dirt in the gasoline tanks.


Policeman Sans and fellow
ofiicer, the only policemen on the
scene, said they were forced to look
on as the violence grew. The police
officers said they exchanged shots.
however, with several carloads of
men which were conveying the milk
trucks.


The convoy was armed with piS-
tolls, sawed of shotguns and ma
chine guns, Policeman Sans said.
He described them as Chicago
hoodlums" They forced the police
car of the road and side-swiped an
automobile containing four persons.


About an hour later near the same
place pickets halted and overturned
four more trucks. Embalming fluid
was dumped in some of the milk,
Policeman Sans said.


A force of 100 State policemen was
ordered into the district to restore
order.


I'VE will watch these roads and
keep them clear" State Police Capt.
Phil Renkosiak declared. Union ofIi-
cials here said they had not author.
lied the dumping of milk and sent
out their own investigators before
commenting further.

GUM.

While the British Air Force was

cashire area of England's industrial
northwest in a MASSIVE assault
which continued without letup for
hours, inflicting heavy casulties and
destroying number of buildings.

commercial buildings and church
were damaged or destroyed Thir-
teen persons were believed killed
when high-explosive bomb hit the

Many Left Homeless.


A group of firemen were killed

munal kitchens.

Both explosive and fire bombs

distance in one street.


Germans Active on Coast.


The British assault coincided with
reports of unusual activity along the
German-occupied French coast,
which led to speculation here that

Christmas attempt to invade Eng
land.

signal.


Observers on the English shore
along the Strait of Dover said un-
favorable weather made it impos-
sible to judge the effects of the
British bombardment of the Nazi
invasion ports" this morning, but

night, when the r. A. F.. pounded

SAN FRANCISCO, Jan. "A 28-

The teams, hand picked from all

tailed when Bill Anahu. Santa

converted.


In the second period the West

back, who skirted end for the second

norman, smooth-passing halfback

1-yard line, from where Frank En-

punt from behind his own goal was
blocked and grounded in the end
zone. The Fasteners got two more
in the next period. The West was
backed to its 1-yard line after
15-yard clipping penalty, and Zim-
norman grounded the ball in the
end zone rather than risk a weak
kick.


The West scored its fourth touch
down in the final period when Lee
Artoe, California tackle, grabbed a
bad Eastern pass from center which
sailed over the head of Dick Cas-
siano, Pittsburgh half, and plopped
into the end zone.


Rain kept away some $1,000 fans
would would have seen one of the
most exciting and amusing East
West contests in years. The 60,0OO-
seat stadium was virtually sellout.

for Crippled Children.

dicate that the Dodecanese is being
strangled by the British blockade,
especially since the establishment of
a major British base on the nearby
island of Crete. Wholly dependent
on supply ships from Italy even for
foodstuffs, the large Italian garri-
sons are evidently on short rations,
while the lessening Of air and sub
marine activity from those bases
seems to show that supplies of oil
and munitions are running low.

would be delighted to have this
chronic Italian menace removed, and

conjunction with British sea power,

against the axis powers. Thus the

despite the appointment of General

Autumn is the natural seeding
time and home owners who are
thinking ahead to next spring and
summer will remember that grass
seed scattered now will provide next
seasons lawn.


Most amateur gardeners and
planters believe that spring is the
growing season and that the proper
time for sowing grass seed is shortly
after the winter freezes have
thawed and the ground becomes
soft enough for cultivation. Sea-
soned planters. however, hold that
the ideal time for improving the
lawn is in autumn and cite the fol-
lowing reasons:


/. The soil is usually still warm
in autumn.


2. Nights are cool and dews are
usually heavy


3. There are frequent rains.


4. Weeds begin to die.


Warm soil Is said to increase
both the rate and amount of seed
termination. The soil is warmer in
autumn. for it has been exposed to
the sun all summer Autumn soil
temperatures are most favorable
to heavy growth.


Cool nights, heavy dew and dimin-
ishing sun rays are said to cause
grass to spread. forming a dense
sod instead of Spindly growth Thick
sods are always more resistant 10
weeds.


Autumn rains are seldom the type
which wash gulleys or carry away
the seed. Their frequent occur
renee provide a constant supply OF
moisture for the grass roots


Dying weeds means that young
grass seedlings have less competi-
ton for nourishment Generally,
autumn-sown grass thrives because
1t Is unhampered.
headline:
Fall Is Best Time


To Plant Grass Seed

Maglll and few other friends

title last month.

BERN, Switzerland, Nov. 6.-The
Swiss government today directed its
Minister to London to protest ener-
getically against alleged violations
of Swiss territory by British bombers
during the night.


The government recalled it pre-
viously had received assurances from
London that British planes would
cease flying over Swiss territory"


The Swiss high command earlier
this morning said heavy anti-aircraft
fire had dispersed one squadron" Of
the many warplal;es that flew over
Switzerland during the night.


The communique did not identify
the planes, but said they crossed
Switzerland from northeast to south
east. One squadron, the announce
ment said, took the road back be-
fore crossing the Alps"


The appearance Of the planes gave
Bern and Zurich air alarms which
lasted an hour and one-half.


Such alarms in the past usually
have indicated British planes we're
en- route to or from attacks on OBJ
jectives in Northern Italy.

Sammy West, in the sunset stage of
a creditable baseball career, is
nursing no illusions concerning his
promotion to guardian of WASH
ington first base interests. He isn't

The Cincinnati Reds and Brook
lyn Dodgers bump headlong into
another Showdown" series today,
with the National League cham.
pionship hanging in the balance.


For Brooklyn, at least, the double-
header today and the night game
tomorrow night loomed as the most
vital tests of the season. The Reds
are racing along at an almost un-
believable pace with IA victories in
their last 16 games.


If Cincinnati is going to be kept
from repeating in the senior circuit,
this winning streak will have to be
curbed quickly and the Dodgers
can't count on much help from the
other Eastern clubs the Reds will
be playing In the next two weeks.


Reds Eliminate Giants.


The champs took the New York
Giants apart in three games over
the week end, dropping them II
full games behind first place and
apparently out of pennant conten-
ton for the remainder of the year.


This put the task Of sidetracking
the Reds squarely up to the Dodgers
themselves, and the prospect was
not too promising, even for ardent
Flatbush fans.


The two rivals have met in five
series this season, dividing the first
four evenly, and when the scales
finally tilted it was in Cincinnati's
direction. The Reds beat Brooklyn
two games out of three in Crosley
Field few days ago, helping put
the Dodgers on the skids that
brought them home today five
games behind the lead.


The Dodgers won only six games
and lost eight during their recent
Western invasion and finished with
fat old Freddy Fitzsimmons carry
ing the load as the teams surest
winning pitcher.


In contrast the Cincinnati staf
has been functioning so perfectly
that the starting pitcher has worked
the complete games in 10 out Of the
last IL contests.


Both major leagues shifted
scenery yesterday, an open date, and
came up for new intersectional
stands today.

Reminding that the warm weather
is bringing out more bicyclists and
thus increasing traffic hazards,
Washington l. Cleveland, manager
of the District Division, American
Automobile Association, today sug-
gested these safety rules for those
who ride bicycles.


Ride in a straight line and do not
suddenly change direction; keep
close to the right-hand side of the
roadway; obey officers, stop and 60
signals and stop signs; ride in single
file on busy streets and never more
than two abreast; avoid driving
too fast on hills and slippery or
rough roads: never hitch-on to any
moving vehicle; never carry any one
on the handle-bars; cross all street
car and railroad tracks at nearly
right angles; wear light or white
clothing for night-riding, and keep
the bicycle in good mechanical con-
dition.

NEW YORK, May 21-War stocks
today led the market in one of the
widest breaks in two years as severe
allied reverses brought visions to
Wall Street of a German-forced
quick peace.


Losses ran to 13 or more points
for pivotal steels, aircrafts, electrical
equipments, coppers, motors and
chemicals. The ticker tape fire.
quently was behind floor dealings on
the downswing, slowing on feeble
recovery shifts. Quotations were

close with dealings speedy. Trans
fers were around 100000 shares,
biggest turnover since last Sep
tember.


The list Topped at the start, with
a number of issues late in making
their appearance. due to the in
ability of specialties to coordinate
bid and asked prices.

advances, defeat of the 9th French

Giraud and the approach of the
invading forces to the English Chan
mel. Later bulletins from battle

contingents and, after intermittent
steadiness, the slide was resumed.

though German and Danish dollar
loans moved upward. The free"
British pound sterling dropped sub
stantially, along with the French
franc.

ferers than others, but they were

Rains during the last week i'm
proved crops in many localities from
the Middle Atlantic States to the
Eastern Great Plains, the Weather
Bureau reports, but water shortage
was causing shipments of livestock
out of the Dakotas, Wyoming and
Montana.


The bureau reported that from
the Great Plains westward through
the Central and Northern Rocky
Mountains to the Pacific Coast the
ranges needed soaking rains. Con-
tinued dry weather in the Great
Plains from Oklahoma northward
damaged dry-land crops.


Despite the weeks rains, the bu-
reau said, pastures in large areas
from Ohio and Alabama to the
Mississippi River needed moisture
badly.


In most of the corn belt the crop
was making good progress, although
in portions of Kansas, Missouri,
Illinois, South Dakota and Western
Oklahoma dry weather early this
month had inflicted permanent
damage.


Rains late in the week hampered
spring wheat threshing in some To-
calities.


Cotton made good to fair progress
in most of the belt, and conditions
varied from locally poor to fairly
good.

ical and Metallurgical Engineering

SHANGHAI, Nov. a.-Consider-
able numbers of japanese troops
were reported today to be withdraw
ing from Shantung Province in
Northern China amid evidence of
growing japanese concentrations in
the south.


Advices from foreign sources said
. steady stream of japanese troops
has been leaving Shantung by rail-
road for the past week. These
sources said they were embarking
on transports at Tientsin and
Tsingtao for undisclosed destina-
tions but were believed to be headed
south toward the Japanese island of
Formosa and the Japanese-occu-
pied island of Hainan on the China
coast.


Some casualties among the with
drawing forces indicated that the
Chinese were keeping up their pres
sure on Shantung, where there have
been frequent guerrilla raids re-
Gently on railroads.


Travellers from Hong Kong. at the
same time, reported sighting flve
Japanese transports OF the mouth
Of the Yangtze River, apparently
carrying soldiers withdrawn from
Yangtze garrison cities.


Foreign military sources said they
interpreted these movements as evi-
dence that Japan Is planning a new
southwark thrust, possibly with the
French Indo- China port Of Saigon
as first objective.


HONG KONG. Nov. % tR.-The
Chinese Central News agency said
today that two Japanese warships
sank with many casualties after
striking Chinese mines in the
Yangtze River near Tungliu, South
Anhwei Province.

that later twilight time, however.

NEW YORK, Feb. 10.-The fight
world today held morning-after
head. and through it buzzed the
name of Arturo Godoy, the strange
interlude in the life of Joe Louis.


For Is mauling, bruising rounds
last night. the Hot Tamale from
Chile stood UP to the Brown Bomber,
and when the announcer intoned
THE winner, and still world cham
pion. a thunder of boos
swept from the Madison Square
Garden rafters.


It was that close in the eyes of
many of the 1855 fans who came
expecting another efficient Louis
painting job and left with vague
miSgivings


They couldn't figure out whether
the Bomber was no longer the same
Bomber who wrecked the John
Henry LeWises and the Max Schmel-
ings and the Tony Galentos. or
whether the clowning. grimacing,
bobbing and clutching Godoy was
more than little better than they
figured.


This they did know, that a return
meeting in the open air next sum-
mer is as certain as death. Arturo
can't punch a lick, but he punched
his way right out Of the Garden
and into the open air


One Judge for Godoy.


Not only the gallery thought the
rock-ribbed, IRON jaWed Chilean was
the victor. Tommy Shortell, one of
the judges. gave Godoy the fight
with 10 rounds to five for Louis.
Referee Arthur Donovan gave Louis
10 and Godoy five, the same as the
Associated Press score sheet, and
the other judge. George Lecron, gave
Louis 10, Godoy four, and called
one even.


Sharper, more Furnishing blows
provided the margin by which the
Bomber retained his title. He was
up against a style that baff1ed him,
and left him puzzled and frustrated
as he tried to find a spot for his
famed dynamite fists on crouch
ing, bobbing foe who came out for
the first round squatting like a
Russian dancer. dove for his oppo-
nent's thighs. then crept upward
like ivy until he could bury his
square chin in the hollow of Louis
neck and whale away.


Louis. little relishing the inside
work. did his best to stay clear, but
his straight left wasn't enough to
keep the courageous Chilean away.
Even Joe's uppercuts, landing on
Godoy's battle-scarred face, failed
to slow the Chilean more than mo-
mentarily.


In fact. Joe's week end punches
bounced off him like rain off tin
roof. and he was forever swarming,
swarming. In several rounds he
carried Louis against the ropes and
silently challenged him to a head
to-head slugging bee from which he
seldom came off second best.


Chilean Bulls Champion.


Time after time the Garden was
bedlam as the unorthodoX Chilean
bulled the sloe-eyed champion
about, often making him blink with
looping lefts or rights which. had
they the potency of Galento
punch. would have spelled disaster.
They could not ruffle Louis calm,
however. and he left the ring un-
marked. Godoys eyes and lips were
puffed, and one eye peered over
slight cut.


Godoy appeared to tire midway in
the fight, but he got his second wind
quickly, and in the closing rounds
he appeared strong. In fact, he pro.
vided a clownish interlude in the
fourteenth. coming out of his corner
gorilla fashion, stopped over, arms
dropped to the floor.


Abruptly he stood erect and be-
gan dancing about Louis in a huge
circle, as the champion, statue in
bronze, pivoted like mannikin in
midring and waited for his haunting
foe to lead.


All in all, Louis won, and in our
opinion, won by clear margin, but
1t was Godoy's night to howl. which
he did literally when he realized he
had stayed Is rounds with the dark
destiny and had carried the fight to
his opponent over the route.


1t was Louis ninth title defense
and the second time he was carried
the limit. Tommy Farr was the
other survivor


The show drew gate of only
S88, ,5238 another disappointment
for the Bomber. His previous Gar
den appearances each topped the
100000 mark.

The new distribution of duties
and responsibilities of the Navy De-
partment secretariat was announced
yesterday following the swearing in
of James v. Forrestal as Undersec-
retary.


Effective at once, the Secretary
of the Navy will have charge OF
the budget, the joint board, naval
petroleum reserves, the general
board and public relations. Secre-
tary Knox also will handle depart
ment policy on legislation and will
have under his supervision the
Naval Research Laboratory.


Mr.. Forrestal will act as depart
mental naison officer with industrial
agencies for other than the budget,
Army, material and labor sections.
The Undersecretary's Office also will
handle tax questions, routine leg
islation and contracts.


The Compensation Board, Naval
Examining Board, Naval Retiring
Board and the Board of Medical
Examiners also are included in the
Undersecretary's category.


Assistant Secretary Compton will
handle commissioned and enlisted
personnel, shore establishments and
civil employees. The Army and Navy
Munitions Board, the Shore Sta
tions Development Board and the
chief clerks Office also are in his
jurisdiction, as well as labor mat
tiers of the department.


The redistribution of duties was
necessitated by the establishment
of the office of Undersecretary.

the Saar."


Aerial observers kept pace with the
land scouts. TWO German recon-
naissance flights were reported yes
terday deep over Eastern France,
while French flyers brought back
photographs Of German lines.


Spring-like weather turned snow
and ice into a mass of mud along
the front.

MANILA, Nov. 23.-The steamer
Washington. evacuating refugees
from China, arrived today from
Shanghai with 618 passengers, 1T
of whom were United States avia-
tors and other civilians who dis
embarked here. The others were
mostly wives and children of United
States Navy men.


Nine hundred persons, mostly
Navy families being evacuated from
the Philippines on Navy orders, are
scheduled to leave Monday on the
Washington for San Francisco. A
few other Navy families will sail
later in the week on the Navy trans
port Chaumont.


Naval officials said that when the
Chaumont has sailed all Navy fami-
lies will have been removed from
the Far East.
