RICHMOND. Va, Oct. 2-"Satis-
factory progress" in the harvesting
Of corn, cotton, hay and apples dur
ing the past week was indicated to-
day in the weekly Virginia weather
and crop report.


Temperatures were below normal,
with freezing weather reported at
Floyd, Wytheville and Bedford and
the lowest reading, "a degrees. at
Dale Enterprise. Light to killing
frosts occurred in most mountain
and Piedmont counties. Precipita-
ton. light to moderate was dis
tributed fairly uniformly over the
State.


Most of the tobacco crop has been
harvested, it was reported. Some
peanut growers have commenced
digging, but this work will not be-
come general until about October 10
as the crop Is somewhat later than
usual.


The gathering Of apples has been
progressing satisfactorily, but some
of the growers report that the crop
is not packing out as well as it had
been expected, the report disclosed.
The unusually early frost damaged
late gardens. corn and lespedeza in
few sections. Pastures are still
good and livestock is in excellent
condition.


Following the rain the ground
was in excellent condition for plow-
ing and disking, and the seeding of
barley and rye was making rapid
progress. Early-sown clovers and
grass were also greatly benefited by
the rain.

TOURS, June 11-This white city
on the banks Of the Loire today
became the emergency capital Of
France.


Tours, whose gravest peacetime
concern was placating fussy tour
lists with good food and wine, thus
was turned overnight into the nerve
center of government and diplo-
macy at an historic hour for
France.


Every resource of the ancient city
was requisitioned to house Minis.
tries, Embassies. Legations and
their stats.
Old buildings, some long con-
demned, were occupied by various
French government departments.


Records and Diplomats.


High officials apologized for the
crowding and hastily mobilized car
penters to repair rotting floors and
erect office partitions. -


Along With the seemingly never
ending stream of refugees pouring
into the city from the north-from
the direction of Paris, about $50
miles away-rumbled trucks heavily
loaded with boxes of government
records.


In the same exodus are the luxuri-
GUS embassy and legation limousines.
First arrivals among them were in
a caravan bringing, among others,
the Papal Nuncio, the Ambassadors
OF Belgium, Argentina and Spain
and the Ministers of Uruguay, Ven-
ezuela and Colombia.


They said they had been bombed
en- route by German planes, but had
suffered no casualties, and we're
thankful to the French government
for having reserved quarters for
them in difficult situation.


Moving Days in Europe.


Tension was evident as large
numbers of police insistently waved
on the slow-moving refugee motor
cades through the city. 7S~


Stretching far back over the roll
ing Loire Valley, the line contained
countless children. Peering out Of
every crowded automobile were the
expressionless, uncomprehending
little faces.


Drying laundry, evidently washed
at roadside streams, fluttered from
many automobiles.


AS to how many had passed
through this city since the Nazi
invasion of the Low Countries q
month ago, no one would hazard
guess.


One policeman shrugged his
shoulders helplessly.


"All day and all night it goes on. "
he said "A little while ago 1t was
the Spanish coming north. Now
our people are moving south. It is
formidable, is it not, these moving
days in Europe?"

Maryland taxpayers welcome the
announcement by Governor O'Conor
that he will favor reduction in the
States income tax. The reduction
can be achieved, the Governor has
noted, through raising the exemp-
ton levels. Many taxpayers, how
ever, also will favor a reduction in
the rates If the States financial
status will permit.


Governor O'Conor has described
Maryland's fiscal condition as
healthy" He announced that State
departments have saved about $780,
900 during the past fiscal year and
that the State surplus has climbed
to $4,000 Despite the uncer-
tainty of world conditions, the
executive believes that with such a
comfortable surplus Maryland can
consider easing the State tax burden.
He has proposed that the levy on
persons having small incomes from
investments, now taxed at the rate of
SIX per CcllI VII paw dllO ONSAJ NC
reduced by raising the 5000 mini
mum. Along the same line he sug-
gests raising the $1,000 exemption
for wage earners and the $500
exemption for dependents. Persons
having ordinary" income now have
to pay two and one-half per cent
on all earnings above the exemption.


The States taxpayers were shocked
last year when nominal one-half
of one per cent income tax rate was
abruptly changed to the two and
one-half and six per cent scale, and
the exemptions lowered. While the
new rates did not quite produce the
100000 sought, the returns, cou-
pied with the economies practiced
by the O'Conor administration, have
been more than sufficient. The
effect of the income tax now is being
studied by a State Tax Revision
Commission which will make recon-
mendations for revisions to the
Legislature which meets in January.
Members of the Assembly, acutely
conscious of the public reaction to
the tax, can be expected to expedite
the passage of any legislation that
will make it lighter.

public hearings.


These measures will be part Of

The Commissioners were closeted
for about two hours yesterday with
Corporation Counsel Elwood Seal
and Auditor Daniel j. Donovan re-
hash1ng a number of bills offered

the program for the coming session.


The two measures decided on

interstate trucks may take through

AMSTERDAM, April 2O.-A Ger
man warplane crashed in Southern
Limburg Province, extreme South
astern Holland, today after being
fired upon by Netherlands anti-air-
craft guns.


The five members of the crew
one of whom was wounded, were
interned.


The crash occurred near Bunde
about 6 miles north of Maastricht
where a narrow finger of the
Netherlands juts south between Bel
gium and Germany.


Earlier three planes, apparently
German, attacked two others, pre-
sumably British, near Siebengewald
Northern Limburg Province. Ma
chine-gun fire was heard and after
a few minutes the two planes being
attacked disappeared to the north
under cover of smoke screen.

outposts that German labor squads

advance positions. German bat

merely nothing to report

ports said, took advantage of the
first clear weather in several days
to send out reconnaissance flights

the German lines and met IL enemy
ships, reports said, but the lone
ship outdistanced them and re-
turned to its base.

running. She was too worried not
to. But the Merry Little Breezes
kept right beside her, and it was
not nearly as hard running now as
it had been.


Have you seen Farmer Browns S
Boy?" painted Granny Fox.


"Oh, yes! We saw him Just a
little while ago over near your house
Granny Fox. We pulled his hat of
just to hear him scold," shouted the
Merry Little Breezes, and then they
tickled and laughed as If they had
had a good time with Farmer
Browns Boy.


But Old Granny Fox didn't laugh
oh, my, no indeed! Her heart went
lower still. and she did her best to
run faster. Pretty soon she came
out on the top of the hill. where
she could look. and then it seemed
as If her heart came right up in
her mouth and stopped beating.
Her eyes popped almost out of her
head. Ihere was Farmer Brown S
Boy standing right in front of the
door of her home. And while she
was watching what should Reddy
Fox do but stick his head out of the
door.


Old Granny Fox saw the gun of
Farmer Browns Boy pointed right
at Reddy, and she clapped both
hands over her eyes to shut out the
dreadful sight. Then she waited for
the bang of the gun. 1t didn't come
Then Granny peeped through her
fingers. Farmer Browns Boy was
still there, but Reddy Fox had dis
appeared inside the house.


Granny Fox sighed in relief. 1t
had been a terrible scare-the worst
she could remember.

States Lines today sold eight of its
idle transatlantic ships. including

to Belgian corporation for a re-
ported sum of about $4,000, 900.


President John M. Franklin of the
U. S. Lines confirmed the sale, but
declined to disclose the price.


The purchasing firm was identified
as the Societe Maritime Anversoise.
The ships start operations between
New York and England, France
and Belgium within few weeks.


The seven other vessels sold were !:
American Merchant, American
Banker. American Importer, Ameri-
can Shipper, American Trader and
American Traveller, all of about 1000
gross tons. Except for the President
Harding, veteran Of the North At
lantic passenger and cargo service,
all are cargo ships.


With passage of the revised Neu-
trality Act, U. S. Lines ships were
withdrawn from the transatlantic
service, but the Washington ana
Manhattan now are In the New
York-Italy trade, and the firms
eleventh vessel. the President Roose-
welt, is in Bermuda service.


The sale was authorized by the
U. S. Maritime Commission.

NEW YORK, Feb. % (R.-Stock
brokers are wiser, but hardly any
richer, from six months experience
with war markets.


If it means anything, the interval
since Hitler turned loose his legions
on Poland has afforded brokers the
first good opportunity to study
action of security prices under the
impact Of modern war and total
itarian controls.


Unlike the opening phase of the
World War, the stock exchange has
continued to do business at the old
stand. Except for the September
boom, the business hasn't been pro-
ductive Of much revenue for COM
mission houses. Transactions, in
fact, begged down into the slowest
markets in nearly two decades.


At that, it was a better break
than commission houses got in 1914,
when the stock exchange closed for
five months to keep from being
swamped by foreign selling. And,
since hope springs eternal in the
speculative camps, there are many
in the financial district who think
history may repeat with another
wartime bull market.
headline: Brokers Wiser, Not Richer.

IhlS month more than 10000 COL
lege students in 670 colleges and uni
versities are starting training as air
plane pilots under the Civil Pilot
Training Program. All of them have
pledged themselves to enter the mill
tary services if qualified and all of
them have passed the regular mill
tary physical examination.


For the first time since it's inception
nearly two years ago, the great Civil
Pilot Training Program has taken on
military characteristics which were
not present during earlier courses.
The $4,000 students who have been
taking primary and secondary
courses during the summer, begin
ming July l, and who are to COM
plete their training by the end of
this month, and the 10000 trained
last winter and spring were under
no obligation to apply for military
training and only small percentage
OF them have done so.


While the original purpose of the
Civil Pilot Training Program, as its
name indicates, was not military, it
was undertaken with the hope that
1t would provide a reservoir of par
TALLY trained civilian flyers from
which the military services could
draw in case of emergency. With
the state of military emergency now
existing, few persons interested in the
defense of their country will quar-
rel with the new requirement that
students trained at Federal expense
should be required to pledge them
selves to continue military training.
Evidently, from the fact that all
quotas for the fall course have been
promptly filled, even before the OPEN
ing of the colleges and universities,
the students themselves have had
no hesitancy in giving such a
pledge. Their spirit speaks we'll for
the future safety of the Nation in
the face of threatened aggression.


1t Is encouraging to note that in
spite of great expansion and speeding
up OF the civil program, safety stand
ards higher than any ever before
known in civilian pilot training are
being maintained The most con-
crete evidence of this record is the
voluntary action of insurance COM
panies in reducing, for the third time,
premium rates for insurance covering
student pilots in the program. These
rates now are less than third what
they were at the time the program
began year and a half ago.


The Nation will join in wishing
these new fledgling aviators well and
take comfort from the fact that their
training will increase the future
strength of both military and civil
aviation in America.

NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 4.-To any
one wondering how the same Tulane
team could drop three straight
games and then polish off Rice.
North Carolina and Clemson, the
answer is-it was not the same
team.


The Green Wave which washed
away most of Clemsons bowl hopes,
1870, last Saturday was far diff
ferent type of surge from the ripple
which scarcely wet the claws Of
Boston Colleges Eagles five weeks
ago, and later lost to Auburn and
Fordham


For most of the afternoon the
Greenies looked as they did last
year when they came through I'M
defeated. They gained more than
400 yards, including 383 rushing,
and held the enemy to 81.


Team Greatly Improved.


"Were running harder, blocking
better and playing more headsup
on defense" generalized Coach Red
Dawson today. "Inexperience and
injuries were our big troubles The
sophomores have learned plenty.
The line has been strengthened
since Tommy OBoyle has been able
to plav again and Jack little was
shifted from quarterback"


Errors in early Games startled
and disheartened Tulane followers.
Sophomore guards played too close
on defense and were repeatedly
driven in. Ends were sucked in.
The secondary let pass receivers
get into the clear.


Blockers forgot their assignments
or missed their men, ball carriers
pointed" the plays or failed to cut
properly over the tackles and ends.


Tough Test for 'Bama.


But recently the guards have been
impossible. the ends fooled rarely,
even by Clemson's super tricky re-
verses. Pass defenders have hung
onto their men like leeches. AL
though North Cardinals Jim La
lame punctured the Tulane goal line
by air, Rice and Clemson found
their aerial attacks did them more
harm than good.


After watching Tulane lose its
opening game to Boston College,
Coach Frank Thomas of Alabama
asserted ''in six weeks Tulane would
beat Boston College"


Developments have added weight
to his prediction. but Thomas prob
ably is wishing he was wrong.
Next Saturday the six weeks will
be up. and next Saturday Tulane
plays Alabama.

DETROIT, Sept. 12-Pennant
fever gripped Detroit's baseball
thousands today as the New York
Yankees came to town for three
game make or break series.


Realizing that the championship
hopes of both teams were at stake

stop the Yanks.'


Long lines Of fans formed at the
ticket windows to obtain paste
boards for the series and the Tiger
management announced its advance
sale for Saturdays game ALREADY
had exceeded that for any other
single contest this season.


Rowe Holds Tiger Hopes.


The scene was almost repetition
of Detroit's pennantwinning days
of 1884 and 1885. even to the Tiger
pitching choice Back in those days,
Schoolboy Rowe was usually called
upon to stop the Yanks. and it was
the Schoolboy, hero of one of base
balls greatest comebacks this year,
whom Manager Del Baker picked to
do the job today


There was a possibility that Baker
might switch at the last minute to
Tommy Bridges, but Bridges. the
only other Tiger pitcher who was
with the club five years ago, would
hardly detract from the illusion.


Marius Russo, 26-year- old south
paw, was slated to bear the Yankee
mound burden.


The Tigers went into the series
boasting six victories in their last
seven starts. three of them over the
Cleveland Indians third party to
the tight little clique sitting Oh top
of the American League standings.


Detroit Has Season Edge.


In addition, the Detroiters have
a u to 7 edge over the Yankees in
the 10 games the two clubs have
played this season.


That's just half of it, though. The
last time they met the Yankees
swept three straight games in New
York and sent the Tigers tumbling
five and half games out of first
place. A repetition of that feat at
this late date might spell another
league championship for the Yanks
and disaster for the Tigers.

warplanes which attacked Naples
before they could do extensive dam
age.


The casualties, the high command
said, were caused by bombs which
fell on Surbo, in Lecci Province east
of Naples and nearby Sanvito Del
Normanni.


An Italian torpedo boat also was
credited with sinking British sub
marine which attacked an italian
convoye in the Central Mediter-
ranean.

British bombers returned to
the German naval base at
Hornum, on the Island of Sylt,
today, dropping more bombs and
blasting German defenses with
machine gun fire after the big
gest British air raid of the war
last night and early this morn
ing.


British air ministry sources
said the bombers went back
principally to take pictures of
the damage, caused by a fleet of
80 to so planes, which partici-
pated in the seven-hour raid.


Reports from Tonder, Denmark,
said that the British attacks today
were carried out with violence almost
equal to the earlier raid.


British Air Minister Sir Kingsley
Wood said that many hits were
made last night on strategic jetty
and railway points on the island,
and that hangers and oil storage
tanks we're set afire. Only one
British plane failed to return from
the raid and all came back from to-
days flight, according to the British.


Sounds of Explosions Heard.


The sound of exploding bombs
rolled in over Denmark's coastal
settlements, leading to belief that
many planes were in action, al
though accurate determination was
impossible. Indications from the
Danish coast we're that British
hombers were sweeping back and
forth over the narrow island in six
attacking units.


The morning attack lasted 20 min
utes, with the conclusion of explo-
sions so intense that houses on the
Danish coast were shaken. Nu-
merous German pursuit planes later
were observed flying to and from the
island to the mainland.


Observers, unable to see clearly,
Judged the number of attacking
units by the successive waves of
bomb explosions accompanied by
terrific anti-aircraft fire.


Watchers from the Danish shore
said numerous observation planes
flew over Sylt at 3 pm. Machine
guns barked, but no fire of heavier
guns was noticed


When fog lifted at pm. shore
observers saw that one of four anti
aircraft towers between the main
land and Sylt was missing, appar-
emily the victim of a direct bomb
hit. The towers are manned by
machine gunners.


Machine Gun Attempt Reported.


1t was reported that an unidenti-
fed foreign plane, fired on by DAN
ish anti-aircraft guns at Esbjerg
during the first big British raid,
later descended and tried to machine
gun the Danish gun crew.


A Danish naval vessel in the Esb-
jerg harbor fired on this plane.


During last nights raid six bomb
ers circled low over Hvide Sande
(white sands about midnight and
dropped three large bombs on that
narrow strip of Danish soil about
midway the west coast.


Several hours afterward another
group of planes appeared over Hvide
Sande and dropped several light
bombs which apparently fell into
the water.


1t was reported also that bombs
fell inside Varde, Danish city
about Is miles from the Danish
coast. in the early morning. Sew
eral craters were found, but no
casualties were reported.


Danish authorities began an in
vestigation to determine nationality
of the planes which dropped the
bombs, and a formal protest was
considered likely. 1t was pointed
out that the planes probably were
British.


Danish anti-aircraft guns again
fired warning shots this morning as
foreign planes flew over Danish ter
ritory.

ROCKVILLE, Md. Nov. a.
Funeral services for Mrs. Clara Bliss
Finley, 88, physician and for many
years active in religious and welfare
work in Washington and Mont
gomery County, were held from the
home this morning. The Rev. John
C. Palmer, pastor of Washington
Heights Presbyterian Church. con-

woman to graduate from the medi-
cal school of Columbian College.
now George Washington University,
and practiced medicine in Wash
ington for number of years.


The Woman's Clinic, Woman's
Gymnasium and Business Women's
Club, all of Washington, were
among the organizations Mrs. Fin
ley helped form, and she was
charter member of the Women's
Anthropological Society, Of Wash
ington; the National Congress Of
Mothers, now the National PARENT
Teacher organization; the George
town Industrial Center and the
Montgomery County Social Service
League. She also was largely in
strumental in founding the Italian
Mission in Washington, now the
Italian Baptist Church, and other
religious groups in Washington and
Rockville.


Mrs. Finley is survived by
daughter, Miss Bliss Finley of
Rockville. She was for many years
a member of Washington Heights
Presbyterian Church

Eighty-eight of the Fascist planes,

Cooperation between ground, sea

described.


British (air) fighters maintained

Associated Press War Correspondent.


WITH BRITISH FORCES OUT
SIDE BARDIA, Dec. 21-British
pressure continued on Bardia, Italy's
beleaguered Libyan port, today, but
the action slackened in severity.


The arrival of new British con-
tingents, however, made it plain
there was no thought of giving up
the attack on this Fascist strong
hold.


On the other hand, it seemed
equally as certain that the Italians
were not planning to abandon the
port, but were preparing to put up
stiff resistance.


While some detachmentS have
been withdrawn to Tobruk, farther
west in Libya, the bulk of the fight
ing forces-perhaps two divisions
remains in the besieged town.


Italian aircraft have been more
active in the Bardia region than
at any other place or time since
the British offensive began 13 days
ago. British pilots reported encoun-
tering big groups of italian planes,
several of which, they said, were
shot down.


Officers express satisfaction with
the performance of their troops in
the desert. The rains have stopped,
but temperatures have hit new lows
in the desert, with freezing weather
reported during last night at some
inland points on the escarpment.
The temperatures for the past two
weeks have been about eight de-
grees below average for this time
Of year.


Egyptian Premier Husein Sirry
Pasha today toured the British
desert military and air establish
ments.

STOCKHOLM, April 10.-Nor-
wegian troops. defending their gov
ernment and its new capital, fought
a fierce battle with invading Ger
man forces today at the town OF
Elverum, rs miles north of Oslo, on
the Swedish frontier, according to
advices reaching here.


About 200 Norwegians were re-
ported killed and wounded, while
German losses were not immedi-
ately known.


The Germans were reported send
ing reinforcements to Elverum
speedily, but the town still had not
been occupied by 4:30 pm.


Volunteers joined the regular Nor
wegian troops to defend the new
capital from the invaders. The
royal family and the government
of Premier Johan Nygaardsvold had
fled to Elverum from Hamar
whittier it had gone yesterday just
ahead of the German occupation
of Oslo.


Supported by Planes.


German troops were supported
in their action against Elverum by
warplanes, travellers reaching here
related.


Reports from Moscow to the
Stockholm newspaper Aftonbladet
said Russia was remaining neutral
regarding current events in Scan
dinavia, but that she regarded Eng
land as responsible for the fate
of Denmark and Norway"


Political circles in Moscow were
said to regard Russia and Finland
both as being out of the field of
action of the great powers, but nev-
ertheless Russia was said to have
concentrated troops in the north
and to have her Arctic navy ready
Tor any eventuality.


Ferry traffic between Denmark
and Sweden, which was cut OF yes
terday with the German occupation
of Denmark. was expected to be
opened by tomorrow.


No telephone calls or telegraph
transmission still were permitted be-
tween the two countries, however.


Danish fishermen reported that II
German warships were in Copen-
hagen today, and that 10000 Ger

Largest Warships Lost.


Norway lost her two largest war
ships, the antiquated 4,l66-ton
coast defense ships Norge and Eds
void, and 500 men in the short
lived resistance which preceded the
German capture of Narvik yester-
day morning, according to Nor
wegian refugees reaching Sweden.


The Northern Norwegian ore port
itself, they said, was occupied with
out a fight by German troops who
had previously been brought Sc
cretly into the harbor on whaling
vessels. The refugees gave this ac-
count of the capture:


A Norwegian customs officer
boarded a German whale oil boiler
ship for the usual inspection, but
was prevented by the Germans
from returning to the shore to give
the alarm that the vessel was actu-
ally a troop transport.


Populace Awakened.


The Narvik populace was awak-
ened at dawn by a warning shot
fired from the 40-year-old Norge
when two German destroyers loomed
out OF the dense snow and fog in
the outer harbor.


The Germans replied by torpe-
dong the Norge. Her sister ship,
the Eidsvold, then opened fire. but
was sunk before her two semi-ob-
solete 8.2-inch guns could take ef-
feet.

went down with her colors flying

John Borican, fast-clipping Colored
flyer, representing the Shore A.C. of

nifcent fashion in his triumph in the
thrilling Lapman 1000-yard race at
the Boston Athletic Associations lus-
trious track circus at Boston Garden
Saturday night. laundering over the
boards against razor-keen competi-

"Long John" Woodruff, Olympic

and Don Smith of Maine, the New
England college mile champion. This
event, which was sagging with high
anticipation, was clipped by the swift
striding Borican in two minutes, and
twelve seconds, a new meet and Bos-

Borican called on his reserve and
bristled ahead of "Long john" tearing

clip that brought the 1894 fans to

five yards behind his adversary who
breezed nonchalantly into the final lap.

or victory, and closed in on the artist
runner with his eyes on the tape.
Wayne Rideout also made furious
last lap bid, finishing third behind
Woodruff.

afternoon when the Ricketts, home

sister, Mrs. Gail Dodson, near

SHANGHAI, Jan. ~ (R.-The cap
tain of the British coastal steamer
Wing Sang reported yesterday that
a Japanese naval boarding party
searched and detained his ship for
more than Is hours in apparent
retaliation for the British seizure
of 81 Germans from the Japanese
liner Asama Maru.


1t was reported that the British
intended to protest.


The captain said a japanese de-
stroyer halted the Wing Sang Tues
day night off Matsu Island in the
vicinity of Foochow by firing two
blank shots.


Japanese officers, an Interpreter
and 81 armed men boarded the
ship, inspected the register and
searched the vessel without exam
lining cargo, the captain said.


The 3.560-ton British ship, en-
route from Hong Kong to Shanghai,
then was required to anchor all
night. Next morning the japanese
returned aboard and the captain
said he still refused to sign a state
ment authorizing the search, but
finally did sign one that the jap
anese were orderly and did not
offend passengers. He then was
allowed to proceed.

The glamorous screen star, the
debutante and the girl who works
for living all follow the same path
in their quest for beauty. They
start with the skin. If that is clean
and clear and healthy they have
the perfect foundation for their IA
vorite complexion makeup.


One of the causes of complexion
troubles is piling on layer upon layer
of cosmetics without preliminary
soap and water washing and with
out thoroughly washing off old
makeup before new makeup is ap-
piled. In winter particularly, pores
very quickly become clogged. Soon
the complexion begins to look dingy
and if the practice is continued
blotches and eruptions are almost
inevitable.


The literal and fgurative base of
complexion beauty is thorough soap
and water washing and drying with
clean towels. Unless the skin is
clean and clear and healthy there's
no magic in the makeup kit.

Associated Press Foreign Correspondent.


GALWAY, Ireland, June 1.-The
United States repatriation liner
President Roosevelt, with 824 Ameri-
cans fleeing the dangers of war
aboard her, stood anchored a mile
offshore tonight, ready for an early
sailing tomorrow.


One hundred ten passengers who
had booked standing room" were
told at the last moment that orders
from Washington specified no such
passengers would be permitted to
sail.


Many of those left were without
funds to domicile themselves but
the Galway hotels took them in
despite their lack of ready cash and
it was moot question who would be
responsible for their keep.


There are reports that the liner
Washington. now en- route to Bor-
deaux, would call here to pick up
those who couldn't get passage on
the President Roosevelt.


Children, matrons and perturbed
fathers stood in line for hours to
board tender for the liner.


The majority of the returning
passengers were women and chill
dren. Husbands and fathers stood
on the quay to wave a farewell.
Many strove to hold back their tears
as the tender wormed its way
through the Channel to the liner.


There was little apprehension
about the voyage, and aside from the
natural sorrow at parting the chief
emotion displayed was annoyance
over the rigid examination of lug
gage.


The youngest passenger listed was
Elizabeth Ellen Kennedy of West
Orange, N. j., born only two months
ago. Her father, an Englishman,
stayed behind.


The President Roosevelt arrived
last night and took on 900 tons Of
fuel and other supplies. Customs
men searched all baggage, and ex-
planned that they had been told
that someone was trying to take
out considerable money"


Unoficially, it was explained that
they were looking for explosives.


Americans here were told they
could take out only EGO (about $64)
out Of England, and many spent
their surplus on Irish linens and
laces.

The blossoming cherry trees-a
colorful border around the Tidal
Basin-drew more visitors today, to
add to the thousands who visited
the scene of the annual festival
yesterday.


Today's gray skies continued the
plague of bad weather which hung
over the festival during the week
end. But the weather did not dis
courage Washingtonians and Wis

Park police estimated that more

points.

traffic division reported today the
check indicated an average of 1916

and Constitution avenue; Wiscon-
sin and Massachusetts avenues and

avenue.

LONDON, Feb. 22.-Great Britain
will await Norways answer to Ques-
tions concerning the Altmark, Ger
man prison ship raided last week by
the British Navy in Norwegian
waters, before replying to Norway's
protest, a reliable source said today.


Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax
handed a series of questions last
week end to Norwegian Minister
Erik Colban. These included whether
the Altmark was searched and, if so,
what was found; what action the
Norwegian authorities would have
taken had they found prisoners
aboard, and why Norwegian war
ships were with the German vessel
If she were considered a merchant
man.


Norway, protesting against the
raid in which British prisoners were
freed from the Altmark, demanded
respect for Norwegian neutrality in
the future and said she expected
Britain to hand over the prisoners,
pay damages and give satisfaction. -


Since then Foreign Minister
Halvdan Koht reported to Norway s
Parliament that the Altmark had
the right to navigate in Norwegian
waters, regardless of whether she
carried prisoners, but denied that
Norway knew British prisoners were
aboard the vessel.

CANTON, MASS.-The nationally
known Peter Pan House on Miss
Josephine Crawford's palatial estate
which comfortably houses over one
hundred children will open its private
school program for girls, Sept. 26,


Miss Crawford for the past few
years has successfully operated the
only private school for our girls in New
England. We are well acquainted with
Miss Crawford's beautiful summer
camp whispering Willows" which
always has had a very timely and in
teresting program for girls between the
ages Of six and twelve. Miss Crawford
this year opened a new spacious build
ing for nursery and kindergarten
children from three to five years of age
which she is happy to announce was a
great success. The Peter Pan House
has always had nursery and kinder
garten children included in its school
program each year.


The rates for Miss Crawford's
Private School are the same popular
rates for the summer season. Why not
offer the best physical and mental edu-
cation to our children when the oppor-
tunity presents itself. The oppor-
tunity is here, communicate with Miss
Crawford at the Peter Pan House call
Stoughton 288R or write to her at 808
West Street, Canton, Mass.


Miss Crawford, a great humanitari-
an is not interested in financial affairs,
but is greatly interested in the educa-
tional advancement of our race. Why
not use to the best advantage the
private excellent tutorship offered by
Miss Crawford including a healthy
winter camp program.


A few years back you wouldn't
believe that today we would have such
beautiful summer camps in New Eng
land for our children to enjoy. Per-
haps today you never thought that
your little girls would ever attend a
private school; only the rich could
afford it. Today through the thought
fulness of Miss Crawford your little
girl may have that opportunity of
private tutorship at very little cost.


Let's be a member Of the Crawford
family and give our little girls a real
start toward the best colleges in the
country.

Nawa returned to Honolulu last

yesterday.

force the Germans to strengthen
their defenses with troops needed

fronts.

/. Weakening of the German

Road patrols of militarized po-

Those who have attended the an
nual benefit supper for the Mont
gomery County General Hospital in
past years are anticipating with
pleasure the event this year, Tues
day evening, on the Sherwood High
School grounds at Sandy Spring,
Md.


The suppers have won an enviable
reputation and include many dishes
made from famous old Maryland
recipes. Few who have enjoyed the
beaten biscuits, home-cured hams.
fried chicken, jams and jellies made
In local kitchens forget the repast,
which is served under the auspices
of the Woman's Board of the Hos
pital.


Preparations will be made this
year for more than 1900 suppers, as
1,640 were served last year. Those
who come for other attractions are
expected to swell attendance to
$500. Booths for the sale of candy,
flowers and other articles are set
up each year, and there are pony
rides and amateur theatricals.


200 People to Serve.


More than 200 people will prepare
and serve the food, most of which is
to be prepared the day of the event.


The supper is one of two major
events promoted each year by the
board, the other being the donation
day tea held at the hospital in
December.


Funds raised are used for the up
keep, housekeeping and oversight
of the hospital and nurses home.
The largest annual expenditure is
for linen, and the marking and
mending of these articles is never
ending work.


The new nurses home was COM
pleted in 1888 the Woman's Board
having contributed $6,500 toward its
erection. The board also super
vised its furnishing and decoration,
while individual rooms were fur
nished by the Woman's Club of
Chevy Chase. the Howard County
Auxiliary and the Woman's Demo-
cratic Club of Montgomery County.


Other Clubs Contribute.


For many years bed in the hos
pital has been maintained by the
Woman's Club of Bethesda. The
nursery was furnished by the Wom-
ans Club of Chevy Chase, and new
equipment was added by the Junior
Auxiliary, which also has made i'm
provements and additions to the
delivery room, Office and waiting
room. New equipment for the ac-
cident room was given by the Jun

Chevy Chase Garden Club. The
library is under the management

new books and book cart, from

The Woman's Club of Silver Spring
has been particularly active in sew

of the Supper Committee this year.
and Mrs. Charles G. Tumbleson is
chairman of the Woman's Board.

Two governments with active in
terests in the Paciflc-the United
States and Austraia-drew closer
together today by establishing dip
lomatic relations.


The biggest island of the South
Pacific, hitherto represented in
Washington by the British Ambas-
sador, announced Its first minister
to this country would be Richard
G. Casey, Australia's present Min
lister of Supply.


The step leaves New Zealand the
only British dominion without its
own representation in the United
States. Canada and the Union OF
South Africa have ministers here.


Australian interests in the United
States hitherto have been repre-.
sented by the British Ambassador
and a special Australian counselor
at the British Embassy, Keith
Officer.

Australia has become increasingly
apprehensive over Japan's advances
on the Asiatic Continent and has
been anxious for closer ties with
the United States, the only Western
power with a major navy in the
Pacific.

have been drawn closer together
also by trans-Pacific air travel.

The submarine, in the public view,
has one function, namely. to un-
leash a deadly torpedo. And that
certainly is its most important sin
gle duty. But it has many other
uses, such as in scouting enemy
fleets, observing his ports and coasts,
patrolling home coasts and laying
mine fields Our Navy's submarines
range from about 1000 to 5000 tons,
and the larger craft have substantial
cruising capacity. These ships mount
guns as we'll as torpedo tubes. To

recent legislation.

pletely equipped floating base which
has great cruising range and Is re-
markably fast. The Navy now has
six carrier in service, four are build
ing and eight more have just been

Before analyzing the fleet air arm,

varied ships already described are
by no means all of the Navy's float
ing equipment. There are numerous

cludes both mine sweepers and mine

Europe's widespread gasoline ra-
tioning has ended joy-riding,
doomed bicycle sales, trotted horses
back into the picture and started
American exporters of petroleum
and automotive products worrying
about the future of their markets.


A survey of motor fuel restric-
tions, based on Commerce Depart
ment cables, showed today that
gasoline consumption had been cur
tailed severely and prices and taxes
increased throughout Europe as a
result Of wartime Enforced econo-
mics and transportation hazards.


Whether American petroleum
shipments to belligerents for war
use have increased enough to Offset
reduced civilian consumption is a
question.


In addition to strict rationing, all
European countries are encourag-
ing or requiring utilization of sub
stitutes, including mixtures of alco-
hol with gasoline, gas manufac-
tured from solid fuels, compressed
Illuminating gas carried in bags or
cylinders, and electric batteries.


Faced with inability to secure suf-
ficient gasoline, increased prices and
driving restrictions, thousands of
Europeans have stored their cars
and are using trains, buses, bicycles
or their feet for transportation.


Drivers of automobiles still oper-
ating carry distinctive signs, are sub
ject to police questioning and must
produce vari-colored rationing book
lets or cards at gas pumps to get
their daily scanty allotment.


Many taxi drivers are forced to
accept passengers only for destina-
tions they can reach with the gaso-
line still in their tanks.

Under plans approved by the
Inter-American Development Com
mission, group of American re-
tail experts will 60 to South and
Central America next month to help
Latin American producers build a
new inoustry-supplying American
consumers with the handicraft
merchandise formerly imported from
Germany, Poland, Czecho- -Slovakia
and other European countries.


BY creating a new industry, the
commission, headed by Undersecre-
tary of Commerce Noble, hopes to
increase the cash income of Latin
America, boost its purchasing power
and make it better able to resist
economic penetration by totalitarian
powers


Millions Involved.


Before the war, according to
Commerce Department officials, the
United States imported annually
about $50,000000 worth of handi-
craft goods from Europe. Other
estimates place the value of these
purchases at considerably higher
figure. Since the outbreak of the
war, imports into the United States
from Europe have sharply declined
and American retailers have been
unable in many instances to supply
their customers with handicraft
goods from Europe.


South and Central America have
the raw material and the skilled
workers to produce these goods. In
order to sell their products sue
cessfully in the American market,
Latin American manufacturers,
however, need two things. First,
a knowledge of the type of goods
which will appeal to American
women. who make up the bulk of
the potential purchasers, and sec
ond, an advance forecast, from
American experts, of probable style
trends in the United States.


To Give Style Pointers.


On their forthcoming trip, the
retailers will tell Latin American
manufacturers how they can best
meet the requirements of the Amer
ican market and give them some
pointers on styles, present and fu-
ture. They will also guarantee to
take a definite amount of Latin
American handicraft for sale in
American retail stores.


The handicrafts previously i'm
ported from Europe cover a wide
range. The articles listed by the
Inter- American Development Com
mission include linen damask, crash
luncheon cloths, handmade bridge
and luncheon sets, needlepoint
tapestries, rayon damask, childrens'
sweaters, wicker sewing baskets,
wool bead hand bags. earthenware
dinner ware, lead and semi-crystal
stemware, crystal ash trays, cut
crystal perfume bottles, metal,
stone and wood bookends, women's
novelty shoes and lapel ornaments.


Made as they are by hand, these
and similar handicrafts do not COM
pete in any serious way with Amer
ican industry, according to Federal
officials. Now that imports from
Europe have largely been cut off,
the recently appointed inter-
American Development Commission
sees an excellent opportunity for
Latin American products to take
the place of the merchandise for
merly supplied by Europe.

MACON, Miss. Aug. 24.-Camp
fires burned today on the Noxubee
County Courthouse grounds as In
dian tribesmen assembled here for
the murder trial next week of Wes-

chief.

Rabbit. which State prosecutors say

NEW YORK, Sept. 17.-War-
throttled trade routes into the
Mediterranean got a new lease on
life today with the announcement
by Garcia e. Diaz, shipping agents,
that the steamer Anghyra sailed
yesterday from New York for
Piraeus, Greece and Istanbul
Turkey, and the steamer Patrai left
Piraeus today for New York.


The vessels, sailing under the
Greek flag. are owned by the Greek
company, Hellenic Lines, Ltd.


Cargoes are fully navicerted.


A regular schedule of sailings
will be offered, the agents for the
Greek line said.


Departure of the vessels marked
the resumption of Mediterranean
trade interrupted in mid-June
When Italy entered the war sail
ings under the United States flag
were banned by the Neutrality Act.
War hazards induced other nations
to curtail activity.


On the eastbound voyage the
Anghyra carried general cargo
which included steel. automobiles,
cereals, beans, cocoa and cotton.


Westbound the Patrai will bring
such products as olive oil, tobacco,
Smyrna figs and raisins.


The war risk insurance rate on
the eastbound voyage was said to be
around Is per cent of the cargo's
value. In view of this, the agents
said. future cargoes probably would
be in the high-grade class; that Is.
merchandise on which shipping
costs are in relatively small proper
tion.

downtown restaurant. The smells

titles, but don't fill their plates.

kitchen-din room, where some

double bed and the folding cot. Two
little boys and the oldest girl sleep
on cots in the room back of this,
and in the third room Jack and his
older brother. These persons live
only from day to day, always hop
ing for some unexpected event
like a hearty meal, but not TOO dis
appointed when nothing happens.

her husbands foot was torn of and

ing Saleve Cliff, just across the

Sirens awakened Geneva residents

BY WILLIAM j. HUMPHREYS,


Associated Press War Correspondent.


A SOUTHEAST COAST TOWN,
England, Aug. 22.-Huge ''big ber-
thas" concealed on the French shore
shelled a mile-long British convoy
threading the dangerous English
Channel today, but after minutes
the ships passed through Dover
Straits without apparent casualty"


Observers estimated that at least
100 shells were fired. at a 20-mile
range, and that at times the Ger
man batteries were sending them
over at the rate of one minute.


The bombardment diminished
after the convoy passed Dover.


Then German dive bombers sud-
denly roared out of the East and
began a new attack on the ships.
British guns brought one Of the
bombers down, and the convoy ap-
parently escaped damage.


Fire in Batteries of Four.


The German guns fired in bat
teries of four, and guns along the
French coast all the way from
Calais to Boulogne appeared to be
taking part.


Every time they fired their posi-
tions were betrayed to observers
who noted the blotches of bright
flame from their cordite charges.


Most of the shells, aimed at the
group Of small merchant ships and
its escort Of war vessels, fell into
the sea.


A few seconds after the flashes
were seen, the shells burst near the
ships. The German gunners
changed the range and the shells
fell closer to the convoy. But sub
sequent shells dropped between the
ships and the English shore.


Crowds Gather on Shore.


The explosions shook the ground
on this side of the Channel. Crowds
began gathering on the shore to
watch.


Shortly after it started, two of
the British warships laid a smoke
screen to keep the Germans from
spotting their target and note where
their shells fell.


It was believed here that the
gunners were getting firing range
from Nazi plane flying high in
the skies.


The convoy stretched out more
than q mile, sailing in close to the
towering English cliffs, 20 miles
from the gun emplacements.


While the warships weaved in and
out in the smoke screen, British air
fighters suddenly appeared over
head. There were no German
bombers on hand, however.

water front of all save soldiers,

BOSTON, April 8.-Earnings Of
most meat packers during the cur
rent fiscal year, which began No
vember l, are expected to show con-
siderable improvement over results
in the 1938-39 period, says the
United Business Service in its cur
rent weekly report.


Meat prices, particularly pork, are
relatively low, due to the increase
In supplies. Profltwise, however, this
Is more than offset by larger sales
volumes and more rapid inventory
turnover resulting from greater
consumer demand, due to both i'm
proved family income and reduced
retail meat prices.


The 1899 spring pig crop was 20
per cent larger than a year earlier
and the fall crop showed 16 per
cent gain over 1888 results. This
expansion resulted in total produc-
ton making new all-time high
last year and forced prices down to
the lowest level in five years. Con-
sequently packers were able to build
up inventories last winter at a very
profitable price.


AT the same time expanding con-
sumner purchasing power assures
continued heavy demand for meats
and this, together with probable
heavier exports later in the year,
will enhance packers income and
inventory profit possibilities.

Boxing in Washington was dis
tinguished by the second feather
weight championship fight in the
citys history and the introduction
of mixed matches.


Petey Scalzo and frankie Covelli
met in scheduled 15-round affair
for the National Boxing Association
126-pound crown after that body
withdrew its recognition of Joey
Archibald's title claims. Scalzo won
on technical knockout in the sixth
round of dull, one-sided argument.


Bill Mcdowell and Cocoa Kid
manufactured the first mixed match.
Cocoa winning a decision. Cocoa
enjoyed string of victories before
losing to George Abrams. Charley
Burley, an outstanding Pittsburgh
middleweight, and Henry Armstrong
at that time welterweight champion
were other topnotch Negro ringmen
who appeared here.


Phil Furr's astounding technical
knockout over Steve Mamakos was
the years biggest surprise. The
Golden Greeks stamina was expect
ed to give him the nod over the
ageing Furr, but he fell victim to
PhlPs arroWlike rights and was
dropped no less than seven times
before being led to his corner.


But MamakoS made startling
comeback by twice whipping Milt
Aron, the National Boxing Asso-
cations No. 1 contender for the
world title


In a promotorial way, the period
was marked by the termination OF
a long partnership between Pro-
motor Joe Turner and Matchmaker
Goldie Ahearn after a series OF
financial reverses. Turner appointed
Gabe MenendeZ as his matchmaker
and the pair showed marked prog
reSS.


Jimmy Erwin, who piloted Pete
Sarron to the world featherweight
title several years ago, and who
enjoys a handsome reputation in
the sport, was signed as match
maker by Severine Leoffler for Riv-
erside Stadium, but resigned after
the first two shows failed to strike
a responsive chord at the box office.


Ray Alvis, once one of the games
most influential managers, took over
matchmaking at Riverside with
Ahearn serving as aide de camp, but
also found the financial road beset
with trouble. Ahearn resigned his
position after the second show to
devote his efforts to other interests.

By the Associated Press.


Icy blasts again swept the North.
ern sections of the Nation today.
with temperatures ranging from
freezing to below zero, but relief was
in sight.


The Weather Bureau forecast
rising temperatures in the Plains
States by tonight or tomorrow.


Meanwhile, the number of known
dead in the storm ravaged areas
reached 108, not including 81 missing
sailors.


Eighteen sailors were known to
have perished in Lake Michigan
during the weeks storms. Hopes Of
finding the missing creWmen alive
were virtually abandoned.


Crews of boats that rode out the
gale termed the storm the worst in
their experience. The oil tanker
New Haven Socony reached East
Chicago, Ind, yesterday covered
with ice and extensively damaged.


"All Over Lake Michigan


"We've been through hell" said
Boatswain Frank Myers. And we've
been practically all over Lake Mich
igan."


One lifeboat, a raft and the pilot
house were swept away by the wind
and waves. The ship reached port
with her compass dead, navigation
charts washed away and the radio
out of order, but with all hands safe.


Capt. Robert w. Parsons of the
lake freighter Thomas F. Cole
brought his ship into Milwaukee yes
terday after being swept almost
from one end of Lake Michigan to
the other" Capt. Parsons, veteran
of 30 years on the Great Lakes, said
the storm surpassed any in his men,
ory. The 81 men in the crew were
uninjured, although the boats in
terror was smashed as water crashed
into doors and windows "a feet above
the water line.

By the Associated Press.


Life began for young Mr.. 1910 to-
day, and he liked it.


For the first half dozen hours of
his life the infant year heard MOTH
ing, but laughter and music, saw
nothing but gayety and merry-mak-
ing. That was in America.


He stumbled around in confusion
in Europe-entering the war-strick-
en- countries guided only by the
flash of cannon. The nightly black
out was somber setting, but there
was not much gayety across the At
lantic.


Americans hit the jackpot of hi
larity in the dying hours of 1899
and then spent their enthusiasm
welcoming the New Year.


The celebrators-there were hun
dreds of thousands-aided by the
Sabbath holiday started early and
stayed late for the business at hand.
Some of the merrymakers had their
celebrations slightly curbed because
of the Sunday liquor laws, but for
the most part there were no restric-
tions. and millions of dollars were
spent in night clubs, bars and hotels.


Bowl" Cities to See Games.


Today's football games brought
thousands of visitors to the bowl"
cities and they Joined in the reVelry.
Los Angeles had the widest cele-
bration in decade The central
downtown area was blocked off to
all but pedestrians. The movie
celebrities were at the high-priced
Hollywood and Beverly Hills cafes
and night clubs. Amusement piers
and nearby beach towns were
jammed.


Miami-in the midst of the
Orange Bowl festival-had a riotous
celebration. Harried policemen gave
up efforts to control traffic and
pedestrians. In New Orleans, an
other bowl city, the merrymakers
crowded wide Canal street in horn
blowing jamboree and night clubs
turned away crowds.


New York's Times Square and
Chicago's Randolph and State
streets were massed with horn
tooters and cowbell ringers. The
swank Everglades Club at Palm
Beach had its largest party and
other resort night clubs had sellouts.


States where liquor was not sold
on Sunday included Pennsylvania,
Washington, Colorado, New Mexico,
Utah and Missouri, and celebrations
in some cities in these States were
somewhat hampered. Some cities
observed Saturday night and held
private parties last night.

BERLIN, May 8.-German airmen
were reported today to have made
successful" raids on marching COL
umns Of allied troops near Narvik,
Northern Norway, and to have
scored new bomb hits on two British
cruisers.


The reports were given out by
the German high command, whose
daily communique follows:


Another German air attack on
enemy naval vessels outside Narvik
was carried out. Two cruisers were
hit.


Enemy positions and marching
columns were successfully bonn
barred. One English chaser (pur-
suit plane) was shot down In an
air fight east Of Narvik.


"The situation at Narvik Is un-
changed.


Among large quantities of booty
recently captured In the Andalsnes
region were 460 English tankguns
with ammunition, 40 other guns.
among which were 40 English anti
aircraft guns; go grenade throwers,
355 machine-guns, $500 rifles,
4,500,000 rounds of infantry am
munition and munitions train with
800 tons of ammunition.


"The last vestiges of Norwegian
resistance in South Central Norway
have now vanished. Parts of a
Norwegian infantry regiment sur
rendered at Vinje. A large amount
Of equipment, weapons and explo-
sives was captured there.


"On the west front an attack
south of Saarlautern by enemy
shock troops was repulsed with
heavy loss for the enemy"


DNB, the official news agency, in
supplementary war report, told
Of heavy artillery exchanges, q
French infantry thrust against a
German position and occasional
fights" between patrol units on the
western front.


The agency said French COM
pany attacked the German-held
village of Merten yesterday morn
ing. but was thrown back after
losing between Is and 20 men. One
wounded French corporal who was
taken prisoner died later.


DNB said that in the mountainous
Warndt region there was much
accommodating activity by both sides,
leading to several clashes.


Nazi Patrol Withdraws.


South of Forbach. DNB reported,
a German patrol withdrew fighting
after being attacked by a superior
French force of 10 men. The agen-
cy said the enemy lost several men
in this action but there were no
German losses.


DNB said heavy artillery action
developed yesterday between the
Moselle River and the Palatinate
Forest when enemy batteries
opened fire and German guns re-
Piled.


The agency also asserted that
German planes shot down and re-
ported missing in the Norwegian
campaign did not exceed 80, but that
10 enemy planes were brought down.
1t said enemy assertions that the
Naz air force lost 235 war planes
IN one month obviously was in
tended to weaken the impression OF
German control Of the air over
Norway which even the enemy now
admitted"

wall, but can be most effective

Hold onto your hats, bcys, the
Cincinnati Reds are riding that
roller coaster


The National League champions,
whom everybody said couldn't slump
because they had pitchers who just
couldn't be beaten in succession,
have managed to lose five out of
their last six games.


That kind of travelling has got
be labeled a slump, even if it ends
right there and the Reds start win
ming again. They still have one
claim unshaken. they haven't lost
more than three games in a row
this season.


They dropped one of their dearest
possessions yesterday when the Bos-
ton Bees Inundated them with two
victories, 1913 and 4-3. It was the
first time that Cincinnati has lost
a double header this year. The
champs had won 10 and split hve.


Bees Murderous to Reds.


Before the session yesterday the
last-place Bees had lost nine straight
games. But Stengels lads couldn't
have been any more fearful of play
ing the champions six games in three
days than the Reds were of facing
the Bees.


Boston has been murderous to
the Reds all year and their triumphs
yesterday gave them an even break
for the dozen times the clubs have
met. This made the Bees the only
team in the league over which the
champs don't have an advantage.


They still have double-headers to
play today and tomorrow and the
Reds may be able to recoup their
record.


The only runs they were able to
get of Nick Strincevicks six-hit
hurting in the first game came on
a three-run homer by Frank Nc
Cormick. The second game went
IL innings before the Bees finally
loaded the bases and Rookie Chet
Ross singled home the deciding run.


Dodgers Are Set Back.


The Reds difficulties would have
been more costly except that the
Brooklyn Dodgers lost and the
third-place New York Giants divided
double -header.

edged out the Dodgers, 40, with
busy Claude Passeau striking out the
last two batters in rescue act that
gave Larry French his 11th victory
of the year.

In the ninth inning, to give the
Giants a 5-4 victory over the st.
Louis Cardinals in their first game.
but Carl Doyle checked the New

game in front as both the Tigers
and the Cleveland Indians were

Joe Cronin hit for the cycle-a
home run, triple, double and single
to guide the Boston Red Sox to a
1873 triumph over the Tigers. Jimmy
Foxx also hit his 23d homer and
young Dominic Di Maggie smacked
one with two on to rout Buck New
som, although the leagues leading

game that was SCARED by nine

CHUNGKING, China (Corre-
spondence of the Associated Press -
Chungking's police are striving
against strong popular opposition
to make this wartime capital safer
from bombing raids, already re-
sumed, which killed several thou
sand civilians last year.


Because existing air raid shelters
can accommodate fewer than U.s.
600 persons, police program calls
for departure of all "unessential"
residents. BY the middle of April,
however, not more than $4,000 had
taken advantage of inducements
such as free transportation and
5000 low-rent houses built in out
lying suburbs.


After the seasonal cloud bank set
tied over the upper Yangtze Valley
last fall Chungking nearly forgot
the danger from the air. Residents
who fled during the air raids
f1ocked back by the tens of thou
sands, shops reopened and the
theater and restaurant business
doomed.


With the springtime lifting of
the fog and the approach of the

Generalissimo Chaing Kai-shek,
stated to enforce a program of
compulsory removal of civilians, de-

mated wintertime population of
100000.

several raids on Chungking's out
skirts and towns in Szechwan Prov

NEW YORK, Nov. 4.-Pro foot
balls major sectional titles were
lust about settled today, with new
champions imminent in both East
ern and Western Divisions OF. the
National League.


The Chicago Bears all but
clinched the Western crown by
whipping the defending titlehold-
ers, the Green Bay Packers, for the
second time, while Washington's
Redskins continued their undefeated
march to the Eastern crown by
chalking up their seventh straight
victory at the expense Of the Pitts
burgh Steelers.


Record Crowd Sees Game.


A record-breaking pro crowd for
Chicago, As ,434, saw the mighty
Bears win, 14-7, when the champs
failed to capitalize on any Of five
scoring chances in the second half.
Joe Maniaci rushed over for the
Bears first touchdown in the OPEN

hit Don Hutson with an 11-yard
touchdown pass to tie the score

the half was over, the Bears second
team pounded As yards for the

two of their remaining four games

The New York Giants chung to
their Eastern title hopes by beating
the Brooklyn Dodgers, 10-7; Ward
Cuffs 25-yard field goal in the sec

the Giants and Dodgers scored
touchdowns in the last quarter, the

Barnum to Hank Soar and the losers

climaxed a 7o-yard drive. The de-
feat practically eliminated Brooklyn
from title consideration and left

uation of being forced to win all Of
their last four games while the Red
skins are losing theirs.

victims for third place in the West
ern Division. Sharing the honors

In the building of logs and planks
hewn 10000 years ago, Prof. Gryaz-
nov of Moscow, Russia, found at the
foot Of the Altai Mountains, so feet
deep in the ice, 10 sorrel horses sad
died and bridled, ready for that last
journey their masters never called
on them to take.


They were not skeletons, but flesh
and blood horses with every hair of
their coats intact, even their eyes,
the blood in their veins, and the
half-digested remains of their last
meal in their stomachs. For hun
dred centuries these horses, en-
balmed in the eternal frost of North
ern Siberia, have stood like marble
statues, their frozen eyes looking
for the summons that never came.

NEW YORK, Aug. 26.-The cot
ton market had another quiet week,
with price movements small. With
the advent of the new crop spot
prices have declined by close to !
cent a pound in the last two months,
but prices of new crop futures have
held within a range of about "a
cent. During the last week active
future deliveries on the New York
Cotton Exchange showed no net
change to an advance of 4 points.


The new crop is later than usual
but pickings and ginning are rap
idly expanding. That has resulted
in increased hedge selling in flu
fureS.


Crop weather during the last two
weeks was generally favorable Trade
ideas as to the size of the current
crop probably are somewhat higher
than the Government estimate is
sued August 8. However. this has
had no pronounced effect on price
levels since the trade assumes that
any excess over the Government
estimate would 60 into the new loan
stock.


On the theory that new crop cot
ton going into the Government loan
stock would not be available next
spring and summer except at prices
much above those now prevailing
for deliveries at that time, there was
some buying of the more distant fu-
ture deliveries early in the week
Such buying did not carry through
however, and the market Subse-
quently dropped


The Government announcement
of new export subsidy rates on cot
ton products effective August 26,
much higher than present rates,
probably would have had a bullish
effect in normal times. The market
did not respond, however, because
of uncertainty as to the European
situation and the very poor outlook
for cotton exports.


Exports continue to establish new
low records for several decades.


Trading on the New York Cotton
Exchange during the week ending
last Thursday totaled 211,000 bales

By the Associated Press.


GJOSS1NGFJORD, Norway, Feb
20.-While Norway, Germany and
Britain wrangled over the status
Of the German prison ship Alt
mark, the ships captain frankly
acknowledged his vessel served as
a German naval auxiliary.


In eulogizing the seven German
sailors killed when British sailors
boarded the Altmark Friday night
to remove British prisoners, Capt.
Heinrich Dau declared:


You were not of the German
Navy, but you served your country
bravely and venturesomely by Civ
ing that navy auxiliary service, by
supplying its needs far from home" i"


After speaking at funeral services
yesterday, Capt. Dau told news
men his ship was just outside Port
Arthur, Tex, with a cargo of oil
when the war started. The Alt
mark, he said, remained at sea
transferring fuel to Nazi raiders and
taking aboard Seamen taken from
destroyed British ships.


The Altmark's sailors who stood
knee-deep in snow around the
swastika- -draped coffins in a Nor
wegian graveyard at Hauge clearly
showed the effects of their long
months at sea. Their clothing was
tattered and torn, and few wore
anything resembling uniforms.
, In describing the attack on the
Altmark, Fourth Officer Jorchin
Wieshert said the Germans were
unarmed, but that the British
boarding party carried pistols, rifles
and machine guns.


German officers showed corre-
spondents the marks of about
dozen bullets on their ship.


The ships officers said the British
lined up many of the German sea-
men, apparently with the intention
of transferring them to British war
ships as prisoners, but changed
their minds at the last minute.


Before leaving the ship, the Ger
mans said, several British prisoners
thanked the Altmark's officers for
the treatment they had received.

Stores that set fashions are dis

IT'S the contrasting neck details of a
trock that can make her look pretty
and most women would rather
look pretty than just smart.


Dresses for daytime are trimmed
with beaded revers, embroidered
collars, and contrasting neckline
borders. There are brightly colored
beads, make-believe gems, gold and
jet sequins and beads-all softening
the severity of plain necklines, all
adding a feminine sparkle to simple
dark dresses.


Restraint is used in these touches;
collars and revers are small, band
ings and borders are narrow. A
little sparkle can do a big trick.
Alencon and Venise laces, brightly
colored velveteen or bengaline coll
lars are being used to brighten basic
dresses which are such excellent
folls for the new neckwear. If a
woman wants to look pretty, there
is delicate pink neckwear to give
a fiattering glow. For gaiety and
freshness, there's red. Little red
velveteen or pique touches make
stunning accents on blue, gray or
black basic dresses. Some of these
little collars in red are beaded in
jet scrolls to give a further con-
trast.


For real elegance, the newest and
smartest idea in fattering neckwear
is the beaded deep yoke of fine Alen-
con or corded Venise lace. Charles
Armour, famous American design
er, started this fashion with his SIM
ply draped afternoon dresses, the
set-in beaded lace yokes being the
only trimming. These designs have
started the vogue for separate plas-
irons and yokes of lace which are
elaborately beaded to dress up a
black gown.


For femininity nothing has yet
been devised to equal the softening
effect given by lovely neckwear
which is wisely chosen.

LINDING snow, driven as only the
irresistible winds of the Western
- plains can drive it, swirled over
pair of figures plunging desperately
along narrow country road in the
Texas Panhandle.


In his arms Noel King, Of Guymon,
Oklahoma, carried his two-year-old
daughter Loretta. Behind him floun-
dered Mrs. King, trying frantically to
keep the cold from seven-months-old
Oracle Fay.


They had left their car lying on its
side in the roadside ditch. 1t was
already beginning to lose its identity
as thick snow clouds drifted over it.
Ahead, they hoped. would be shelter
from the worst blizzard the area had
experienced in a decade.


The couple struggled forward as the
sobs of their frostbitten babies filled
their hearts with terror and their limbs
with new strength. Hours later, after
four heartbreaking miles of exhaust
ing, knee-deep snow, they staggered
into an oil-pipe-line booster station.


There they found food and warmth
Il food for all but Oracle Fay. for she
required a special formula. And there
was no doctor to minister to Loretta,
whose arms were frostbitten from ell
bow to fingertips. All four we're suffer
ing from cold and exposure, but it
would be days before help could reach
them.


A telephone call to Bartlesville,
Oklahoma, brought first-aid sugges-
tions; the mother and father and sta
ton attendant worked over the chill
dren, praying that help would come
before Loretta's arms became infected.
The attendant telephoned Perryton.
Texas, the nearest town, and asked
that help and medicine be sent as soon
as the twenty-four miles could be
traversed.


Psnyton's Flying Cowboy


lWO hours later the drone of an
airplane penetrated the roar of the
storm. Overhead, circling carefully,
was Texas's first ski-equipped airplane.
With it came life, for Harold Hawk,
Perryton's flying cowboy. brought
medicine and the baby's special for
mula.

man of thirty two, had heard of their
precarious plight and had flown

AMSTERDAM, July 6.-The Ger
man military commander in Holland,
Air Corps Gen. Friedrich Christian
sen, issued a sharp communique
today accusing the Dutch Army and
population of an unloyal attitude to-
ward the German occupation.


He said the character of British
bombing attacks proved Britain was
obtaining information from the
Dutch side.


The communique warned against
any demonstration in favor of the
Dutch government.


Gen. Christensen said the free
dom granted by Fuehrer Adolf
Hitler had been misused and that
the military had not shown proper
discipline to the German Army of
occupation.


In connection with his charge
that the British air force had been
aided by information from the
Dutch, Gen. Christensen said all
actions would be investigated and
that the guilty persons would be
punished according to German law.
Such actions would be considered
high treason, punishable by death.

The Cincinnati Reds are making

them to repeat for the National
League pennant look good


At the end of the first water

are at the top of their circuit with
three games won and none lost, but
that isn't the whole story.


They never have been behind In
any OF the games. Their three prize
pitchers have gone the full nine
inning route in every case. No more
than l run has been scored against
them in any contest. The team
hasn't committed single error.


The 6-1 depth bomb they set off

day was the most emphatic indica-

that they are travelling the same
trail they took year ago.


They made mockery of the chal-

Walters, who kept the Cards shut

and used is pitchers, including

games and three days in a row.
! One week doesn't make a season.
but a champion has to win approxi-

counts just as much as one in
August or September.

ROME, July 6.-The Italian high
command announced today that
two enemy attacks with strong
forces" were repulsed at the forts
of Capuzzo and Birsleman in North
ern Africa.


Fighting by fast-striking columns
and airplanes was reported by the
high command in Libya, near the
Egyptian frontier.


British air raids on the Sicilian
bases of Augusta, Palermo, and
Catania was said to have resulted
in little damage.


Meanwhile, the Italian cabinet
approved an appropriation of $685.
100000 lire ($13,250,O0O for the i'm
provement of naval bases.


The cabinet, meeting with Pre-
mier Mussolini, also approved a
series of minor wartime measures
which included provisions for re-
imbursing private citizens with gov
eminent bonds for war damages.


War pensions for injured civilians
also were authorized.


Marshall Rodolfo Graziani was
appointer governor general of Libya

placed former Governor and Air

plane crash recently, as commander

ternazionai said Marshal Graziani's
succession to Marshal Balbo meant
the beginning of 'wide-scale oper-
ations to re-establish italian domi-
nance" in African Mediterranean
territories, which have been part

posed law compelling moving pic
ture theaters to show war propa-
ganda films

diplomatic because Premier Musso-

ton of the German government.


The latest parley of the axis allies
was the Munich meeting of Mus
solini and Adolf Hitler June 16.
when they drafted terms for armi-
stices with France.

heard nothing of reports that King
Carol of Rumania was coming to
Rome to consult the Italian gov
eminent.

unusually hard conditions"

TOXIC, March 22.-Foreign Min
lister Hachiro Arita told the Jap
anese Diet today that Japan will
not put any obstacles in Germany's

or America" during the European
war.


Arita added that Japan was Ger

A member of the Diet, expressing

Europe by United States Undersec-
retary of State Sumner Welles were
predicated on the assumption the
allies would be defeated, asked Arita:


Don't you think Japan should
discard her policy of uninvolvement
and openly side with Germany and
Italy?"


Arita replied that Japan was solely
concerned with the construction of a
new order in East Asia and that
entry into the European conflict was
inadvisable

ister's remarks. Naval Minister
Admiral Zengo Yoshida asserted
that I'VE are going to dispose of the
China incident with out eyes wide
open to the world situation"
Cooperation With Axis Suggested.


Arita delivered his statement after
an interpellator had asserted that
the government, while mouthing
phrases about uninvolvement. has
promised Britain not to transport
German nationals or armament
homeward,' and asked:


"Since both Germany and Italy
appear to have recognized Japan's
aims in East Asia should not Japan
take some positive measures to CO.
operate with them?"


Both Admiral Yoshida and War
Minister General Shunroku Hata in
dorsed Arita's reply, but Hata
added:


However. we will not countenance
any interference in the East Asia
fight by either the British-Ameri-
can or Italian German blocs"


Earlier War Minister Gen. Shun-
roku Hata had announced that Gen.
eralissimo Chang Kai-shek's

men and that "the holy war; for
"a new order in Asia" would con-

Appearing before the Budget

he said that neither the formation
of the new Japanese-supported
Wang Ching-wei government for
China nor the lnsistence of foreign
powers on the validity of the Nine
Power Treaty would deter the Japa-
nese Army from the completion Of
its mission.


During the same session Arita re-
iterated that the latest United States
credit to China ($200O0,0OO) was
"disagreeable' to Japan, but he said
that Toxic had no intention OF
taking counter measures. He ex-
pressed belief that Congress would
not agree on an embargo on goods
to Japan.


"The ultimate purpose of the cur
rent China affair."" Gen. Hata told

expansion.

Apparently these products are

ings, or from money received from

This condition raises justifiable

The Greek governments an
nouncement of special victory post
age stamp bearing the legend Koritza
SymbolizeS the most amazing mill
tary exploit of the present war. In
exactly twenty-five days, the rela-
lively small Greek Army has not only
broken the sudden onrush of Italy's
numerically superior and heavily
mechanical war machine but has
Stormed the main italian frontier
base with its vast stores of arms and
other supplies Moreover, the cap
ture of Koritza is merely the out
standing feature of general often
sive all along the front which is
driving deep into Albania at sew
eral points. Already, ArgirocaStro,
Italy's chief supply base in Southern
Albania, and Porto Edda, Italy's only
debarkation point in that region,
are menaced by the oncoming
Hellenes. Nowhere do the Italians
seem capable of making a stand, and
their morale is obviously deterior-
ating. Athens dispatches speak of
$4,000 prisoners in the Koritza sector
alone, together with captured arms
and munitions sufficient to equip
several fresh divisions of Greek
reServists.


Unless the Italian high command
can somehow manage to stem the
onrushing tide, the world may be
about to witness a colossal military
disaster, with the expulsion of Italy
from Albania and the destruction of
an army numbering at least 100000
men. Every day, the Italian situation
becomes graver. Anglo-Greek war
fleets menace Italian communica-
tons across the Adriatic Sea; Anglo
Greek air forces blast ports of de-
barkation and Strafe Italian troops
and transport over Albanian noun
tain roads. The wild Albanian tribes,
bitterly hostile to the Italian occu-
patton of their country, are already
forming guerrilla bands fired by the
lust for vengeance and loot. Incl
dentally, Albania contains a strong
Greek minority which welcomes the
Greek troops as liberators and aids
them in every way.


The chief factor which may pre-
vent the Greeks from fully exploiting
their glorious victory seems to be
not italian resistance but the grow
ing German-Bulgar threat against
Greeces northeastern frontier, Many
of Greece's best troops must be kept
there, to man the strong defense line
erected against the chronic Bulgarian
threat. When the war with Italy
began, Greece probably did not have
more than 10000 first-line troops.
Captured Italian equipment will pre-
sumably enable Greece to call to
active service many more reserviSts
from pool of trained manpower
running as high as 100000 Also, the
very magnitude of Greek successes
will doubtless spur Britain to take
chances by diverting from its Near
Eastern strongholds more materiel
and even men.


All these are bright spots in the
picture. The darker side is the black
cloud of German-Bulgar power loom
ing on the northern horizon. But
one thing is sure: Even though that
thundercloud bursts in a torrent
which sweeps Greek resistance aside,
the triumph and its fruits will be
German. The military strength and
prestige of Fascist Italy seem to be
utterly Debated

The slightly crippled but climbing
Washington Eagles, ebony -hued
nags of the Eastern Amateur
Hockey League renew their pursuit
Of first place tonight at Riverside
Stadium, meeting the lowly, pesky
Jersey Skeeters.

fourth Of what they hope will be

leads of the Baltimore Orioles and.

night in Baltimore, is in a position

Of the second-place Rovers, for the
Orioles have played four more
games than either New York or
Washington.

The Eagles. by splitting even in
the four games they must make up,

tonight would trim Baltimore's mar

Sunday, while Knipfel has reinjured

Johnny McTeer sub for Knipfs

Chiefly responsible for the Skeet-

NEW YORK, Dec. 26.-The Ger
man liner Hamburg, once called the
floating athletic field" may have
been sunk while operating as q
raider off the Portuguese coast
Capt. Joel Comes of the freighter
Concalo Vehlo said today.


Capt. Comes said on his arriva
here that he had sighted an empty
lifeboat bearing the name Ham
burg 200 miles due east of the
Azores December IL.


The 22,117-ton Hamburg was laid
up at Hamburg after an exciting
fight from New York wnen the wal
began. British warships sighted her
carrying French Line colors, but
she escaped in fog.


Built in 1926, she normally carried
crew Of 440 men and had accom-
modations for 1,151 passengers.


Capt. Cornelius Arundel of the
British freighter Haxby, which was
sunk by raider off Bermuda, said
recently that the raider was a huge
ship equipped for three-year voy-
age of mine-laying and ship sinking.


Shipping men then believed that
she might have been the Hamburg
or her sister ship, the Deutschland.

BERN, SWITZERLAND, Oct. 81
P).-British long-range bombers
bound for Northern Italy thundered
high over Swiss territory last night
and early today for the first time
since September 5.


An army communique said Swiss
anti-aircraft guns fired at the planes
and there were alarms just before
and just after midnight in Bern,
Zurich, Geneva and other cities of
Western and Central Switzerland.


The planes came from the north
west, crossing the Jura Mountains.


After a series of violations of neu-
trail Swiss territory by British bomb
ers during August and the first week
in September, the British govern
ment was said to have promised that
its aviators would be instructed to
keep from crossing the Swiss from
tier


The army communique said:


During the night of october 20
to 81 our territory was violated
many times by English aviators.
These planes crossed the Jura from
tier, flying in southeasterly direc-
ton, in many places. Our anti
aircraft batteries opened fire on the
invading planes"
