Hitler's legions wiped out and
scattered untold thousands of fam
lilies as they crushed through Po-
land, but to the OStrower brothers
they caused the end of a 29-year
separation.


In fearful but happy reunion on
the Union Station platform this
morning. DR.. Meyer Ostrower,
Washington optometrist, and his
wife and daughter met his brother,
Alexander Ostrower, who, with his
wife and daughter, fled his Warsaw
law Office just ahead of the Nazi
invaders.


The train from Chicago which
was bearing the three on the last
lap of their long journey was late
and DR.. Ostrower, his wife Jean
and 18-year-old daughter Henrietta
waited for more than an hour.


When the train did pull in DR..
Ostrower's face did not light up
until the last three persons came
down the platform. One was a man,
stocky, well dressed, the other a
woman, slso smartly dressed, and
the third little girl-each carrying
a suitcase, each looking around with
wide-eyed expectation.


Recognition Is Mutual.


The brothers recognized each
other at once. They did not say
anything, but walked quietly, up to
each other, shook hands and kissed
on the cheeks. In sii~ace the wives
embraced, and then the spell was
broken as DR.. Ostrower's daughter
Henrietta picked up 7-year- old
Irene, her new" cousin, kissed her
and burst into flood of tears.


I'm so glad you're here" she
sobbed. That was too much for the
others. All cried.

banks of the Yangtze River yester-

bassador Nelson T. johnson and
Rear Admiral William Glassford
and other American officials.


The incident occurred, the Jap
anse said. about 20 miles above
Wuhu. The gunboat was coming
down river from Hankow.


The Japanese said Japanese
transport was about 500 yards up the
river from the Luzon and it was i'm
possible to tell at which ship the
Chinese were firing as shrapnel fell
around both.


Mr.. Johnson was returning from

commander of the American
Yangtze patrol.


Others aboard the gunboat in
cluded Maj. William Mayer, military
attache, and Maj. James McHugh,

sought to take advantage of the
presence of the American craft by
launching a bombardment against

NEW YORK, Nov. 22-Turkey,
cranberry sauce and other "fxin's"
were bought this year more plenti-
fully than last in the States cele-
brating the Thanksgiving holiday
this week, the weekly trade survey
of Dun & Bradstreet, Inc, revealed
today.


Retail merchants also saw early
nibbling at Christmas gift offerings,
although most stores have not yet
started to push Yule merchandise


The review said:


Gold weather gave impetus to
the seasonal upswing at retail, en-
abling many merchants to chalk up
sales gains over the preceding week
despite the inclusion in that period
of exceptionally good Armistice Day
results


Reports from the 80 States cele-
brating Thanksgiving this week ~
dicated increases in food volume
over year ago and unusually sat
isfactory response to special promo
tions of table accessories.


Gift Buying Starts.


Although the holiday shopping
season was not yet officially opened,
city stores reported strong early
interest in gift purchases: buying
extended over wide variety of
merchandise, including handbags,
lingerie, costume jewelry, hosiery
and occasional furniture pieces.


THE improvement in retail turn
over in the past two weeks has
usually been more marked in win
ter clothing than in any other
regular lines. Furs, coats, heavy
underwear, hosiery and gloves are
said to have sold in substantial vol
ume. In children's wear depart
ments snow suits and Logging sets
have rolled up sizable totals


Despite these gains in wearing
apparel, retailers report that home
furnishings lines still make by far
the best relative showing. This
week heavy purchasing of china,
glass, silverware and linen in pre-
Thanksgiving promotions added to
brisk sales of furniture and floor
coverings.


Compared with the correspond
ing period last year, the total vol
ume of trade was estimated to 10
per cent higher. This was broader
margin of gain than a week ago de-
spite the fact that the automobile
trade, now against the peak sales
period of 1899, was no longer chalk
ing up the exceptional year-to-year
increases of october and early No
vember.


New England Active.


Regional sales gains were broad
cast this week in New England, in
the North Central and in the South
ern States. Trade in the North
west still felt the effects of last
weeks blizzards, but volume main
tanned a slight advance over last
year.


For the seven major regions of
the country, percentage changes
above the 1899 level we're as follows:
New England, 6 to II; East, to 8;
Middle West, to 10; South and
Southwest, 9 to Is; Northwest, to
4; Pacific Coast, to 7.'


Wholesale buying, the report said,
appeared to be mostly for the
balancing of stocks New business
was small. There was reordering of
some cold weather items and some
small retailers were placing late
Christmas gift orders.


Relatively few buyers were in
wholesale trade centers, the review
found. and those appeared to be
principally concerned with getting
delivery on merchandise already
ordered. Shipments on old orders,
however, were mostly going out on
schedule.

able speculation in trade circles.


Last weeks approximately 122, 900

cess of retail demand, despite the

the aggregate volume undoubtedly

Trade authorities have been OBJ
serving for more than a fortnight
that tapering of in factory out
put was about due, but there has

leveling off would take place. The
trade has begun to speculate upon

can be maintained and to what

servers say this is wholly probable,
but. they question the capacity of
the new car market to absorb that
volume.


Even with the increased buying
power expected to result from ex-
panded employment, they say. there
will be large inventory of used
cars to be liquidated along with
the heavy factory output.


The belief prevails in some quar-
tiers, however, that the production
division of the industry has deter
mined to keep a certain volume
ahead of actual demand and that
the leveling off will not come until
very definite slackening in present
new-car demand appears.
Whether that is anything more
than guess is yet to be demon
Strated.


Output of the automobile fac
tories this week, according to
Wards Reports, Inc, will to-
tai 102,340 cars and trucks, re-
duced chiefly by the Thanksgiving
holiday. Last weeks assemblies
numbered 120,943, highest level since
the summer of 1887. A year ago this
week 1880 vehicles were completed.
Wards said that production would
turn upward next week, when five
day schedules become general again.
but added that the levels of earlier
November would not be reached.

Is this the same wind blowing east.
Upon the stiffened bones of steel?
This wind once combed the hair of


corn,


But now factory ticks her heel.
This wind once laid her cool hands on
The golden urge of rye and wheat.
Now her sad litany is heard
In the rude squalor of a street.
Vulgarity of city steel,
And smoke stacks of blasphemy,
Reach for her riveted thighs, and feel
Freedom in her impotency.
This wind once combed the hair of


corn,


And quenched the thirst of western


hills,


Now silent lies her harvest song
In the thunderous, grinding mills.
Her amber thighs and starburnt hands
Embrace the thieving pouch of


death,-
Which hold this secret contraband:
Bones and blood and riveters' breath.


MARY AHLQUIST.

baSsador, acting for New Zealand;

lister, and Richard G. Casey, Austral-
ian Minister.

April 2 between the United States
and the Union of South Africa.

Mrs. Mary Van zandt Morgan, 80,
widow of Dr. Edwin Lee Morgan
and daughter of Capt. Nicholas
Biddle Van Zandt, died Wednesday
at the Louise Home, 1900 Massa-
chusetts avenue NV. Mrs. Morgan
was lifelong resident of Wash
ington.


Surviving is her sister. Mrs. Jean
Cabell O'Neill Herbert of New York
City. Mrs. Herbert, who wrote under
the name of Jean Cabell ONeill,
was correspondent for the Brook
lyn Eagle during Gen. Pershing's
punitive expedition in Mexico in
1914 and later wrote historical ar
ticles for the Associated Press.


Funeral services were arranged for
$3.50 o'clock this afternoon at the
chapel in Oak Hill Cemetery, with
burial following in the Van Zandt
plot there.


Mrs. Morgan's grandfather, for
whom her father was named, was
the first Government historian in
Washington. The elder Van Zandt
married sister in-law of President
Madison. Her father, a naval officer,
left the service to fight for the
Confederacy.

ANNAPOLIS, Md, Aug. 19-
Washington regatta riders who sell
dom miss a Chesapeake Bay race
were rewarded for their consistency
after two trying days of competi-
ton in the fifth annual Annapolis
Yacht Club regatta, which ended
here yesterday in a last squirt OF
light airs and bright sun.


Annapolis Yacht Club trophies
presented at the club late yester-
terday included a first place for
R. Ernest Covert, a second for Clark
Daniel and third for Col. Jack
Jacobs, all Washington sailors, who
made a clean sweep of the comet
division.


Ralph Youngs of Alexandria, Va,
was presented the top prize in the
little penguin class after nosing out
13-year-old Phelps Hunt of Wash
ington.


Washingtonians who came
through with second place trophies
were Jack thinner, 20-foot Division
I; Henry Strong. star class, and
Prentice Edrington, 2O-foot Divi-
sion II.


Egret Places Big Boats.


Light airs and successive rain
squalls, which marked the week end
racing, persisted through the morn
ing's final races for the smaller
classes, while the larger cruising
and racing yachts-racing out in
The bay-Were favored with a light
northerly in the afternoon.


The fast cutter Egret sailed by
c. Porter Schutt of Wilmington, Del,
captured the major honors in the
big fellows, winning the Annapolis
Y. c. Trophy for the first yacht to
finish in the cruising division and
another for first boat in Glass B.


Uncle Sans middies, sailing their
44-foot yawls built last year,
brought their Alert and Intrepid
into second and third positions in
Glass B on corrected time. The big
ketch Vamarie, also of the Naval
Academy, won Class A.


Covert Pressed in Win.


Covert, who has been leading
comet sailor at nearby regattas this
summer, was hard pressed for his
No position, finishing only three
points, in final tally ahead Of
Daniel. The latter nosed Covert out
for first place in the final race by
less than boats length following
a see-saw battle in battling airs and
head tides.


The Capital Yacht Club skipper,
however, had saved enough points
from Saturdays two heats to main
tain his lead.


Young Hunt, tied with Youngs at
the beginning of the day, found the
light going too much for him. He
broke out oars to paddle home, but
with sufficient points over his nearest
rival, Hunt took second prize.


Commodore Pete H. Magruder Of
ficiated at the pres entation.

By the Associated Press.


LONDON, April 20.-The allies,
squaring away for major opera
tions" against German forces in
Norway, proudly announced today
their troops had reached the new
battle-ground without a single life
being lost.


"This achievement proves more
than anything else the complete
control the allied fleets have over
sea routes" said the Press Asso-
citation, authoritative news agency.


The numbers landed were held
secret (though Swedish dispatches
said two British and one French
divisions reached the west coast
Of Norway, but the press said, Day
after day our transport ships have
carried heavy artillery, tanks and
army equipment together with
thousands of troops over 400 miles
of sea to ports in Northern Norway
without mishap."


French Already in Action.


France disclosed that her troops
had landed at several points in Nor
way.


Soon after military spokesman
said a French expeditionary force
landed yesterday and already has
taken part in engagements" au-
thorities said the first landing of the
French in the north was followed by
successive landings at various other
points.


The number of troops involved
and details of their movement north
we're not given though some sources
estimated there were 10000 men in
the landing party first announced.


Military observers expressed the
opinion that the allies strategic
position in Norway was considerably
improved by the past weeks opera
tions which saw syncroniZed attacks
from sea and air on German bases.


Nazis May Have $4,000.


There were no official estimates
of allied troops in Norway, but Scan
dinavians said Germany had from
10000 to $4,000 soldiers there.


London commentators insisted the
Germans would encounter serious
difficulties in supplying food and
arms for their large forces but that
the allies, due to naval superiority,
could pour reinforcementS and sup
plies to their troops by sea.


Swedish frontier dispatches indi-
Gated allied and Norwegian forces
were massing for a double -barreled
Trondheim. after the landing of
British troops described as picked
soldiers fitted especially for noun
tain fighting in the rugged western
region.


Reports of initial clashes in the
Trondhelm area were unconfrmed
by the War Office, which thus far
has issued only two communiques
totaling % words on the subject
saying that the British troops have
landed and that operations are
proceeding"


Expect Drive to Take Months.


Britain's chief strategist, First
Lord of the Admiralty Winston
Churchill, indicated in a speech
last night that the allies expect the
Norwegian campaign to take some
months, Welcoming home survivors
of naval warfare off the Norwegian
coast, Mr.. Churchill told them they
were the vanguard of allied armies
which will use this summer to
purge and cleanse the soil of the
Vikings, the soil of Norway, from
the filthy pollution of Nazi tyranny"


Diplomatic quarters, meanwhile,
appeared to take more serious view
of Premier Mussolini's "saber-rat-
Ting" though the recently pro-Ger-
man tone of the Italian press slack
ened somewhat yesterday.


The Times, which frequently re-
fleets British government opinion,
bluntly replied to Italian press at
tacks with the assertion Britain and
France have both the power and
determination to intervene forth
with" If called on to defend the in
dependence of small country.


The Times pointedly added that
the allies instant reply to the at
tack on Norway has made it i'm
possible to suppose they would re-
main inactive in the face of an as
sault upon the integrity or inde-
pendence of any Balkan nations"

Chuck another line coach on the
fire. Throckmorton, and we'll cele-
brate Georgetown's 26-12 victory
over Waynesburg last night at Grif-
fifth Stadium-if that calls for q
celebration.


Didn't look as though there would
be anything to yell about for while,
rdid it? What happened? Well,
everybody undereStimated Waynes-
burg from the waterboy to the towns
leading grid expert and Georgetown
wasn't ready for the blistering brand
Of football thrown at it. AS a mat
ter of fact it wasn't ready for a fast
game of spin -the-bottle, mentally
speaking.


Certainly the boys were warned
about Waynesburg Jack Hagerty
and his aides talked themselves blue
in the face, wagged warning fingers
and showed them past performance
records but the squad thought they
were practicing for a hog calling
contest and laughed it off. Waynes-
burg beat the greatest team in
Georgetown's history? C'mon, pal,
act your age


Hoya's Line LifeIess.


Well, that wasn't the greatest
Hoya team out there last night nor
even a fair imitation. If anybody
wanted to press the matter they
could have the squad arrested for
impersonating. The line didn't
charge-simply leaned against op-
posing linemen as though very. very
tired, and the blockers seemed to
be working for Waynesburg. The
secondary hung back rather shvlv
waiting for its name to be called
before rushing in TO plug a gaping
hole or collar stray ball carrier.
And the way Waynesburg shook
loose potential pass receivers, tch,
tch.


But enough of criticism. George
town paid for its sins-paid through
the nose. Fullback Jim Castiglia is
in the hospital with a torn ilium
muscle and will be out at least two
weeks; Augie Lio's right knee Is
pulled up like penny balloon, Mike
Kopcik has charley horse, Jules
Koshlap is hobbling around on a
twisted ankle, Lou Ghecas is nurs-
ing couple of bruised ribs and the
entire squad has fine assortment
of bumps and black eyes. 1t was not
exactly tea party.


Three Georgetown touchdowns do
not appear in the summary because
they were nullified by penalties and
that was the blow that almost killed
poor Poppa. One came early in the
fray-Kopcik taking fast peg from
Koshlap and going over unmolested.
Another happened in the last few
seconds when Bill Mclaughlin
gathered in a Waynesburg pass and
galloped half the fields length to
pay dirt. Nice plays that didn't
mean a thing.


Kopcik, Perpich Okay.


Kopcik, incidentally, shared what
honors the line receives with George
Perpich, a rookie tackle. Mike made
catches that would have shamed
Ossie Bluege and Perpich dug in to
salvage what he could of George
towns line prestige. 1t was large
order the way the line was miSbe-
having. "Mush" Dubofsky wouldn't
have recognized his pupils.


Waynesburg had a fair r-to-mid-
ding passer in Bernie Mazer, who
spread woe and CONSERVATION
throughout Georgetown ranks when
his arm was right, and Paul Brooks,
a halfback who could play on any
body's football team, and they did
most of the damage. Brooks scored
the first touchdown midway of the
first period on a screened pass, then
marshaled an 81-yard parade for
the second, Crawford going over for
the score.


Waynesburg's most potent weapon
was simple reverse, and the way
1t picked up yardage you'd think
the Hoyas were having their first
glimpse of it. And they selected
their stuff wisely, catching George
town off balance or out of position
quite often.


Defensively, it was Waynesburg's
sliding line that caused Georgetown
the most grief. The visitors refused
to charge straight but drifted to
either side and always were in posi-
ton to harass the Hoya blockers.


Jack Doolan, rookie back who
looked very good extensively and fair
on defense; Bill Mclaughlin, Jack
Spencer and Bill Wixted accounted
for Georgetown's scores. Wixted re-
covered a Hoya tumble in Waynes-
burg'S end zone for his touchdown.

After trailing an unprepared In.
consistent Maryland team through
the first two periods, Mount WASH
ington's stout stickmen hit the jack
pot for seven goals in the last two
to shake out an 8-3 victory over
the Terps In the seasons opening
lacrosse match yesterday at College
Park.


Playing in biting cold wind, the
Old Liners appeared on their way
to another upset decision over the
Baltimoreans as they peppered the
net with three pay-of shots in the
first period. They even sneaked a
cripple" by the visitors usually
foolproof goalie, Fritz Stude. and
played circles around their first line
of defense.


Even In the second period, when
rip" Hewitt, playing against his
former buddies, sprinted the fields
length and whammed a hot ingot
into the cage for Mount Washing
tons initial score, the Terps didn't
look bad.


Wolfpack Stages Rally.


Then came the deluge. Three
goals the Wolfpack planted in the
net in riotous third period to 20
ahead and four in the fatal fourth
to seal their hosts fate. Maryland
fell apart. 1t couldn't pass, couldn't
run and couldn't make its plays
click. 1t also lost the services of its
all-America defenseman, Milt Mulitz.
who was obliged to quit the field
when his lef muscles tightened up
on him.


But it wasn't the defense that
begged down but the attack. Mark
land Kelley's work at goal was
superb. Although literally show
cred by Mount Washington shots
he managed to stave off a majority
and clear the ball, but one man
couldn't beat the experienced and
crafty Baltimoreans.


Maryland lost the ball time and
again, dropping it at the feet of
Mount Washington men who
promptly scooped it up and sent it
zinging downfield. Nor could the
Terps pick up innumerable loose
balls that came their way. And
with the foe cracking with each
advancing minute Mount Washing
ton sent its telling cluster Of salvos
into the sinking ship to drive home
the victory and avenge last years
defeat.


Terps Get Fine Start.


JACK Mueller personally account
ed for Maryland's first goal shortly
after the game began. Oscar Me-
wares took pass from the same
Mueller, who was behind the cage,
and tipped it over his right shoul-
der from a 45-degree angle for the
score after 31a minutes and Gordan
Sexton scored on a pass from Bill
Bond in IL minutes to complete
Maryland's counting. The Old Liners
were close many times after, but
couldn't get the rubber by Stude.


A pass from Hewitt to Fred
Stieber gave the eventual victors
flying start midway of the third
period and Tome Dukehart and
Jack Turnbull followed in quick sue
cession to knot the count and send
the visitors out in front, 4-3.
Two goals by Dukehart, one bv
Guild and another by Turnbull COM
| pleted the scoring in the final period.

The Supreme Court today out
lawed another company union"
but said that rights that employees
had obtained under individual con-
tracts negotiated through the Or
ganization were not foreclosed.


The case involved the National
Licorice Co., which had appealed
from a ruling of the United States
Court Of Appeals for the Second
Circuit Affirming board order. The
Supreme Court. however, modified
the order to protect the rights of
the employees who had not been
Joined in the proceedings.


The court also agreed today to
review the 15-year-old case CENTER
ing around the efforts of the Fed
eral Power Commission to require
the Appalachian Electric Power Co.
to take out a license for its
$ll.000,000 hydro-electric develop
ment on the New River at Radford,
Va. The Fourth Circuit Court of
Appeals had denied the Govern
ment the right to require this
license which gives the Federal
Power Commission authority to pre-
scribe rates and charges for the
power development and gives the
Government the privilege of taking
over the projects after so years.


Stone Reads Decision.


The decision in the National
Licorice Co. case was read by Justice
Stone. In separate opinion JUS
tice Douglas and Justice Black said
the Labor Board order should not
have been modified. Justice Murphy
did not participate in the case.


The case rose in August, 1887,
when an A. F. L. local, the Bakery
and Confectionery Workers Interna-
tional Union of America, filed
charges Of unfair practices against
the company. which has plants In
Brooklyn and elsewhere. The union
charged the company with interfer-
ence with its collective bargaining
operations and with attempting to
form a company union.


The board later issued q COM
plant against the concern and in
the following May ordered the COM
pany to cease dominating or inter-
fering with its Collective Bargaining
Committee as the representative of
its employees and to completely dis
establish it. The board said also
that the company should not give
effect to wage contracts that the
committee and individual employees
had made with the company.


Refusal to bargain collectively with
the union and to interfere with the
right of the employees for self organ
ization also was barred.


Order Modified.


The Second Circuit Court then
feafnrmed the order but modified it
to the extent of providing that bar
gaining with the union would de-
pend on whether the labor group
was certified as the proper bargain
ing agency by the board after an
election.


While these proceedings were in
progress the employees of the Brook
lyn plant sJruck, but later came back
to work. They obtained a five per
cent wage increase and other en-
ployment benefits which were agreed
to under the controverted contracts


When the board order was affirmed
by the Circuit Court, the company
appealed. For its appeal the COM
pany raised the question of whether
the employees had not been necessary
parties to the board order to abro-
gate these contracts.

The Civil Aeronautics Authority
and the Weather Bureau became
units of the Commerce Department
today, while the Food and Drug
Administration was placed under
the Federal Security Agency.


President Roosevelt's reorganiza-
ton order of last spring provided
for the shifts, but the effective date
was delayed until beginning of the
new fiscal year, July l.


The G. A. A. was created by Con-
gress two years ago as an inde-
pendent agency to assume func-
tions that had been performed by a
bureau of the Commerce Depart
ment. The Weather Bureau and
the Food and Drug Administration
were shifted from the Agriculture
Department.


Col. Donald H. Connolly is slated
to become Civil AeronaAtics admin
istrator, succeeding Clinton M. Hes
ter, who is resigning to enter pri-
vate law practice.


The reorganization moves, effec-
tive today, also provided for the
Maritime Commission to assume the
former Navy Department response
bility for cooperating in mainte-
nance and supervision of four State
nautical schools.


The Maritime Commission will
take over responsibility for furnish
ing Government vessels and equip
ment for school ships and for match
ing State contributions up to $25,-
600 for each school. The Navy will
continue to lend ordnance and other
equipment used in naval science
courses which prepare graduates for
enrolment in the Merchant Marine
Naval Reserve. Retired naval Of
ficers will be appointed superin-
tendents of the schools.


The four institutions are the Cali
fornia Maritime Academy, the
Massachusetts, Nautical School, the
New York Marine Academy and the
Pennsylvania Nautical School.

Every home gardener sooner or
later tries Strawberries with sur
prising results. If the plants are
everblooming and properly planted
they will produce excellent results
the first year-from warm weather
to late fall. Next season the yield,
despite extra fertilization. is a dis
appointment. The reason is that
strawberries deteriorate from year
to year unless new beds, with new
plants, are made each season.
Select runners from the most pro-
life producers for continued sue
cess.


Take runners when the fruit is
ripening or has just fruited. The
most successful amateur method of
taking runners is to bury four-inch
pots near the parent plants so that
the runners can cross them. Anchor
the runners over the soil-filled pots
with clods of dirt and in six weeks
the pots will be full of roots. sepa-
rate the runner from the parent,
and set the new plants aside in
frame until early fall, when the
strawberry bed may be remade with
the new plants, which always bear
heaviest during their first year after
setting out.


If you do not use the pot method
for obtaining runners and depend
on straight cutting and transplant
ing, use extreme care in setting the
new plants in their permanent
homes. Too shallow planting causes
the roots to dry out; If planted
so that the crown is covered, the
crown rots. Plant with the crown
at the soil surface for sure-fire
results.

Howard A. Gray, director of the
bituminous coal division of the In
terror Department, said today min
imum prices for soft coal at the
mines would become effective Sep
tember 3 and range from 10 cents a
ton for low-grade Indiana coal dust
to $525 for high-grade lump pro-
duced in Washington State,


Secretary Ickes said Gray had
completed work on the long awaited
minimum prices, intended to stabil-
ize the bituminous industry. and
had already started mailing the
schedules to members. He said,
however, none of the specific prices
other than the high and low would
be announced until after they had
been officially released through the
mails and after Gray had completed
the task of duplicating the sched-
ules


The Secretary said the first sched-
ules covering mines in the Rocky
Mountain and Far Western States
were placed in the mails over the
week end and those for the remain
ing districts would be in the mails
by August or shortly after.


The prices, Ickes continued, cover
substantially all commercial bitumi-
nous coal and reflect the differences
in quality. Producers who are mem
bers of the coal code may not sell
their coal at less than minimum
prices without risk of loss of their
code membership. which loss would
subject them to 1912 per cent tax
and possibility of suit for triple
damages by code member compete
tors. Producers not members Of the
code are permitted to sell their coal
at any price they wish, but their
sales are subject to 1914 per cent
tax.

added

LONDON, July 31.-The British
armed merchant cruiser Alcantara
fought a battle with German
raider, a fast converted merchant
ship, in the South Atlantic but was
unable to prevent the raider escap-
ing, the Admiralty announced today.


The Admiralty said the German
ship, mounting four guns on each
broadside, turned away immedi-
ately after she was hit, using a
smoke screen to escape.


The Alcantara, however, chased

her speed, the report said.

killed and seven wounded.

joined the British South Atlantic
Squadron last March.

coast of England, continuing blows
they have been delivering In this
region almost necessarily for the

PASADENA, Calf, Dec. 28.-
Stanford's football squad headed
into another lively workout today
for the clash with Nebraska in the
Rose Bowl, and once again Coach
Clark shaughnessy intimated he
would stress his aerial offense.


Aerial drills have dominated the
Stanford preparations since they
reached Pasadena, with Southpaw
Frankie Albert, the Indians all
America quarterback, and Thor
Peterson tossing.


Stanford boasts several splendid
pass receivers, but Fred Myer, right
end: Glen Tomerlin, spindley-legged
reserve wingman, and Hugh Gal
larneau, halfback star, stand out in
this department. Myer generally is
rated the best.


Milt Vucinich, second-string full
back, continued to avoid drills be-
cause of his injured knee and the
belief is growing that he will not see
action at all New Year Day. Rob
Parker, 188-pound senior, may re-
place Norm Chg Chief Standlee if
the latter's trick ankle gives way in
the game. Parker is a hard line
plunger, but has seen little service
this fall.


The Stanfords will rest tomorrow,
taking a busman's holiday by at
tending the professional football
game in Los Angeles between the
Chicago Bears and the National
League Au-Stars.


Nebraska arrives Sunday morning
and a delegation of Tournament OF
Roses officials, flanked by scores OF
Nebraska enthusiasts, will greet the
Huskers.


No rain is predicted for the New


Year game.

Associated Press Sports Editor.


NEW YORK, Dec. 5.-Boston Col
lege, unofiicial champion of the East,
places three men on the all-Eastern
football team compiled today by the
Associated Press.


Drawn from the Boston array
which will face Tennessee in the
Sugar Bowl New Year Day are
Charley O'Rourke, brilliant back;
Chet Gladchuk, huge center, and
George Kerr, scholarly guard.


Cornell, although 1t dropped its
last two games, and with them the
Ivy League title to Penn, gains two
places on the all-star team. The
other places are shared by Harvard,
Penn, Pitt, Georgetown, Yale and
Fordham.


O'Rourke's backfield mates on the
mythical team are Walt Matuszczak,
Cornell quarterback; Francis Xavier
Reagan, sensational Penn star. and
line-cracking George Kracum Of
Pitt.


With Gladchuk and Kerr in the
line are Loren MacKinney of Har-
ward and Alan Bartholemy of Yale
at the ends, Nick Drahos Of Cornell
and Joe Ungerer of Fordham at the
tackles and Agostino Lilo, George
town veteran, teaming up with Kerr
at guard.


OF these all are seniors except
MacKinney and Bartholemy, who
are juniors. Drahos and Lilo are the
only repeaters from the all-star
team of 1899. The 1910 team aver
ages 202 pounds in the Line and 1876
in the backfield, where ORourke's
158 pounds cuts sharply into the
average.


Versatile Reagan a Standout.


Reagan's place on the team was
secure beyond any challenge, for the
great Penn triple threat stood out
head and shoulders beyond any
Eastern rival for an-around value
Only in the Michigan game was he
stopped cold, and in that test Penn's
line was clearly outplayed.


But the other three backfield
nominees all had to Withstand real
competition. MatuszcZak, husky
blocker and play-caller for Cornell,
barely beat out another great block
er, Boston Colleges Henry TocZy-
lowski. ORourke, a standout in
Bostons vital game with George
town when Georgetown's 23-game
unbeaten streak was broken, found
a half dozen serious challengers
on his heels, among them Andy
Tomasic of Temple, Hal McCul-
Tough of Cornell, Dave Allerdice
of Princeton, Len Eshmont of Ford
ham, Bill Busik of Navy and Henry
Mazur of Army.


Kracum beat out such other full
back aces as Steve Filipowicz, Ford
ham sophomore, Mort Landsberg
of Cornell, Jim Castiglia of George
town and Walter Zirinsky Of
Lafayette.


Flank Competition Keen.


Competition over the end posts
was sharp all the way. Bartholemy,
a fine pass catcher and great de-
fensive player, was Yale's most
consistent player all season. Mac
Kinney, who did most of Harvard S
kicking. performed brilliantly, par
ticularly in the closing stages OF
the season when Harvard began to
move. But their edge was small
over such rivals as Alva Kelley of
Cornell, Hugh Barber and Joe Sic
gal of Columbia, Vince Dennery
and Jim Lansing of Fordham and
Len Warner of Penn.


One of the East's finest wingmen
Gene Goodreault of Boston College
drops back among the honorable
mentions because injuries suffered
in the Georgetown game kept him
out of the Eagles important games
with Auburn and Holy Cross.


The toughest choice of the lot
was at center, where the East had
a banner crop including the 242-
pound Gladchuk, Leon Gajecki OF
Penn State, Don Snavely of Colum-
bia, Lou de Filippo of Fordham
Ray Prick of Penn and Frank
Finneran of Cornell.


Few could challenge Kerr and
Lilo at the guard positions, and
Drahos and Ungerer were equal
standouts at the tackles, where
the field was limited to an extraor-
dinary degree.

The German-speaking capital of

GENEVA, June ~ [P.-The Ger
mans gained few mountain miles
tonight in their effort to join forces
with the Italian Alpine armies.


The town of Bellegarde, near the
Tort, was captured by the Germans,
lost and then regained between
dawn and dusk. Bitter fighting
continued in this section without
respite.


The fort is 5 miles northeast of
the town, commanding the entrance
to the wide valley between the Lower
Jura and the Alps.


Fort Stormed in Morning.


Large German forces stormed the
fort this morning, but were thrown
back. Two tanks which reached
the top Of the hill found the road
way blasted away in front of the
fort, with a 900-foot drop into the
Rhone gorge before them.


The Germans retreated to Belle
earde under a pounding from the
Tort guns. A French counterattack
followed and drove the Germans
momentarily from Bellegarde.


Just before sundown the Germans
again took the town, but found that
French engineers had dynamited all
bridges.


Little Progress South Of Lyon.


South of Lyon German motor
lied columns have made little prog
ress. Near Grenoble and Scham-
berry in the Lower Jura foothills
French forces yesterday drove back
their opponents. French sources
said the Germans apparently are
awaiting reinforcements from Dion


Other unoncial reports said the
French have reorganized their forces
and closed their ranks across the
Saone Valley, shutting out German
motorized columns.


The Italians seem to be awaiting
q further German advance before
trying to join hands with their axis
allies across the Alps.

COLON, Panama, April 13-Cut-
ting swath is blocks wide through
Colon, wind-swept fire tonight de-
stroyed hundreds of frame tene-
ment houses and left approximately
10000 persons homeless before it
was controlled by a small army of
firefighters.


The fire ragged for hours in this
city on the Atlantic side of the
Panama Canal before United States
Army officials announced its spread
was stopped. It's origin was not de-
termined Immediately.


The Army officials also said it
was impossible to estimate immedi-
ately the property damage.


No casualties were reported.


Traffic Cut on.


The fire never reached the Amer
ican town, New Cristobal, but it did
cut off traffic between Cristobal, seat
OF the port administration, and New
Cristobal. where United States en-
ployes of the Panama Canal reside.


1t was said unofficially that there
was no suspicion of sabotage.


The United States Navy rushed
sailors and marines and all available
naval craft from the Coco Solo base
to assist in fighting the fire, and the
United States Army and Canal Zone
officials placed equipment at the dis
posal of Colon officials.


Five freight cars loaded with $50
men and six trucks arrived from
Panama.


The Panama Canal engineering
division dynamited buildings in the
path of the fire.


The Army assembled tents and
other relief equipment to aid the
victims, many of whom were la
borers employed in the Canal Zone.


The city's principal thorough
fare, Paseo del Centenario, became
a camping ground for thousands of
the destitute homeless who lost
their belongings.

THE HAGUE, The Netherlands,
April l3.-The Netherlands faced
tonight its most critical period
since the outbreak of the European
WARMTH its armed forces fully
alert to strike back at any invasion,
new strategic areas under martial
law and the government reiterating
its vow to maintain policy of
complete independence despite pres
sure from the warning powers.


Belgium, too, invoked new defen-
stve measures, posting military
guards at all public properties
radio stations, ministries, airdromes.


The Netherlands merchant marine
suffered another loss in the sinking
Of the steamer Velocitas, 1877 tons,
which struck a mine off the English
coast last night with the loss OF
three lives. The Velocitas was
bound from England to Antwerp
with coal.


Martial Law Extended.


Strengthening the hands of
elderly Premier Derek jan de
Geer's government and the army
high command. Queen Wilhelmina
of The Netherlands tonight issued
a royal decree extending the nations
manifold martial law areas.


The military was given control
over additional zones in the south
eastern province of Noord Brabant,
where the main first defense lines
are located, and in northern and
eastern provinces.


Since last November's first lin
vasion scare" The Netherlands
literally has been dotted with these
martial law zones, covering points
which are component parts of the
elaborate Dutch scheme OF land,
sea and water-line defense.


Heretofore, however, the north
eastern provinces of Groningen,
Drenthe and Overijssel, fanking
the broad reaches of the Ijsselmeer
(zulder zee), had no such zones,
and other provinces were not COM
pletely encased in the state of seige.


Concern Felt in Low Countries.


Since the war spread to Scandi-
navia, within easy striking distance
Of the coasts of Groningen and its
of shore islands, much concern has
been manifest in both The Neither
lands and Belgium.


There have been charges both
from Germany and from the allies
that "the other side" Is threatening
a surprise attack on the low coun-
tries.


Netherlands radio programs were
interrupted tonight for a special
broadcast of British denial of ru-
mors that English troop transports
are on the way to Holland.


The communique said the report
apparently had been carried by the
German radio and published in the
Berlin newspaper Nachtausgabe.


The average Hollander seems
heartened by the strong defense
measures which his government has
taken (their exact nature is a mill
tary secreD and by the knowledge
that well-eQuipped army and naval
forces are fully prepared to resist
any surprise attack, either on the
eastern frontier or along the North
Sea coast


Foreigners Are Uneasy.


However, there are signs of un-
easiness among some foreigners.


British nationals, for instance,
have been advised to report to their
consulates at Amsterdam and Rot
terdam the moment any emergency
arises.


The government press service en-
phasized the governments deter
mination to stick to its policy of
independent neutrality (Holland has
no defense or non-aggression pacts
with any country, not even Bel
gium). It said the government
would make no advance arrange
ments with any belligerent for aid
in case of attack


The army guards in Belgium were
described ofiicially as precautionary,
because Of the general tension"
Additional army leaves were banned.

HELSINKI, Finland, Nov. 28.-
Kyosti Kallio, Finland's 67-year-old
President, has resigned because Of
continued poor health, the Govern
ment Information Bureau announced
today.


President Kallio suffered q heart
attack August 20 and since then
Premier Risto Ryti has been Acting
President.


In September the German official
news agency DNB published an er-
roneous report that Kallio was dead,
but this was quickly denied In Hell
sinki, where his condition was re-
ported improving.


The son Of peasant farmer, Kali
lio climbed through the political
ranks as q member of the Agrarian
party to become cabinet minister,
Premier and finally the fourth Presi-
dent of Suomi, the Finnish Repub-
lie.


Despite his failing health, he was
extremely active in executing the
national program of reconstruction.

NEW YORK, Jan. 22.-More fast
streamline trains will be skimmine
along over the Nations railroads
this summer than ever before In
history. Some will be Diesel
powered. Others will be steam
driven. The controversy over the
relative merits of the oil-fed Diesels
and the traditional coal-fueled To-
comotives still RACES.


Chicago. Burlington & Quincy
one of the first big roads to put

trains in service at the time they
were introduced back in 1884, still
thinks the Diesels are tops. The
road has just ordered new

The new unit will be composed of

$555,000. The present streamliner
the pioneer zephyr" will be as
signed to another division of the

In addition, the Burlington has
plans drawn up for two proposed
Texas zephyrs, to operate overnight
between Denver, Fort Worth and
Dallas.


Central Fav0rs Steam.


New York Central Railroad, on
the other hand, stoutly approves
stream line steam trains Its stream
line steam driven Twentieth Gen.
tury Limited, operating between
Chicago and New York City, has
now become an institution.


Moreover, the roads stream line
steam-powered Mercury" plying
between Cleveland and Detroit, so
pleased the management that a
second Mercury" train was built
and now operates between Detroit
and Chicago.


Altogether there are between rs
and 80 Stream-line trains now in
operation, with Diesel-power most
prominent in the West and steam
power in the East. Which, one un-
biased railway official says, is as
it should be.


He holds the Diesels are pre-
ferred west of Chicago mainly be-
cause tracks are straighter out there,
towns are further apart, and the
oll-electric units prove highly eff
cient in swinging the trains along
at 80 and 100-mile-an-hou clips
across the Plains Moreover, coal
mines are overwhelming in the East,
and oil fields in the West.


Preferred in East.


On the other hand, some rail
executives contend steam will al
ways be preferred in the East. They
claim steam trains accelerate faster.
making better overall average speed
winding around curves, slowing for
frequent towns and climbing grades
in the more hilly and thickly popu-
lated territory this side of the Mis-
sissippi.


Most rail experts seem to think
that even though there may be
great expansion in the use of Diesels
for passenger service and for yard
switching service. that steam will
never be supplanted as the basic
rail motive power for freight trains.


They claim steam still is best of
the two for moving long, heavy
freights big distances from the
standpoint of power, operating eff
cheney and locomotive life. To back
this up, they point out that prac-
tically all users of Diesel-power pas
senger trains still cling to steam for
long freight hauls.


Pennsylvania Railroad has been
the one big Eastern road to lean
away from steam, Shun oil and elec-
trify some of its important lines
past committing territory. Electric
power, before the Pennsylvania be-
gan extending it on long lines, had
proved successful on such short-line
passenger carriers as the New York,
New Haven & Hartford and the
Long Island.


The Pennsylvania now has main
lines electrified between New York,
Philadelphia, Washington and out
to Harrisburg. But steam carries
traffic from there on to Chicago and
other Western points.

harbor at Tampico, Mexico.


The Van Kinsbergen took possess

the first intimation here that
Netherlands warships were operating

ern waters.

Nazi crew attempted to Scuttle their
vessel to prevent its seizure by the
Van Kinsbergen. An independent
source asserted that the merchant
man also had been set on fire when
tne destroyer closed IN.


Idarwald Scuttled Sunday.


Another German freighter, the
5,033-to IdarWald, which steamed
out of Tampico with the Rhein No.
vember 20, was scuttled by her crew
Sunday when intercepted by the
British cruiser Diomede


AS early as November IS, the
Rhein, Idarwald and a sister ship,
the Phrygia, had attempted to steal
out of the Mexican gulf port, with
disastrous consequences for the
Phrygia.


The Phrygia's master, believing he
was about to be captured by enemy
ships which had been reported lurk-
ing outside the harbor bar, ordered
his vessel scuttled. A fourth Ger
man cargo vessel, the Orinoco, was
halted by engine trouble before she
could clear Tampico Harbor, and
still is there.

her Mexican sanctuary, her radio
dispatched this message: "Rhein
being followed by warships."


Further word of her fate was lack
ing until announcement of her cap
ture.

not set the time that the Rhein was
overhauled by the Van Kinsbergen.

said that other units of the Dutch
Navy were operating with the British
patrol in the Western Atlantic. The
number and types of the ships were

NEW YORK, Jan. 3.-The stock
market today dared the hazards of
the convening of Congress and
presidential message by rallying
briskly in continuation of yesterdays
advance.


While business started off quietly
it gained rapidly later and leaders
pushed up fractions to points or
more.


Veterans of the trading floor re-
called that January market psychol-
ogy is usually better than that OF
December and that for 38 of the past
80 years the first months prices have
been better than those of the pre-
ceding period.


Much of the support, brokers said,
came in the investment stocks and,
while there was a fair turnover of
lower priced issues, the big money
was for the blue chips including
the steels, motors and rails.


Neither the meeting of Congress
nor the presidential message ap-
peared to have much effect on the
course of buying, many professionals
thinking Mr.. Roosevelt's hint of
higher taxes for national defense
would not increase the country's bill
much if other budget items were
reduced.


Transfers approximated 100000
shares.


Prominent on the upturn were
United States Steel, Bethlehem,
Chrysler, Santa Fe, PENNSYLVANIA
Railroad, New York Central, Sears
Roebuck and American Telephone.
both of which made new l939-4O
highs; Consolidated Edison, North
American. Anaconda, Westinghouse
Electric, Dow Chemical, Du Pont,
Allied Chemical, Johns -Manville,
United States Gypsum, Loft and

CLEVELAND, July 6.-Held hit
less for four frames by bespectacled

White Sox to keep their grip on
first place.

was succeeded by Johnny Allen.

Hundreds of children from Wash
ingtons settlement houses and Or
phanages will attend the Maeter-
linck play, "Seven Wishes" at the
National Theater Friday through
the sale of so-called pleasure
fund" tickets.


The Wellesley Club of Washing
ton is sponsoring the play for the
benefit of war relief for British
children. Those who purchase
pleasure fund tickets, however,
will turn them over to designated
groups and thus make Christmas
merrier for Washington boys and
girls who might otherwise not at
tend. More than 800 tickets of this
kind already have been sold in
addition to the regular admissions.


The play will be presented by the
Children's Theater of New York.


Among agencies which have re-
ceived pleasure fund" tickets are
the Americanization School, which
will send orphaned refugees of all
nationalities; the Christ Child Soci-
ETY.. the Police Women'S Bureau,
Georgetown Children's Home, st.
Johns Orphanage, the Health
School for Crippled Children, the
Junior League social welfare de-
partment of Children's Hospital,
the Jewish Social Agency, Oppor-
tunity House, Neighborhood House,
Friendship House, the Metropolitan
Police Boys Club, Hampshire House
and Goodwill Industries. Another
group which will attend the show
is from country school in nearby
Maryland. where the pupils have
never seen play or a moving pic
ture.


Between acts the youngsters will
sing carols and hear program by
the Police Boys Club Harmonica
Band. A transcription of Princess
Elizaabeth's address to the British
children will be played Gay souve-
mir programs and holiday decora-
tons will add to the festive at
mosphere.


Both pleasure fund tickets and
regular admissions are available at
the Children's Theater headquar-
tiers, 1884 F street NV.

SUN VALLEY, Idaho, Nov. a.
New ski runs, a new toboggan run,
a new woodland cabin retreat for
ski tourers. a new gameroom in
which bowling is featured and new
physiotherapy conditioning" rooms.
coupled with the fact that all of last
years ski runs have been widened.
are some of the developments win
ter season visitors will find here.
A brand-new emile long trail is
Broadway Run, starting at the
9,200-foot summit Of Baldy Noun
tain, running the mountains entire
length and joining Sunnyside Run
some 5000 feet below. At the start
of this run, the United States Forest
Service has built a stone lookout
station, fitted with stoves and COM
Portable lounge. At the top Of
Broadway Run there are also six
ravines suitable to all types OF
skiers. Good snow is assured from
early December until May.


The narrow canyon run is now a
rolling highway down the mountain
side, at some points being more
than 100 yards in width. Skiers
now may continue down Riverside
Run to the bottom of Baldy Noun
| tain.
Along Riverside Run a toboggan,
run mile and half long has been
laid out, designed for thrills with
safety.


The new cabin retreat, designed
particularly for late spring skiiers,
is being constructed in the Galena
Summit region. To reach this wood
land haven guests must travel 18
miles north of Sun Valley through
scenic mountain country.


Innovation at Sun Valley Lodge
is the installation OF the physio-.
therapy conditioning rooms, where
aches or pains resulting from a days
vigorous exercise on the ski runs
and ice skating rinks are treated.


Installed in the new game room
are four standard size bowling al
leys. Pool tables and other games
also are available.

BEAUMONT, Tex. July 90
Sheriff Chris P. Fox of Ell Paso told
the Dies Committee that Com
munists had obtained recruits by
promising when the revolution
comes" Mexican citizens will re-
ceive the land taken from them"
by the United States.


He mentioned Texas, New Mexico
and several other Southwestern
States as the prizes to be devided.


The sheriff also laid before the
committee yesterday a report he
said had been given him of meet

Teachers, Students Listed.


This report, which he said came
from person who attended the
meeting, identified numerous teach
ers and students of State schools as
Communist party members. At one
school almost the entire football
and basketball squads were listed.


Plans for 1910 were made at this
meeting, Sheriff Fox testified, with
particular emphasis" on the State
gubernatorial campaign.
El Paso was pictured as the focal
point Of Communist operations be-
tween the United States and Mex
leo, with a former Mexican Consul
there as the ''ringleader.


Earlier, John L. Leech of Port
land, Oreg., and George Bertholon
Of Los Angeles told the committee
the Communist party plans to OBJ
tain social equality with white per-
sons for Negroes


Mr.. Bertholon, 20-year-old for
mer student at the Los Angeles
Junior College, said the Young Com
munist League had gained control
Of the student government at that
school.


Negro Communist Work Described.


The Laborers' Non-Partisan
League and the California Fedora
ton for Political Unity, which he
described as being important polit-
ically in California; the Workers
Alliance and the American Youth
Congress all were under leadership
of Communists, he testified.


Mr.. Leech said the Negro-Com-
munist work was active throughout
the South. Among other things,
Communists are seeking for the
Negroes the right to marry white
persons. enfranchisement and gov

Negro population constitutes the
majority.


Force will be used if necessary

text:
Special Dispatch to The Star.


SALISBURY, Md, Feb. 12.-Mrs.
Annie Savage Pilchard, brought to
the hospital early today with a pis-
tai wound in her back, told police
she had spent the night in the attic
Of her farm home, hiding from two
robbers who had criminally assaulted
and shot her after killing her hus-
band.


She was found this morning on
the roof of her home, where she
had crawled at daybreak. Firemen
raised ladder to bring her down
and rushed her to the hospital.


Mrs. Pilchard told police the
bandits walked into her home near
Stockton about 8 o'clock last night
and demanded money. Mrs. Pill
chard handed over her pocketbook
to one of the men, who fired a shot
gun point blank at her husband,
Harvey Pilchard, 61-year-old farmer.


He was killed instantly and his
body was found this morning on
the nving-room floor. Mrs. Pilchard
said she screamed and ran when her
husband was shot and one of the
bandits fired pistol at her.


The bullet struck her in the back
and she fell to the floor. The rob-
bers fled and Mrs. Pilchard groped
her way up to the attic to hide.
She said that while she was hiding
she heard the two men come back
to search for her. At dawn Mrs.
Pilchard 'crawled out on the roof,
where she was found by John Man
uel, a fireman from a nearby saw
mill.


Police indicated they knew the
identity Of the killers, said to be
colored men, and. an arrest was ex-
pected.


Feeling mounted high when word
Of the shooting became known and
officers moved cautiously to avert
possible violence.

sides for supplies.


Soon after Joachim Won Ribben-

last August 20, German economists
visited Russia and presented their
menu" of Russian raw materials in
which Germany was specially in
terested.


In return, q Russian trade dele
CATION toured Germany Inspecting
many industrial plants, after which
they submitted their requests for
goods in exchange for raw materials.


Expands Present Accord.


Another German delegation head
ed by Special Ambassador Karl Rit-
ter visited Moscow, and authorita-
tive sources said the treaty then
was concluded.


These sources said the treaty
covers items beyond the $50, 900 ,0GO

The Russian German trade agree
ment before the war started was

Authorized sources in commenting

The 1880 iron lung which Dis
trict Legionnaires purchased for
Providence Hospital demonstrated
its usefulness as a life saver even
before the donors presented it
formally to the hospital last night.


No sooner had the mechanical
respirator been installed than man
near death from an asthmatic con-
dition was placed inside it. Attend
ants said the respirator save the
patients life.


The presentation ceremonies were
held last night in the lobby of the
hospital. Sister Rosa, superintend-
ent, thanked William T, Slattery,
past department commander of the
Legion. and his fellow Legionnaires
and auxiliary members for the gift.


All Legion posts and auxiliaries in
the District participated in the
fund-raising programs to obtain the
iron lung. The campaign started
last May.


Col. Joseph Randall was chair
man of committee in charge, con-
sisting of William H. Hargrave, Hey
wood Saunders, Anna Frame, John
J. Mulvey and Charles Kohen.

ings.

PARIS, June eff the French
Army can hold for 48 hours more
against the terrific drive by two
German armored divisions of
about 500 to 1000 tanks and sew
eral infantry divisions in one
small sector the situation is
probably saved.


The second day of the German
drive for Paris found a heavy Ger
man offensive in the Peronne-Sois-
sons area met by vigorous French
counter offensives. Tank met tank,
the French tanks usually the larger
and often superior in quality, if in
ferior in numbers.


But at noon, the German advance
was nowhere great. In some places
German tanks. which had advanced
ahead of their infantry, found them
selves surrounded and were then
subjected to air, artillery and anti
tank gun attack.


Planes Armed With Cannon,


At Chaulnes, 40 German tanks
were destroyed, airplanes fitted with
cannon sweeping to only a few
meters over the monsters and
emptying their cannon into their
lightly armored rear.


In at least three regions German
tanks were cut off and completely
isolated, apparently having ex-
hausted their gasoline.


The French counterattacks came
at moment where they apparently
disturbed the German assailants
most.


This fighting is not like the battle
OF Flanders. The French no longer
attempt to oppose tanks by rifles.
They take shelter in strong spots
and allow tanks to pass, trusting
that they will be stopped and de-
stroyed by French tanks and air
forces before they have gone far.


Quickly adapting themselves to
the new situation, the Germans lin
tied their thrusts in depth and in
same cases returned almost to their
point of departure.


Gain Only at One Point.


The advance into France was, ex-
cept in one spot, no deeper at noon
today than it was last night-in
some places less deep. The German
infantry divisions following the
tanks had mached all the way from
the German border in the last three
weeks and showed some signs of
fatigue. Moreover, they were of diff
erent units which had been united
for the purpose of this attack.


North of scissors the fighting
was also heavy. A third German
attack south from Abbeville along
the coast has made some progress.
but the intruders were being fiercely
counterattacked this morning.


The morale of the French troops
impresses this correspondent. OBJ
viously, the Germans cannot hope
for a repetition of the panic they
created on the Meuse.

BY the Associated Press.


STOCKHOLM, April 26.-Re-
ports reaching Swedish news
papers late today indicated the
allied and Norwegian forces on
the front below Trondheim have
inflicted considerable losses on
German advance units, forcing
them back to a point 5 miles
south of Roros.


The allied troops, coming down the
Glomma Valley from their concen-
tration point at Storen, brought light
artillery into action.


Behind the Nazi advance column,
German units were reported digging
in in the Osterdalen valley some
10 to Is miles below RoroS, after re-
tiring from that city.


Artillery had come into play by
late afternoon on both sides, and
the cannonading could be heard
from the Swedish frontier, some 20
miles from the scene of the fighting.


tReports reached London that
Norwegian bands descended in
the rear of the Germans who yes
terday drove as far as Roros be-
fore retreating south of the city
and had DESTROYED their line OF
retreat back to Elverum and Oslo,
the Chicago Daily News foreign
service reportedD


New Equipment for Allies.


There was evidence, also, that the
allies had received new aerial equip
ment. German air activity in the
Trondheim sector fell off consider
ably. and there were reports of
minor air battles in several places
between British fighter planes and
German bombers.


One German plane was reported
shot down after fight with three
British planes over the Swedish
frontier.


The British also were said to have
curbed German air activity at their
Namsos landing point, above T>rond-
helm, by installing anti-aircraft bat
teries.


Roros, from which the Germans
retired when the allies moved down
from Storen, is 10 miles southeast OF
Trondheim.


In the Gudsbrandsdalen Valley to
the west another flying NaZi column
appeared to have begged down at
Ringebu, some 100 miles south of
Trondheim.


French Arrivals Reported.


The British position around
Trondheim itself, meanwhile, was
reported improved by the arrival OF
crack French troops, including For
eign Legionnaires and Alpine SOL
diers.


The Germans continued, how
ever. to pour a steady stream OF
reinforcements into Trondheim by
air transport, each capable of carry
ing 80 men. There also were re-
ports that German ship had man
aged to evade the British blockade
and enter Trondheim Fjord with
supplies.


The German situation at the
Arctic port of Narvik was said to be
becoming more precarious. Some
sources estimated that the Nazi
force there, carrying on from noun
tain positions around the town with
the aid of munitions flown in by
plane, now numbers less than 500
men.


Fighting Between Small Units.


In general the fighting throughout
Norway appeared to be between
small units, maneuvering swiftly for
position. All reports agreed, how
ever, that the German detachments,
regardless of their size, were armed
to highly effective degree with
automatic weapons.

text:
Two years ago the conditions under
which thirty-f1ve thousand Wash
ington girls and women earned their
living became Subject to the Dis
trlct's minimum wage law. Whatever
doubts may have existed as to the
wisdom or effectiveness of that act
have been dispelled in the subse-
quent months. Most recent statistics,
made public by Mrs. William Kittle,
chairman Of the Wage Board, at Mrs.
Roosevelt's press conference, indicate
that the law not only has stabilized
employment and made regular jobs
for thousands of part-t time workers,
but more women are earning more
money in private employment than
before the act went into effect.


These figures, which show that only
a comparatively few part-time work.
ers still receive less than the legal
minimum, are directly important
only to the employees who have so
benefited. But the methods by which
these results have been achieved are
important to the community. They
represent a tribute to the co-opera-
tive effort for fairness and honest
dealing among employers and en-
ployeS alike. 90.


In eighteen months six commit
tees, composed in each case of three
representatives of the workers, three
employers and the three members of
the Wage Board, worked out to their
mutual satisfaction the basic mini
mum scale required to provide a
proper living for those engaged in
various types of enterprises. Within
these groups there were disputes and
debates. But resulting scales were
arrived at without later dissension
and without recourse to pressure.


And the subsequent decisions OF the
board have been accepted as reason
able and proper. That these decisions
invariably have been unanimous is
evidence enough of the tact and rea-
sonableness of those intrusted with
administration of the act.

BARCELONA, Spain. Oct. 19.-
Torrential rains in the Eastern
Pyrenees today further burdened
flooding Spanish rivers whose known
toll already had mounted to 1873 dead
or missing.


With telephone, highway and rail
communications shattered through
out Barcelona and Corona Prov
inces, it was believed the final total
might pass the first estimate of
200 dead in the waters Of the ram
paging Ter River and it's tribu-
tarieS.


Rain which has fallen for three
days continued to pelt down
throughout the night and morn
ing The government rushed relief
supplies into the stricken area.


Houses Crumbled.


Rivers in the Lerida section and
throughout Navarro also flooded as
the rainfall drained swiftly off the
mountains. In Torello, where 200
houses crumbled in 20 minutes, the
toll Of dead and missing climbed
to 108. Two passengers drowned
when Barcelona train went
through the collapsing bridge there
one of three trains derailed by
the floods. Many persons died in
Torello when they returned to their
homes prematurely following re-
ports the flood was receding.


Ironically, the people of Corona
were asked to conserve water for
fear breakage of the mains might
bring shortage.


18 Drowned in Corona.


Eighteen persons were reported
drowned in the city of Corona, So
miles northeast of Barcelona, when
bridge was swept away. Water ran
deep in Gerona's streets, reaching
the balconies of homes in low places.


Generalissimo Francisco Franco
ordered relief sent Immediately to
the families of flood victims. The
Ministry of the Interior headed a
list of donations with 100000 pesetas
approximately $4,000.


Three days of continuous rain
preceded the floods. Virtually all
towns on the lower side of the
Llobregat River near Barcelona were
flooded Crops in that fertile valley
were ruined and poultry and live
stock losses were heavy.

STOCKHOLM, June 5.-Air raid
alarms were sounded briefly in
Northern Sweden today when at
least two foreign planes were sighted
at great height over the iron ore
port of Lulea. heavily fortified Boden
and Pitea. another northern port.


The planes disappeared before
they could be identified.


British. French and Norwegian
troops smashing eastward along the
Narvik Railway were reported in
Swedish press dispatches today to
have stormed the German defenses
at Sildvik, about halfway between
the Arctic ore port of Narvik and
the Swedish Norwegian frontier.


Narvik in Allied Hands.


Narvik now is in Allied hands and
Allied forces are trying to free the
railway into Sweden from the Ger
mans.


The dispatches said the Germans
were yielding under the heavy rain
of shells from British destroyers and
land batteries.


A final onslaught against the main
German forces at Bjornfjell, about
miles from the Swedish frontier, is
expected within a day or two If the
present advance continues.


The Allies and Norwegans are now
moving in accordance with well
plans.


The battle-ground is a mountain
railway which burrows through IA
long tunnels.


Casualties Reported Heavy.


Inside these tunnels the Ger
mans are fighting furiously, in many
instances heroically holding on to
the last man. Into the mouths of
the tunnels fly showers of shrapnel
from the guns of British destroyers
lying in Rombakfjord, alongside the
railway, and from Allied mountain
artillery.


Taking advantage of this bar
rage but still exposed to German
air attacks, the Allied troops are ad-
vancing along the railway from
Narvik to force their way through
and around the captured tunnels.


Casualties are reported heavy on
both sides.

NEW YORK, Dec. 4.-Marine un-
derwriters disclosed today the Brit
ish government had prevented a
sharp increase in commercial war
risk insurance rates despite current
heavy English shipping losses.


The British war risk Office in
Sures all cargoes between United
States Atlantic coast ports and the
west coast of the United Kingdom
for a fiat 212 per cent.


Commercial interests in the United
States and England charge 10 per-
cent, which has ben in effect for
months.


A few exporters and importers
pay the higher rate, insurance men,
said because they fear delay in
payment of British policies because
of government technicalities and
prefer dealing with United States
firms with which they are familiar.
In addition, some are afraid England
might be subjected to quick defeat,
1t was said.


Domestic underwriters claimed
they were not doing enough busi-
ness in Europe bound cargoes to
keep in postage stamps, largely be-
cause of the British rate. Most,
insurance business now comes from
Far Eastern and South American
shipping, they said.

80 In the first two days that this

for the same period year ago.

Another report said insurance

during recent years would not con-
sent to a tenant sealing his corn
under the long term.

ROME. July 4.-The Italian high
command reported today that Ital-
ian troops from Libya have pushed
across the Egyptian frontier to
Musaid, near Sollum, while native
Dubat troops from Ethiopia have oc-
cupied the British fort at Moyale on
the Kenya border.


Sollum lies just at the border of
Libya and Egypt on the Mediter-
ranean coast.


The communique said:


"On the Cyrenaican front our
column reached Emusaid, in the
Sollum zone, throwing back small
groups of armored cars while our
air force attacked and dispersed
an enemy motorized column.


Farther south repeated English
attacks on the Capuzzo redoubt
were completely repulsed.


One of our submarines has not
returned to its base.


In East Africa our Dubats oc-
cupied the fort at Moyale, keep
ing it despite fruitless air raids
with which the enemy reacted.
On the Sudan frontier our squad
rons bombed enemy fortresses at
Akopo and Gallabat.

By the Associated Press.


LONDON, Sept. 2O.-British fight
ers repulsed more than 200 German
planes in a massive battle over the
Southeast Coast this morning and
the raiders were seen racing in
disorder toward the French Coast,
British sources reported today, fol-
lowing night-long Nazi raids on
London and heavy R. A. F. counter
blows against German inland con-
tinental bases and invasion ports"
The authoritative British Press
Association said British fighters,
hidden in the clouds waiting for the
. Germans, pounced on them as they
reached the Kent Coast and a free
for-all followed


. The press associations correspon-
dent, describing the battle, said the
raiders were driven relentlessly back
eastward and the fight continued
over the sea. Later a formation of
Hurricanes and Spitfres came flying
home to the cheers of watchers
below.


Near Dover one German fighter
spun out of the sky trailing smoke
and crashed in hills near the Chan
mel port. German raiders also ap-
peared over London and the Thames
Estuary during the morning.


Anti-Aircraft Barrage.


Londoners, warned to air raid
shelters when the attackers ap-
peared, emerged again shortly after
noon, when it was believed the
danger had passed. Anti-aircraft
batteries kept up a thunderous bar
rage against the Estuary raiders
until British fighters sped to the
attack.


British bombers, striking at Ger
man bases while the Nazis were
subjecting London to its 18th con-
secutive all-night attack, blasted
the Dortmund- Ems Canal and other
vital communications in Germany
proper and number of ports and
airdromes in German occupied ter
ritory, the Air Ministry announced.
Resuming daylight raids, nine
German planes roared through the
clouds over the London area, but
dropped only two bombs. Addi-
tional raiders appeared simul-
taneously over a southeast inland
town.


Later rooftop observers heard the
drone of planes over the capital.
but they were flying too high to tell
whether they were British or Ger
man.


One explosion was heard during
the morning in London, but it may
have been a time bomb dropped in
last nights raids, described officially
as ION a smaller scale and less ef-
fective than of late"


London Main Objective.


London again was the main OBJ
jective of the night attacks, but
bombs also were dumped in Lanca-
shire. Essex, Surrey, Berkshire, Kent,
the Midlands and Southwest Eng
land


A formation of dive bombers cap
ped the night attacks with violent
assault on the northwest and east
sectors of London just before dawn.


One German raider brought down
by anti-aircraft fire over Southwest
London crashed into the side of
house so yards from hospital at
Merton Park. Its wing tips dam
aged four houses before it struck
the fifth, exploding with such force
that the building was demolished.
People in nearby air raid shelters
were endangered by the spreading
flames but escaped.


Some fatalities were caused when
a bomb hit an escape hatch of a
public shelter in a North London
park. The East End also suffered
some casualties.


Many Incendiaries Dropped.


Damage in Central London was
less than on previous nights, al
though numerous incendiary bombs
were dropped. High explosive bombs
made direct hits on two streets. In
one a jewelers. shop and many
apartments were demolished. Peo-
pie in a basement shelter of one
wrecked building were rescued un-
hurt.


One man was killed and many
persons were injured in another
street. A gown shop and a hair
dresser's establishment were badly
damaged.


Although gaping bomb crater
was left in the sidewalk few feet
from West End provision shop, the
shop opened as usual, half the staff
sweeping up shattered glass and
the other half serving customers.


Lord Beaverbrook, Minister for
Aircraft Production; Sir John An
derson, Minister of Home Security,
and Lord AShfield, chairman OF
London Transport, last night in
spected the Holborn underground
station where thousands of East
Enders have been taking shelter
nightly.


The japanese Embassy, in fash
ionable Portman Square, has suf-
fered damage, mostly broken win
dows, in recent raids and the staff
has been forced to move to nearby
building.

sened the blows of Nazi raiders
until after midnight, when the moon
broke through to light the way for
the dive bombers

BY the Associated Press.


CANNES, France, March g.
Maxine Elliott, 81, famous Ameri-
can actress who achieved success
both In Europe and the United
States, died last night at her
chateau at Juan Les Pins.
For many years since her re.
tirement from the stage Miss Elliott
had lived on the French Riviera
at her Villa L'Horizon. where Euro
pean royalty and other notables
were frequent guests.
A famous beauty in the early part
of the century, Miss Elliott made
her tast stage appearance in 1920
at her own theater in New York
after 81 years as an actress.


All attempts to get her to return
to the theater were refused with
the assertion that she wished to
grow middle-aged gracefully"


Suffered Heart Ailment.


Since last June Miss Elliot. had
been suffering from a heart ailment.
Her sister. Lady Forbes Robertson,
the former Gertrude Elliott. is due
to arrive from London tomorrow
Funeral arrangements have not been
made


Her ill-health had prevented ex-
tensive war work during the present
conflict, but when the World War
started she was an early volunteer
Red Cross nurse.

CHICAGO, July 5.-Traders on
the Chicago Mercantile Exchange
today expressed little optimism over
the possibility of increased exports
of dairy commodities to England
despite elimination of the rich Scan
dinavian and Low Country sources.


They had held out some hope for
increased exports to England when
the Scandinavian and Low dairy
lands came under Nazi control and
this optimism was reflected in mar
ket prices about two weeks ago when
the British Purchasing Commission
placed its first orders for canned
milk


Washington officials, however, were
quick to assert that these purchases
would not be in amount large
enough to cause any extensive boom
Department of Agriculture estimates
indicated that with the exception of
prepared milk and eggs, there is no
immediate prospect of any substan-
tial increase in produce exports.


Other Markets Closed.


Even though several years will be
required to restore Scandinavian
and low dairy land production of
normal, traders question whether
Germany. with her barter trade sys-
tenn, will import dairy commodities
from this country.


Furthermore, should domestic pro-
duction be geared up to meet any
possible demand from Central Eu-
rope, producemen wonder what
would happen to the domestic mar
ket when conditions in Europe re-
turn to normal.


Before the World War Denmark
was England's chief source of but
ter imports, and this source was
almost entirely eliminated during
the war. Since then, however, New
Zealand and Australian exports
have rapidly increased until before
the present conflict they and other
dominion countries supplied Eng
land with so per cent of her butter
imports. England imported only 80
per cent from Scandinavian coun-
tries. Moreover, reports indicate
that England had been accumulat-
ing considerable butter and has re-
placed much of the lost supply with
home-produced oleomargarine. Eng

From the doorway of Happy
Jacks house the softest of soft
voices came down to him. dee,
dee, dee! See me, see me! Happy
Jack, Happy Jack, come to the
Christmas tree before Chatterer and
Sammy Jay take away all the good
things you like so WE'LL" it cried.
dee, dee, dee, dee! I'm as happy
as can be-" 1t was the voice of
Tommy Tit the Chickadee.


This time Happy Jack became
enough interested to climb up and
poke his head out of the doorway.
At first he could see nothing at all,
for the million jolly Little Sum-
beams blinded him with their
brightness. And the million little
crystals of ice flashed in his eyes
and dazzled him.


But he could hear, and what he
heard were the jolliest sounds and
the merriest, sounds and the hap
pieSt sounds and the cheerieSt
sounds that ever were. They came
from the Old Orchard and from
beyond in Farmer Browns door,
yard. They we're the mingled voices
of Tommy Tit and Drummer the
'Woodpecker and Sammy Jay and
Yank Yank the Nuthatch and Chat
terer the Red Squirrel, all talking
at once as fast as their tongues
could go and not making a single
quarrelsome sound. And with them
mingled the jingle of merry sleigh
bells as Farmer Browns Boy pre-
pared to go for a ride.


Hardly believing his own ears,
Happy Jack started for the Old
Orchard. What do you think he
found there? He found a little
hemlock tree standing in the snow
where no hemlock tree had been
before. In it and around it were
his friends, so happy and excited
they couldn't keep still. You see
that little tree was hung with things
birds dearly love to eat and scat
tered under it and in little boxes
fastened to its branches were big
fat hickory nuts and brown chest
nuts and yellow corn, enough for
all forGmany days.


With the taste of the first nut all
misery left Happy Jack. For a
while he was too busy to talk. Then,
with his stomach filled until he
couldn't swallow another mouthful,
he scampered to the top of a big
apple tree, spread his great, fluffy,
silver tail and did his best to tell
all the Great World that he was
the happiest squirrel that ever lived.


A door slammed, Farmer Browns
Boy walked across the dooryard and
jumped into the sleigh. He stopped
whistling long enough to look over
toward the hemlock tree in the Old
Orchard. Merry Christmas, every
body!" he cried.


And Tommy Tit and Happy Jack
and Chatterer and Drummer and
Sammy Jay and Yank Yank each
did his best to wish Farmer Browns
Boy Merry Christmas and to
thank him for their Christmas tree.
The sleigh bells jingled merrily, the
jolly Little Sunbeams smiled hap
PLY, Farmer Browns Boy whistled
joyously and far away chimes pealed
softly and oh so sweetly.


Happy Jack looked down. Under
the Christmas tree Peter Rabbit
was dancing from pure joy. The
Jolly Little Sunbeams were dancing.
Chatterer the Red Squirrel was
chasing his tail. In a flash Happy
Jack was down on the snow doing
the same thing and his heart was as
light as his fluffy tail, for into it
had entered the spirit of Christ
mas.


And so for Happy Jack Squirrel
and all the other little people of
the Old orchard, I wish you Merry,
Merry Christmas.
