By the Associated Press.


PARIS, June 12.-"Gay Paree"
was a half-empty shell today, quiet
itself as the sound of battle reached
its streets.


Instead Of the fashionable tour
lists and other customers usually ar
irving at this time of year to patron
lie world-famed dressmakers and
milliners, refugees were arriving in
droves from battle-torn Northern
France.


The dressmakers themselves had
packed up and left. The Govern
ment was gone and the newspapers
were gone Subway trains were run
ming, but in restricted numbers.
Taxis were rare. Some food shops
were open, but most closed


Automobiles were streaming out
of the capital packed with civilians.
Others wishing to leave hoped for
restoration of train service. Poorer
people walked. Most people who
had transportation of any sort had
gone.


Refugees Crowd Station.


Electricity, water and gas were
still available, but not a light
burned in the streets at night.


Platforms of the Care ST. Lazare,
where boat trains from de luxe
liners usually are unloading aris-
tocratic passengers at this time of
year. were crowded today with
bedraggled groups of refugees in
flight from German-invaded Nor
mandy.


Many came part way on foot from
Beauvais, Compeigne and Creil,
towns in region about so miles to
the north where the Germans are
now operating. Many of these were
mothers carrying babies and small
children in their arms. The family
groups carried all the clothing and
household furnishings they could
manage.


Hot, hungry and thirsty in the
June heat, they waited for trans
portation to points still farther
from the battle which followed
them. They we're huddled in little
groups, usually augmented by some
kind of dog.


They sat on suitcaSeS in the midst
of potato sacks stuffed with cloth
ing and baby carriages piled high
with bedding and baskets filled with
kitchenWare and foodstuEs. There
were sick, wounded and palayzed on
stretchers.


Woman Walks SO miles.


Among the travellers forced afoot
was a woman with a 1-year-old
child who had walked from Beau
vais to Meulan 80 miles before she
could get on train for Paris.


Another woman with her six chill
dren walked 20 miles from Com
piegne to take train at a station
which she found blown up when
she got there. No trains we're run
ming, but she succeeded in getting
q lift by automobile to Paris.


Other refugees from the north
came in two-Wheeled peasant carts
drawn by horses in tandem, the lit
tie families sitting atop their house
hold furnishings. Many came by
bicycle. Others walked. pushing
ahead Of them baby carriages and
wheelbarroWs loaded with their
household goods.


Most of these refugees were SIM
ply making their way through Paris
to go farther southwark.


Thousands of Americans Remain.


1t was estimated several thou
sand Americans still remained in
Paris despite repeated warnings by
their Embassy to get out. Among
those remaining was United States
Ambassador William C. Bullitt,
although part of his staff went with
the government to Tours.


Many of the fashionable refugees
from Paris went to BiarritZ, and
with them were many of the famed
dressmaker and millinery establish
ments, practically all of which closed
their Paris salons.


Schiaparelli. Molyneux, Lanvin,
Paquin and Helm are closing here
and opening at Biarritz. Patou has
had a Biarritz branch for several
months and is transferring her Paris
staff there. Worth and Balenciaga
are among the dressmakers closed
here and not reopening elsewhere

Ever since the sudden signing of
the Russo-German agreement in
August, 1889, which proved to be the
dramatic prologue to the present
war, rumors have been rife of an
impending split between Soviet Rus
sia and Nazi Germany. Thus far,
these reports have been baseless, in
the sense that no open rift has
occurred and that effective inter-
course between the two countries
has been maintained.


However, time has abundantly
shown that Russo German under
standing is very hard boiled in char
acter; that each government is
chronically suspicious of the other
and that certain conflicts of interest
exist which have been neither
mutually agreed upon nor COM
promised, The principal zone of dis
agreement is the Eastern Balkans,
running from the Danube delta to
Constantinople. And during the
past few days, streams of press re-
ports have been coming from many
sources which are too definite to
leave any doubt that a real clash
between German and Russian in
terests impends.


The current crisis seems to have
been precipitated by the breakdown
of lengthy negotiations among the
members of the Danube Navigation
Commission. Since the expulsion of
the former British and French dele
gates, its outstanding members have
been the delegates of Germany,
Russia, Italy and Rumania. What
caused the breakdown has not been
officially disclosed, but it is stated on
seemingly good authority that Soviet
Russia demanded control over all
three mouths of the Danube.
Since its seizure of Bessarabia, Rus
sia already controls the northern
mouth. Report has it that this pre-
cipitated violent quarrel between
the Russian delegation and that of
the axis. Certain it is that the dele
gates have gone home and that the
commissions sessions stand ad-
journed-ostensibly until the end of
January. All of which indicates
that something serious must have
happened.


Meanwhile, in Rumania, intensi-
fed prosecutions of local Commu-
nistS by the Iron Guard conceded
with one or more sharp Russian
diplomatic notes to the Rumanian
government complaining of alleged
"anti-Soviet activities" and warning
that these must stop Concurrently
there began the mass movement of
German troops and military equip
ment into Rumania via Hungary,
which is obviously swelling to gigan-
tic proportions. The Hungarian
Railway Administration has publicly
announced the suspension of regular
passenger service to allow the pas
sage of 1,160 German military trains.
1t is conservatively estimated that
this means the sending of 100000
troops and abundant materiel to
Rumania, to reinforce the 100000
German soldiers already there. With
picked Russian divisions reportedly
concentrating in Bessarabia, the
stage seems set for at least a dip
lomatic test between Hitler and
Stain, repercussions of which may
bring almost anything.

COPENHAGEN, Feb. 23.-A Brit
ish-French warship squadron began
today e blockade of the Northern
Russian coast, the newspaper Ber-
lingske Tidende reported, while
uncomfortable rumors circulated
| that clash with the Soviet Arctic
Navy already had been precipitated.


The paper said the allied ships
were strung out for a considerable
distance along the Arctic coast to
prevent shipment of Russian sup
plies to Germany and to halt any
possible attempt to deliver Russian
submarines to the German Navy.


Presence of allied vessels In that
far northern vicinity was confirmed
yesterday.


Aside from blocking trade between
Germany and her friend, Russia.
the British and French were de-
scribed as aiming to prevent any
German ships from taking refuge
IN Russia-as number Of mer-
chantmen did in the early days nf
the war.


Murmansk Connections Maintained.
/ Until now, it was reported that
German merchant carriers had been
maintaining steady connections with
Murmansk, which is an ice-free port
despite its Arctic location on Kola
Bay.


Development of the blockade
magnifled uneasiness OF Scandi-
navian nations over the future of
their neutrality.


In view of the bad feeling that
resulted from British rescue of cap
tive merchant seamen from the
German ship Altmark in Norwegian
waters last Friday night. there were
apprehensions that any new naval
clashes in northern waters would
raise further knotty and embarrass-
ing problems for the neutrals.


The British and French contend
that Norway's coastline, broken by
fjords and screened by offshore
islands, offers a comparatively safe
highway for German ships from
Murmansk and has been used ef-
fectively to evade their blockade
IN the North Sea.


Red Navy Prepared for War.
The Stockholm newspaper Alton
bladet reported yesterday that the
Russian Arctic Navy had been pre-
pared for the possibility of war and
that Admiral Nikolai Kuznetzoff
naval affairs commissar, had flown
to Murmansk to inspect it.
The Scandinavian countries are
coming to the foreboding view that
almost anything can happen in the
waters of Northern Europe.


The Stockholm newspaper Dasens
Nyheter voiced the hope that the
Scandinavian foreign ministers, who
are to confer in Copenhagen Sat-
urday and Sunday. would agree on
uniform rules for the treatment of
belligerents' ships in territorial
waters.

In ancient times, communication

from bondage in Egypt.


Orthodox congregations had
Passover services this morning.

with the rabbis reading the story of
the exodus from Egypt. The Wash
ington Hebrew Congregation also
had special services this morning.


In homes, institutions and syna-
gogues last night, Washington Jewry
gathered around tables to celebrate
the Seder. At the Hebrew Home
for the Aged Morris Maser, director
of the home, conducted the service

ate unleavened bread and drank
the ceremonial wine at services in
the Hebrew Sheltering Society, 407
Massachusetts, avenue NV.


For the sixth year Jewish en-
listed men from the Army, Navy
and Marine Corps were guests OF the
Jewish War Veterans at services in
the Beth Sholom Synagogue.

sufficient to keep many from their
planned jaunts to the coast.

close tab on the movements of the
hurricane off Hatteras. Weather
Bureau advisories were broadcast
here every 80 minutes.

low that of heavily armored battle

strated clearly in the bitter battle

dinavian waters between the British

record of battleships having been

apparently have suffered serious
damage. Cruisers and destroyers un-

with the Nazis boasting Of numerous
sinkings among British ships Of
these classes.

battleships has been able to resist
the heaviest bombs, naval experts
naturally have been giving serious
attention to the problem of provid-
ing better deck protection for the
lighter ships. Secretary Of the Navy
Charles Edison was impressed with
the need for thicker armor above the
water line during his inspection of
the fleet in maneuvers off the West
Coast recently. Simulated air raids
theoretically wrecked the communi-
cations and fire control apparatus of
several vessels. Damage of this sort
would be disastrous in actual COM

Radio waves carry the human
voice across the Atlantic, but this
wonder of the present age has not
taken the place of cables. Gable
lines are busy, and they take mes
sages across the ocean when radio
fails.


The ocean cable is not a new
thing, but its history goes back less
than a century. In 1874 Samuel F.
B. Morse sent telegraph message
from Washington to Baltimore.
That was great step toward the
ocean cable, which is a group Of
telegraph wires under the sea.


Thirteen years later Cyrus w.
Field, an American, worked to
make q dream come true. After
forming the Atlantic Telegraph
Company" he tried to bring about
the laying of a cable from New
foundland to Ireland. Seven copper
wires were bound together to form
cable" 1000 miles long.


The cable was let out from
ship departing from the Irish coast;
it broke after 400 miles had been
laid. The next year a British ship
and an American ship followed
different plan. Each took about
1850 miles of cable to midocean.
There the cable ends were spAced
together and the ships moved apart.
They let down the cable as they
went, but alas! When the vessels
were only miles apart the cable
broke.

full close import ant chapter in American Maritime

To the thousa sands of Americans who showed SUI

CORAL GABLES, Fla, Feb. H.
Having heard very little of Patty
Berg for the last seven months
while the Minneapolis girl was alb
senting herself from serious golf,
the Nation possibly will be inter-
ested in knowing how Patty has
survived her inactivity.


The subject is thus backed into
and approached with caution for
the reason that there came a time
in the late 1905 when there might
have been little too much written
about the red-haired wonder girl Of
the links.


Not that Patty, a sweet girl,
didn't deserve every word written Of
her prowess from tee to green. She
did. because her record since she
quit playing football with the
neighborhood boys and took up golf
had been uniformly wonderful.
But now Patty has had her ap-
pendix operation, she has missed
the National Women's champion
ship and seen the title fall to an
other fine golfer, Betty Jameson Of
San Antonio, and now she's back
to elbow her way down the fairways
again and take up where she left
of.


Erases Two Tough Opponents.
Is she still the best woman golfer
in the country-if not one worthy
of ranking with the greatest of all
time, including the almost immortal
Joyce Wethered of England? The
answer, after having watched Patty
trim two worthy opponents yester.
day in the Miami -Biltmore cham
pionships, and after having watched
her best rivals in action also, would
seem to be yes.


Patty still has little something
on the other girls. and she should
win her fifth straight championship
here.


Patty's two victories yesterday
were the twenty-second and twenty
third straight that she has scored
in the local classic, which possibly
constitutes a record of some sort. In
her first match yesterday she was
only one over fours for Is holes, on
a fairly long and tough course. That
included one glaring six, where she
overdrove on the seventh hole and
rolled into canal some $50 yards
away.


Her Game Appears Improved.
Yes, Patty appears to have sur
vived her operation and her absence
from tournament golf. If anything,
she appears to be hitting her drives
a little longer. to be approaching a
trifle more crisply and to be banging
her puts at the cup with trace
more confidence. That makes her
very good. indeed.


In her semifinal tussle today she
encounters Marion Miley of Lexing-
ton, KY, a girl who has been right
near the top for several years. The
winner probably will run into Betty
Jameson, the national champion, in
the 36-hole final tomorrow Betty's
opponent today is Shirley Ann john
son of Winnetka, ILL.,, who won two
surprising victories yesterday.


A final between the Misses Berg
and Jameson would be natural.

RICHMOND. Va. Sept. l3.-The
heavy rains and floods of August
ruined about 10 per cent of
Vlrginias flue-cured tobacco crop,
the State Department of Agricul-
ture reported


Approximately / or 2 per cent of
the corn in the central, southern
and southeastern districts of the
State was flooded and was a COM
plete loss, the departments report
said, while the prospects for pea
nuts declined II per cent below the
August forecast due 10 the long
wet period.


The wet weather caused some
rotting OF Irish and sweet potatoes:
seriously damaged" the canning
tomato crop in Bedford, Floyd and
other counties in the Roanoke area;
reduced the yield OF watermelons
on the Eastern Shore. and damaged
the bean crops in Carroll and other
southwest counties.


Fruit Crop Hurt.


The rains also carried their havoc
to the fruit crops, spreading brown
rot in peaches and lowering the
quality of that fruit, and causing
considerable rot on grapes.


Some livestock was lost during
the floods. but while this loss was
heavy for a few individual farmers.
the total represented only a small
percentage of the livestock in the
State.


To offset the flood and rain
damage, the Agriculture Depart
ment said that the rains were help
full to dry sections in Northern
Virginia and in parts OF eastern
and western districts where there
was a minimum of soil washing.


Summing up the outlook, the re-
port said that wheat, oats, buck
wheat, potatoes, peaches and hay
were expected to show larger yield
than last year. while the production
Of corn, rye. barley, sweet potatoes,
apples, tobacco and peanuts will
be less than last year.

King Carol and his encourage expert
enced as they fled from Rumania

been Rumanias last shot at its
former ruler and his friends. Carol
and his two chief associates in his

under detention in Seville, Spain,

dition to Rumania, trial and sem

what charges await the trio is
not made clear, but the nature of
some of the revelations in Bucharest

may be.


Leland Stowe of the Chicago Daily
News foreign staff has made some
sensational disclosures of the grip
Carol, Magda Lupescu and his min
lister of palace, Ernst Urdareanu, had
upon Rumania's economy, a grip
from which they are alleged to have
reaped huge profits, particularly on
Rumania's rearmament. But it evil
IDENTIFY did not stop there. Notations
repeatedly found in the Runanian
National Bank indicated that Carol
may have been going beyond his
royal stipend to dip into Rumania's
treasury. The ostentatious display
which not only Carol but his woman
companion effected in Bucharest,
their huge property holdings abroad
and the elaborate character of their
flights from Rumania in a private
train accompanied by vast assort-
ment of baggage lend weight to the
allegation that Carol found the king
ship extremely profitable and helped
make it so for his friends, some of
whom are already under arrest in
Bucharest.


Carol will find few to Sympathize
with him in his plight. Rumania In
all probability would have been far
stronger and better equipped to deal
with the Nazi, Hungarian and Soviet
threats if its regime had not deCayed
during Carols rule. Certainly there
was no unity within Rumania behind
him, due perhaps to the fact that too
many people resented Lupescu's
Vaccinations, her trading in official
positions, and her influence over
Rumania's ruler. Many non-Nazis
could not tolerate such a condition.
When the crisis came, Rumania was
a weak and ready victim for hostile
neighbors. Carols abdication was
not the end of the story for Rumania,
and more of it undoubtedly will be
unraveled if Carol, Lupescu and
Urdareanu are returned to Bucharest.

Twenty-six years ago today, April
21, 1914, an American landing force
swept over the waterfront of Vera
cruz, Mexico. Marines and sailors
landed on the fire-swept beach,
swarmed through the streets and
eventually gained control of the city.
There was bitter opposition. A
sgroup of valiant naval cadets, to
whom life was cheap and honor
priceless, gathered in defense of the
academy. Most of them perished
there. Street fighting is always
bitter and Veracruz was no excep-
ton. Men died, gallant men on both
sides, without even the small con-
ISOLATION of dying for a major cause.


Things like that just don't hap
pen. They are generally the result
of carefully considered plan. Vera
cruz was part of a plan. Behind
the occupation lay two contributing
factors, and strangely enough it
was the lesser of the two that was
offered to the general public as the
casus belli: Honor! Honor has al
ways been convenient peg upon
which to hang excuses of this kind.


Had the true reason been adj
vanced at the time, the public
would have accepted it less readily
than the intangible affront to our
national honor. Although the cir
cumstances justified prompt action,
many Americans would have doubt
less condemned the expedition. for
actually it was on the borderline
between justifiable seizure and
wholesale piracy.


Instead, the "Tampico incident"
was offered for public consumption.
This occurred on April 9, when one
officer and nine unarmed sailors
from the u S. S. Dolphin went
ashore to obtain supplies. Their
boat was tied up to the wharf when
Mexican soldiers Suddenly and mex
plicably pounced upon the Ameri.
cans and placed them under arrest.

The last zero weather experienced

The forecaster expected the mer-
curry to begin a drop this afternoon
after last nights temporary modi-
fication of the cold which has per-
sisted here throughout the rev
year.

polar air has been moving south

forecaster said. 1T now appears to

direction

badly. They said skating would be
resumed tomorrow if the expected
sub freezing weather develops

and Virginia during the last few

last fortnight and thickened the ice

peake Bay.

lures had modified somewhat this
morning.

throughout the brief session, favor
ties managed to tack on further
recoveries of fractions to a point
or so.

War developments and the tax

The first aerial blitzkrieg on
Potomac River fish failed today be-
cause the weather was too good.


For an hour and half, two men,
bers Of the Washington Chapter
of the Izaak Walton League piled
rod and reel from the Goodyear
blimp, Enterprise, cruising slowly
over the Potomac near ST. Gather
ines Island, about 10 miles down
the river. But perfect" weather,
with only the slightest breeze,
forced the blimp to maintain a
speed of 10 miles or more an hour
the fishermen said, and their lines
spanked along the surface of the
water too swiftly for fish to bite.


Bob Wilson, chairman OF the
local Izaak Walton Cotton Thread
Fishing Committee, and Jack Mil
ligan. the other aerial angler, said
that if they could only have had a 10
to 15-mile- -an-hour wind to head
the blimp into, allowing them to
cruise at a virtual standstill over
the water, they would have caught
some fish.


Capt. Werner Smith, commander
of the blimps crew, seconded their
view.

ABOARD AN UNNAMED SHIP
AT A SOUTHERN ENGLISH PORT,
June 21.-Nearly 1,500 British and
foreign refugees from invaded
France crammed on the narrow
decks Of ship intended to accom-
modate only 180, raised a full
throated cheer as they sighted the
green hills of Cornwall.


Before the ship arrived from
France last night food and water
were running short. German bomb
ers had attacked them and these
refugees-including at least 500
women with young children-had
slept for three nights on open decks
as the rescue ship plowed its way
homeward under destroyer escort.


In every corner of the cabin ac-
commodations old and sick lay
wrapped in rugs, coats and even
mats off the floors. Passengers hud-
died in companionways, on stairs
and every available square foot Of
the decks.


fr1eStS ana NUNS ADOdT0.


There were British families from
Paris and the Riviera, students
from Geneva, priests and nuns,
French, Czechs and Polish and Ger
man Jews. There were sailors, ma
rines, army officers from units of
the British Expeditionary Force,
woman ambulance drivers and I'M
perial Airways officials.


There also were the original pas
sengers-settlers and government
officials from East Africa-who
cheerfully surrendered their cabins
to refugees, many of whom seemed
half dead with weariness from their
flight across France. Each had his
own story of adventure or private
sorrow.


For % hours the ship waited near
Bordeaux while refugees poured
aboard. One tender was alongside
when a German plane suddenly
swooped from the sky and tried to
rake the ships crowded length with
machine-gun fire. No one was hit.


French fighters chased the plane
away and few minutes later it was
seen falling in flames, hit by guns
of British cruiser which was en-
barking members of the British En-
bassy staff across the bay.


All Food Is Rationed.


All night the boat lay at anchor
at the mouth of the moonlit harbor
while passengers nervously expected
to be bombed at any minute About
am. shrill whistles sounded the
alert and the ship shuddered as
her anti-aircraft gun began blazing
away at a low-1ying plane believed
to be dropping magnetic mines In
the sea around her.


A nearby jetty was bombed, and
passengers who crowded to the rail
saw plume of jet-black smoke
rise to the sky.


At dawn more refugees scrambled
up the dangerously-swaying accom-
modation ladder. They included six
wounded soldiers in care of pretty
blond nurse who cared for them
increasingly throughout the voyage.


Volunteers tackled the food prob
lem in the limited galley. preparing
and serving lunches where they
could. The ship had just about
enough food to last on limited ra-
tions, although 1t was . month
overdue. having been routed via
Capetown, South Africa, instead of
through the Mediterranean Sea.


The hungry were divided into 10
"sittings." Every one had the same
fare in two meals day. They were
served tea, bread and butter in the
morning; meat, rice and potatoes
at night.

In MASSACHUSETTS about 13O years
ago, the Federalist and Democratic
Republican parties used to poll an
almost even number of votes. Once.
however, the Democratic-Republi-
cans happened to have a majority
in the state senate. The party leaders
took advantage of a constitutional
prerogative that had never before
been evoked. and passed bill redi-
viding the state into new senatorial
districts. Their scheme was to put
those sections that normally returned
preponderant number of Federalist
votes into single district. The Demo-
cratic-Republican governor Elbridge
Gerry reluctantly signed the bill.


When the boundaries of one of the
new districts, Essex County, were
drawn up. it looked like a salamander;
and newspaperman of the time COM
bined this word with the Governors
name to coin the term gerrynsd''de1.
The new word strongly appealed to the
popular imagination. and finally came
to mean any political maneuvering
that was designed to give a party an
unfair and unnatural advantage.
However the next year the wrathful
Federalists elected their own gover-
nor and had the law repealed, but the
word - and the practice - linger on.

LONDON, Jan. 29.-German
bombing planes were reported to
have attacked British ships along
400 miles of Britain's east coast to-
day in the most widespread raids
on shipping yet attempted in the
war


Attacks on vessels were reported
from the mouth of the River Tay
in the north to the Kentish coast
in the south. They continued from
shortly after 9 am. to midday.


Anti-aircraft guns burst into &C
ton in the Tyneside area, and air
raid warnings we're sounded in a
number of northeast coast districts.


British fighters were credited with
driving off the bombers.


Ships Reporting Attacks.


Ships reporting attacks were
listed as the British Officer, $500
tons: Atholl Monarch, Danny Bryn,
Stanburn, 1881 tons; Otterpool,
4,867 tons; Knitsley, 2,272 tons;
Wellpark. 4,649 tons, and the $751;

Scottish coast, which reported that
the attacking bombers were driven
off by British fighters.


Seven bombs were dropped near
the 4,699-ton Llanwern in Tyneslde

The German raids came on a day
of bitter winter weather which
brought British rail and highway
traffic to a state described as the

Violent explosions were heard at
sea off North Yorkshire resort be-
fore the first air raid. warning
sounded in four towns along the

The 1591-ton Norwegian vessel
Hosanger also was sunk A British

STOCKHOLM, Sweden, March IA
NA.N.A).-The prelude to the
Finnish Russian peace negotiations
and the immediate reason why the
Firms started talking peace was the
break-through by the Red Army of
the third line and strongest defenses
of the famous Mannerheim Line at
Summa three weeks ago. This
break through is the most signifi-
cant military feat since the World
War-not only because of its mill
tary Importance, but because of i'm
mediate developments which sent
the Finnish Premier Risto Ryti,
Juho Paasikivi, former Premier of
Finland, and colleagues to Moscow.


What caused the folding up of
this famous and long-held and al
most impregnable line, which was
equal to, and, in some ways, better
than the Maginot and Siegfried
Lines?


Three Reasons for Break.


Three reasons, which, put to-
gether, constitute q hitherto unre-
vealable answer. First, the only
weakness in the line itself was acci-
dentally found by the Russians; Sec
ond, the WEAKNESS Of the Firms and
the impossibility Of relieving their
best fighters; third, but not least
important, was the first use of their
best divisions by the Red Army COM
manders.


The Mannerheim Lines strength
was not the strength of the first line
itself, but the strength of everything
behind that first line. Dugouts, tank

By the Associated Press


LES VERRIERS. Switzerland (At
the French Border. June 1s.-
French troops, 350,000 strong,
escaped today from the lower Magi-
not Line to reassemble with the
southern army and lend force to the
nations insistence upon an honor
able peace


The troops moved south in two
main forces, the first of 100000 and
the second of $4,000.


The larger body was shielded by a
few thousand French Alpine Chas-
seurs, who stood guard in the lower
Jura region while the Maginot Line
troops escaped behind the thin
screen.


The second force of $4,000, mainly
from the Nancy garrison and vet
Grams of engagements around Metz
and the Vosges sector, headed south
IL hours after the others. They made
their way down through the Saone
Valley unopposed except for skir-
mishes with small motorized German
units.


Germans Reach Swiss Frontier.


Their passage indicated here that
although German panzer divisions
reached the Swiss frontier early this
morning, the Alsace Lorraine area
is still far from being sealed OF from
the rest of the French forces.


1t was considered impossible for
the Germans in two days to have
extended its motorized legions over
the area from Verdun TO Jura in
more than thin line.


A lone French motorcycle courier
was said to be maintaining liaison
between the forces.


Artillery fire just north of Basel
ceased today, but the rumble of guns
was still audible from the region
around Neuf Brisach where the
Germans are maintaining bridge
heads at the Rhine and the Rhine
Rhone Canal.


Huge clouds of smoke marked the
passage of French troops in with
drawal. They were burning oil
and gasoline reservoirs, dynamiting
bridges and destroying munitions
dumps behind them


Citizens Feed Soldiers.


In the communities of Eastern
France through which the troops
moved south. the civilians reopened
barricaded shutters and doors to
greet and feed the soldiers.


Everything had been prepared for
the encirclement developments and
the people had been expecting to see
German rather than their own
soldiers.


The main French army of the
south, according to advices reaching
here, is being reasSembled at the
junction of the Rhone and Saone
Rivers.


The feat of the Alpine Chasseurs
IN screening their mates happened
this way.


Sometime between the fall of
Paris and the fall of Verdun the
Maginot defenders were ordered to
send out all available reserves, and
at the same time two divisions of
Alpine Chasseurs were rushed from
the ltallan front to reinforce the
Verdun sector.


Chasseur Force Cut in Two,


Before the Chasseurs reached the
Verdun region, however, the Ger
mans broke through on the Marne
and sent an armored division to
close the door behind Alsace-Lor-
raine and the Maginot zone. On
Sunday they cut the Chasseur force
In two. Less than a division was
left between the Germans and the
Jura Mountains.


Nevertheless, despite their small
force and their weariness from sew
eral days fighting, they stood for 36
hours against the Germans, using
several batteries of 75's and lois
which they found at the position
they took on Little Freese Mountain
about 80 miles from the Swiss
frontier.

A communique issued by the Min

large fires had been caused and no

week. Planes in the raid. which
was Of comparatively short duration,

and delayed action bombs.

when a high explosive bomb hit two

MARY had little lamb, its fleece
was white as snow," is the theme
song for winter evenings. At least,
so it would seem, judging from the
vast array of great coats, capes
OF natural fieeces, and little short
Woolen jackets that are amusingly
realistic.


Never has the debutante gone into
her first winter better fortified
against the cold, and never has her
evening wrap looked the gala part
as 1t does this winter. Made of sim
pie wool weave, her chic evening
coat is not too dressy for her first
winter. 1t gives her a comfortable
wearable fabric that she doesn't
have to live up to. She can gloat
over the fact that she is turned out
as smart as her brother will be in
his new trench coat.


Her trench coat is made of the
new woolen fleeces with often wide
gold belt and military buttons.
There are wonderful duvetyn coats
too, in brilliant colors embroidered
in gold on lapels and pockets. There
are slim fitting soft tweeds and
worsteds in jade green, rust, plum
and turquoise, which are interlined
and warm as toast.


Then there are broadcloths and
fannels, and capes in beautiful pas
tells with huge fur collars which are
finding favor with older women as
well as young. White or royal blue
are color favorites.


There are wool ensembles, sheer
wool crepes, fine fluid broadcloths,
duvetyns, lovely cashmere-like fab
RIGS and marquisette-like woolens
which drape beautifully. Often the
gowns are cut very low and worn
with sequin embroidered jackets
an evening tailleur that changes into
a very formal dinner gown. Beige
and gray are very popular colors.
The gray is frequently combined
with chartreuse, flame red and
jade.


1t is surprising how many women
are choosing a tailleur softly draped
with a very short or wrist length
jacket. Certainly for the woman
who does not have a lot of clothes a
wool formal gown with jacket will
serve for many occasions.

I saw a young and beautiful women
the other day who told me the amazing
fact that she was ninety years old. 1
could scarcely believe her for her
face was smooth and her body unbent
and graceful. I asked for her secret
and she smilingly said it is only this:
Keep busy. She said that she had
never stopped working but had kept
right along with her duties and found
a real joy and satisfaction in them.
And so, with unceasing activity her
blood had been kept pure with it's
hurry through her veins while her
body had never had chance to grow
rigid and bowed. She said, any woman
can remain young and beautiful if
she will just KEEP BUSY.

THE HAGUE, June Most of
the half-million Netherlanders who
fed their homes during their nation s
five days Of war have returned.


Among those not back home are
10000 Rotterdam residents housed
at The Hague and nearly 5000 from
Breda, town near the Belgian border,
who are wandering about between
Client and Bruges.


Mayor Bartholomew Won Slobbe

were forced to flee when their town
was converted into a fortress. He
said, however, that Breda escaped
damage and that all but the group
between Ghent and Bruges had re-
turned.


Thousands of Dutch soldiers still
are in Belgian coastal towns to
which they retreated from Holland
with French troops. After the capi-
tulation of the Belgian Army they
began returning home afoot and are
expected to arrive in few days.

BERLIN, Sept. THE British
Royal Air Force. staged its most
daring. its most spectacular, its
noisiest and Its most destructive
attack of the war on Berlin last
night.


For the greater part of three
hours, beginning shortly after mid
night, the skies over the city were
bright with flares. tracer bullets. and
the flashes of anti-aircraft artil-
lery. Window panes ratified and old
buildings preceptibly trembled with
the shock of explosions, and the
gibber of machine guns flashed
viciously across the road, amidst
the belch and bark Of the heavier
pieces and the drone Of British
motors.


The British flyers did more dam
age in general than they had pro-
duced during any single attack
before.


The most striking feature of the
raid as a spectacle was the audacity
Of the British pilots. Kept of from
the city by the balloon barrage, and
battered at, when they broke
through, by the anti-aircra{t guns,
which seem to have been notably
reinforced in recent days, the flyers,
nevertheless, few so low over Berlin
that the drone of their motors was
plainly audible even in cellars and
the Germans were repeatedly able
to take the planes under machine
gun fire.


Some of the pilots flew with an
enthusiasm so sternly that they
might almost have been unaware
of the heavy fire that the anti-air-
craft guns were putting up. One
man flew low across the center of
the city from east to west dropping
series Of several flares as he went,
then circled about and proceeded to
drop another series from west to
east along almost precisely the same
line again.

LONDON, May IL Sunday The
Royal Air Force, following up morn
ing raids, again attacked German
mechanical forces advancing from
the Rhine toward the Meuse late
yesterday afternoon, the Air Min
istry announced early today.


The Air Ministry's communlque:


German mechanized troops ac-
vancing from the Rhine toward the
Meuse were again harassed yester-
day Saturday by a series OF
attacks made by aircraft of the
Royal Air Force.


Roads leading out of Maastricht
were bombed and a few miles SOUTH
west Of the town on the road to
Tonvres column of small tanks,
armored cars and transport vehicles
were attacked and several direct
hits were obtained"


50 Planes Reported Felled.


At least so German planes were
reported destroyed and many others
put out of action in the first days
raids in the Lowlands.


"The enemy's advance was further
hampered by a series of operations
in which bombs were seen to hit
important railways and road juno
tions and bridges at Alderkerke,
Gelgern, Rees and Goeh," the min
istry's communique said.


Another admiralty announcement
said British naval planes made two
forays against Bergen. scoring three
hits on German ship believed to
be the 14,600-ton training vessel
Bremse.


The second raid, achieved with
complete surprise" was reported to
have fired and heavily damaged
German fuel tanks.


, Claim 20 Planes Shot Down.


Since April 8, the Air Ministry
said, 20 Nazi aircraft had been shot
down of Norway by the fleet air
arm, which is separate from the
Royal Air Force, and that many
others had been destroyed on the
ground. The fleets anti-aircraft
guns were credited with bagging an
additional 81 enemy aircraft.


Fresh from the lesson of Norway,
where lack of air support cost the
allies the rich south and center
regions, the Royal Air Force led the
campaign to hold lowland flying
bases at all costs and delay Ger

can take up positions alongside the
Dutch and Belgians.


Disposition of allied forces was
kept secret. but it was no secret that
one of the big jobs of the allies is to
prevent the German thrust toward
Liege from separating Belgium and
the Netherlands.

NEW ORLEANS, Dec. 31.-Ken-
lucky, victor in two previous Sugar
Bowl basket ball tussles, succumbed
last night, 48-45, to an Indiana
team that covered the court almost
as thoroughly as the varnish.


The Hoosiers led all the way ex-
cept for a few minutes of the first
half, and on two occasions amassed
big leads. But the Kentuckians
rallied both times, and the game
ended with $500 spectators-an-
nounced as the largest basket ball
crowd ever gathered here-yelling
furiously as the clubs matched point
for point until the last few seconds.


Indiana, with practically the same
team that copped the national in
tercollegiate championship last year,
won by superior floor play. The
Hoosiers' guarding and ability to
get the ball off the blackboard kept
the Colonels shooting from dis
tance. while Indiana passes and
dribbles often pierced the wildcat
defense.


The Kentuckians, however, found
the basket with accuracy of the
squirrel guns of their native hills,
while the boys from across the Ohio
tossed many Grip shots futilely over
the hoop.


Curley Armstrong, ace dribbler,
and Bill Menke were high scorers,
each tallying IA points for Indiana.
Lee Huber got II forKentucky, all
on field goals, two coming from close
to the middle. Milton Ticco scored
four field goals and two singles for
the losers.


Kentucky, Southeastern Confer
ence champions last year, beat Pitts
burgh, 4O-19, in 1887 and Ohio State,
$3.50, in 1889 in the Sugar Bowl
game. 1t was Indiana's first ap-
pearance.

BY the Associated Press.


NEW ORLEANS, Dec. 31-Two
football teams with 20 miles of gulf
coast between them, but nary an
alibi. were ending the year and their
practice simultaneously today in the
quiet Of their respective camps as
enthusiasm over their meeting in
the Sugar Bowl classic here tomor-
row slowly worked its way toward
mass hysteria.


At Bay City. Miss, an apprehenslve
Frank Leahy was to send his Boston
College Eagles through mild work
out to brighten any dull spots and
then prepare to spend New Year
Eve worrying in all dimensions about
what might happen tomorrow.


Eastward along the coast at Edge
water Park. Bob Neyland and his
confident Tennessee Vols were to GO
through a similar routine, with the
veteran Neyland, to whom bowl
games have become just an extern
sion department of the regular
schedule, forsaking Leahy's worry
ing role.


Both Teams in Top Shape.


With the recovery of Gene Good
reault, star Boston end, from knee
injury, both squads are in top shape
physically. The Eagles, since their
arrival, have been high-spirited and
kittenish, a fact taken as a good
omen by their followers. The Vols
have been businesslike, which their
fans also view with encouragement.


Meanwhile this alWays-festive city
was beginning to look like all the
county fairs rolled into one as trains,
buses, automobiles and boats hourly
disgorged hundreds of rabid fans.
Hotel lobbies resembled mass meet
ings; streets, from the narrow, an
tique French quarter to the broad
expanse of the main business dis
trict, were thronged with good
natured, jostling crowds, promising
New Year Eve without a roof.


From all lips came one question:
who do you like?"


1t came with a soft, Dixie accent,
or with a crisp Down-East twang.
The answer always brought an argu-
ment.


Tennessee Heavy FavOrite.


Oddly enough, except for the rabid
Tennessee fans and the equally
rabid Bostonians, the choices were
usually based ON a cold analysis of
each team, with Tennessee usually
coming out on top in this kind of
competition. So much so, in fact,
that the Vols early today were rated
2-5 favorites, although the margin
was expected to narrow as the
Northerners increased in number.


Odds or no odds, the belief was
general that $1,000 spectators would
see a great, and possibly free-scor-
ing, battle between two undefeated
teams tomorrow


The two squads were to remain
at their camps tonight, arriving
here about headache time tomorrow
morning. The weatherman has
promised sunny skies.

Black Pussy, the cat who lives at
Farmer Browns house, was starting
out for a walk. To have seen her
you would never in the world have
guessed that she had anything on
her mind beyond getting little
exercise. Hunting was the last thing
in the world which you would have
suspected her of.


Across the barnyard into the Old
Orchard walked Black Pussy, and
paid no more attention to Tommy
Tit and Drummer the Woodpecker
and Happy Jack Squirrel and Chat
terer the Red Squirrel than if they
didn't exist. She didn't even glance
at them, although they called her
ell the bad names they could think
of. But Cor one thing you might
have supposed that Black Pussy
didn't hear them at ALL The one
thing that showed them she did was
the tip of her tail. That twitched.
She couldn't help it. 1t always
twitches when she is angry.


Down along the edge of the Old
Orchard, toward the Green Forest,
Black Pussy walked. You see she
know better than to try to catch
any of those little folks in the Old
Orchard. She had tried too often,
and they knew her too we'll. In
the far corner Black Pussy stopped
at the edge of the brush pile
Farmer Browns Boy had put there
for the Bob Whites. From under
that pile came the scent of little
brown coated birds. Black Pussys
mouth watered. She was tempted
to wait and watch. But after a
bit she decided that she would first
visit the Green Forest


Now, as soon as Black Pussy was
quite out of sight of the little folks
of the Old Orchard, she no longer
appeared to be merely out for a
walk. To have seen her then you
would have known instantly that
she was hunting. She crept along
over the snow, listening, watching.
looking into every bush and behind
every old stump she came to. She
was perfect picture of stealth. She
was hunting just as her cousin,
Yowler the Bob Cat, hunts. She
was hunting, not because she was
hungry, but because of sheer love
of hunting and the cruel desire to
kill.


Black Pussy hoped to surprise
Whitefoot the Woodmouse, or one
of Peter Rabbits half-grown chill
dren, or Mrs. Grouse, or one of
the little feathered folks who had
come down from the Far North to
spend the winter. So she stole from
bramble-tangle to bramble- -tangle,
and snow-covered spruce to snow
covered spruce, a fierce desire blaz-
ing in her yellow eyes.

NEW YORK, Aug. 13.-Granger
railroads-the big Western carriers
that move the grain crops to mar
ket-are feeling a little better about
the wheat situation.


For some time it has been feared
by many rail executives that there
would be a sharp drop in winter
wheat production this year


Now. however, the figures. are just
about complete, revealing that win
ter wheat harvested this season ag-
gregated around $4,000 900 bushels,
or only about 100000 under the
563 100000 threshed in 1899.


Railway grain traffic this year has
been substantially under 1899, due in
part to the fact that much wheat
was placed under Government loan
and is now stored and sealed in
private warehouses and on farms
throughout the West.


But Grain Must Move.


However traffic executives say
this grain eventually must be hauled
TO market and when that time comes
the granger roads will benefit.


Big haulers of winter wheat in
clude the Atchison. Topeka e. Santa
Fe; Union Pacific; Chicago, Rock

Missouri ri-Kansas-TeXas, St Louis
San Francisco and the st. Louis

The wheat export picture at the
moment looks dark. The blockade
of sea shipping brought by the Euro
pean war has for all practical pur-
poses closed continental markets to
American grain sellers. While Great
Britain has been an increasingly
large customer for American goods
since the outbreak of the war, she
has been taking industrial materials
primarily and getting wheat and
other food supplies from her colonies
and dominions, including Canada.
Just week or so ago Britain bought

ada.


Europe to Need Wheat.

conditions for Europe this winter.
With France, Norway, Denmark.
Belgium and the Netherlands-all

ing around 200000,0O0 more bushels

Former President Herbert Hoover,
head Of the European Food Distri-
button Commission, this week started
negotiations with both the British
and German governments to permit
him to move grain through military
blockades into the Netherlands. Bel
gium, Poland and Norway. where
$1,000 900 persons are facing starva-
ton" The negotiations still are in
the conversational stage. but if
movement to Europe's needy is ar
ranged, surplus American grain sup
plies this fall and winter may be
ferried across the Atlantic to Euro
pean civilian hands.


Shipping of grain for war refugees
abroad, railmen say, might start
moving to market winter wheat now
stored in warehouses and bins in the
Western crop belt


And the granger roads would be

This little locust tree. with all its
and millions Of tiney little blossoms, all
together making one huge blossom, was
at the northwest corner Of the house,
not more than 10 feet away.


There are two windows in the upper
room there, one on the west, and the
other on the north.


Through these windows In the early
morning, and especially in the evening,
( came the delicious scent Of the flowers.


And all through the day, from first
light to last light, came the hum-m-m-
m-m Of the bees. gathering the pollen
which they were going to make into
honey.


Do you like honey2


We have always been sorry that we do
not like honey very much. 1t seems such
worthy food, made by such brave,
wise bees.


All day long, and for many days, the
hum of the bees came through the
windows, mingled with the scent of the
blossoms.


1t was almost as if the flowers and
the bees and the sweet smell were right
IN the room there, so close they all were,
and so sweet the odor, fragrant but not
penetrating.


No wonder the bees liked those little
flowers


Then one afternoon the sky clouded,
and storm arose.


1t was early for a storm, but storm it
did, with lightning and thunder, and
all that.


Suddenly there came splitting sound.


The tree had not been struck, and it
had not been uprooted, but one of the
largest branches fall forward to the
south, right in the middle of the wind
storm.


1t was the bees tree, receiving severe
blow from the storm.


Next day, tree men came to look at the
tree.


They took off the splintered bough
and found that the entire trunk was
| hollow, from point about feet from
the ground.


SO the tree had to come down, for it
would have fallen in the next storm
of course.


The stump was cut off about 2 feet
from the ground
The top was followed out, and con-
creted, to make bird bath.
There today scores of birds take their
baths, and drink happily.
An old vine winds up to say hello to
the redbird, and the blue jay, and the
nut hatcher, too.
You see, the good things in this world
are never lost, even though they are
blown down.

Most boys and girls, and probably
few grown-ups, believe that
marines are called "leathernecks"
because Of their exposure to the heat
Of the tropics and the tanning effects
Of the rays of the sun. But the sea
soldiers were given this nickname
for an entirely different reason.


In the days when the marines
wore their hair in long. powdered
braids, they were given stiff, close
fitting leather bands, called stocks,
to wear around their necks. These
stocks held their heads erect in the
approved military manner, and pre-
vented the powder from their hair
from brushing off on the backs of
their uniforms.


This custom was still in practice
nearly 100 years after the soldiers
had abandoned their braids. And
thus originated the nickname
"leathernecks."

BY the Associated Press.


GENOA, Italy, Jan. 23.-Surviv-
ing members Of the crew OF the
italian liner Orazio said today that
the fire which DESTROYED their ship
and imperiled the lives Of more
than 600 aboard started when a
spark from a motor set fire to lu-
bricating oil. which In turn caused
fuel oil to explode.


Other survivors declared many of
the 10 persons reported missing had
died of exposure and told how a
badly burned Peruvian mother
jumped from the flaming ship into
the sea, leaving her baby aboard.


The Italian liners Conte Blanca
mano and Colombo brought more
than 500 survivors of the disaster
into port. About half of the num-
Der were injured or burned in the
explosion and fire which destroyed
the South America bound liner.
= Authorities investigating the cause
Of the blaze found a general agree
ment among survivors Of the crew
that it was preceded by an explosion.
Just where the explosion occurred
was not determined.


Seven ambulances carried the
worst Of the injured to hospitals.


Survivors said some scantily clad
victims died of exposure when waves
dashed over the nfeboats, drenching
the occupants. Others were lost
while being transferred from the
ship to lifeboats in the rough seas.


Seventy of the original SAB pas
sengers and crew aboard the vessel
have not been accounted for. Six
of those missing are believed to be
passengers. The Italian Line, which
owns the Orazio, said SCI persons
had been saved. Twelve Germans
were taken off the liner the day be-
fore the fire by French patrol boat.


The student explosion and fire
were reported to have destroyed
most of the Orazio's lifeboats.


Among II Colombians rescued by
the Colombo was Sonora Cecilia
Santos Ortiz, niece of the President
Of Colombia and wife of Colombias
Consul General at Genoa. She suf-
fered slight leg burns. Her daughter
Maria also was saved.


Enrique Forero, another survivor,
disclosed that he and his wife and
two children had been rescued from
the Netherlands liner Simon Bolivar
when it was sunk by a mine in the
North Sea last November 10, and ex-
pressed joy that their luck still
held.


Carlo Failla, Colombian CONNER
ciai Attache at Rome; his wife, two
children and sister were others
among the rescued.


Planes Continue Search,


Seaplanes continued to search the
Mediterranean in the hope of find
Ing persons listed as missing.


The Orazio's Second Officer Clio
relic, among 48 survivors landed at
Marseille by French warship, said
the fire followed an engine room ex-
plosion, but that he did not know
the cause.

HOLLYWOOD, May 25.-Dras-
tically, Hollywood pushed a re-
trenchment campaign today in the
face of vanished European and
dwindling American revenues-trace-
able directly. say studio heads, to
spearding fires of war.


Distributors in key cities reported
almost without exception that a
jittery public, uncertain of the fu-
ture, is keeping a collective ear to
its radio and collective purse in its
pocket.


Producers discovered long ago
that times of stress bring such a
situation, but this time profess
genuine alarm. Figures on how
great is the past two weeks domestic
box office slump were not compiled,
but one studio spokesman COM
mented:


Its worse than the depression"


Slump Felt Quickly.


Since movies literally are made
today with money pushed into
cashiers cages yesterday, a slack
ened financial flow is felt quickly.
The effect has been a tightening up
all along the line. Budgets are be-
ing trimmed to the bone. Location
trips are being Cancelled and studio
sets built with the least complexity.


In some instances stats have been
cut. Script writers have been told
to plan simple scenes, using few ex-
tras. Authors with stories to sell
are sure to feel the pinch. For every
major studio has million dollars
or more in unused original manu-
scripts. These will be pulled from
files, busted off and turned into
celluloid.


Stars incomes can't be affected.
since all are under contract. But
in at least one plant the economy
rule is brought home to them.
Radios have been banned from all
dressing rooms. Surveys showed too
much time wasted listening to
broadcasts and discussing them
later. And although every studio is
top-heavy with high-salaried execu-
tives and producers, unwillingness to
trim much high up the ladder has
been evinced in past financial diff
ficulties.


Ultimately the theatergoing pub
lie may benefit. For one studio
chief instructed his department
heads:


Make better pictures, with 100
cents OF quality for every dollar.
When people tire of thinking and
talking war, they'll crave enter
tainment. If our brand is good,
we'll get the business"

BUSINGEN, Germany Correspond
ence of the Associated Press).-A Ger
man island in Switzerland some miles
square has been forced into unwilling
isolation due to the European war.


More than 1000 Germans live in the
town of Busingen and its surrounding
farms which form q German territory
several miles inside the Swiss frontiers,
north Of Schaffhausen.


Before war began, Busingen's inhabit-
ants, though German. were allowed free
transit through Switzerland to Germany.


Now everything's different. The 3-mile
area is literally locked up by the Nazis.
Any one entering 1t must have a pass
port. Swiss newspapers are banned.
Scores Of German customs guards en-
force the regular German monetary
restrictions.


Before Hitler came, Germany and
Switzerland were in the midst Of nego-
tiations to have the little island turned
over to Switzerland, but such deal was
hardly compatible with the Nan pro-
gram Of greater Germany and the
talks were halted.


For several years during the Nazi
regime the inhabitants OF Busingen
elected a non-Nazi mayor although the
hooked cross was flown from their city
hall and church steeple.


The Nazis put stop to that recently
by appointing mayor from outside.


The enclave is really hangover from
the Hapsburgs, for the powerful Haps-
burg family kept the little town on
the right bank Of the Rhine in order to
collect Austrian tolls from the barge
men.


Now the whole area Is surrounded
with barbed wire save at the roads
where Man troopers stand guard check
Ing passpoets.

the Idaho Sawtaoth wilderness
one remaining Western frontier-is
the rodeo's real home. In this coun-
try was fostered the hell-for- leather
school of horsemanship.

market.

81 bill compared with $50 last May,
when Germany began her offensive
against the Low Countries.

buyers at the current quotation and

ing was caused by public fears the
United States might enter the war
or block all continental accounts.
Switzerland is still an international
banking center, and much of Eu-
ropes financial business is cleared
through the little neutral nation.


1n New York the Swiss franc was
priced at 2318, United States cents,
highest since early 1888. The price
has risen steadily in the last month
as Swiss money originally sent to
the United States for safekeeping

While Knud Holmboe and Ab
Deslam were visiting the "cave
dwellers of the mountains" they
were shown a we'll which supplied
water for the whole village. 1t was
only about 80 feet deep, but they
were told it always contained plenty
Of water.


The natives had worked out an
odd but clever invention to take
water from the well. Jugs were
fastened to a rude wheel and the
wheel was moved through water IN
the well. AS the jugs came up they
emptied water into trough. Much
Of the water obtained in that way
was employed to give moisture to
growing crops.


The power for the wheel came
from a camel which was driven
around and around. The beast was
blindfolded to keep him from getting
dizzy.


Leaving the village, Holmboe and
his comrade drove to point where
the road branched in two directions.
The map which they carried showed

right, which looked much better.

Special Correspondent OF The Star.


OMAHA, Nebr., Sept. 28-Wen-
dell Willkie brought his campaign
to Omaha this week and Repub-
lican leaders who persuaded him to
sandwich this city into full itin-
erary hope that his visit will help
stem whatever deterioration there
may have been in his Nebraska
prospects.


Omaha has about 18 per cent of
the States total vote. With farm
ers evidently about evenly divided
between Mr.. Willkie and President
Roosevelt. and with residents of the
smaller towns believed favoring Mr..
Willkie, the Republican nominees
performance in Omaha may we'll
settle the issue for Nebraska as a
whole.


The city was heavily Democratic
in 1882 and 1896. In 1888 it re-
elected a Democratic Representa-
tive and gave the Democratic Gov
ernor enough votes to overcome an
out-State Republican lead. Until
September l this year voter regis
trations were running exactly even
between the two parties. This
month the Democrats have taken
the lead and now have 2,047 new
registrations against 1924 for the
Republicans. Even this represents
considerable Republican gain.
In bringing Mr.. Willkie to Omaha
the Republican leaders, of course,
were not thinking entirely in terms
of the national campaign. They
have State and congressional
tickets to worry about, and their
candidates are none too strong.
For Senator, the Democrats have
an acknowledged vote-getter in
Gov. r. L. Cochran, former State
engineer, who became the only
Governor to serve three successive
terms. His Republican opponent is
Hugh Butler, an Omaha grammar
making his first bid for public office
A grain dealer is not the best sort
of candidate to appeal for farm
votes, and Gov. Cochran is gen.
orally given the edge.


The Republican candidate for
Governor is Dwight Griswold. a
somewhat colorless small-town edi-
tor who has made three unsucce ess-
full races for the Office as Republi-
can nominee. His opponent, Terry
Carpenter. oil dealer and former
Representative, was fought vigor-
ously by all Democratic chieftains
in the primary but now has their
united support. Whereas. Mr.. Girls
void indorses the conservative rec
ord OF his Democratic predecessor,
Mr.. Carpenter appeals to old-age
pensioners with promises of in
creased aid.


Barring a landslide, the Repub-
licans are not likely to improve
their situation in Congress. They
now have three seats. The two
Democrats, Representative Nc
Laughlin of Omaha and Repre-
sentative Coffee of Chadron, have
better than average prospects for
reelection.


Thus, Mr.. Willkie may help the
State and local tickets, but they
are not likely to help him.

Warm weather wearables for the
younger generation have a chic all
their own besides all the practical
features that make the new summer
styles for grownups such a joy. No
matter how much rough and tumble

tom boys of both sexes look like

washed and dressed.


OF course, neither the children nor
the clothes will stay that way long,
but what of it? Having to keep clean
would take all the JOY out of playing
ball, digging tunnels, or eating ice
cream. That's no reason for any one
to be concerned, however. Children
well-trained in health habits always
wash their hands with soap and
water before eating, scrub up all
over in the bath tub, then change
to clean clothes at least once a day

BY the Associated Press,


LA PAZ, Bolivia, March 26.-The
Bolivian government this morning
put down short-lived revolt by
1000 members of a regiment of car
abineros (national police which
government spokesmen said was
due to discomfort with the outcome
OF the recent presidential election.


Government sources said the ris-
ing and its suppression were blood
less. The regiment is quartered in
suburban Mirafiores and apparently
the rebels never left their barracks.
No shots were heard in La Paz.


Gen. Enrique Penaranda, former
head OF the army. was victorious in
the election of March 10 and is
scheduled to assume office April 16.


Leaders Surrender.


The government announced that
the rising had been defeated and
its leaders had surrendered. Their
names were not disclosed. Mai.
Celestino Pinto was the regimental
commander. Government sources
indicated that leaders of the rising
might face death sentences.


Provisional President Carlos Quin-
tanilla ordered Gen. Icazo, army
chief of staff, to inspect all mill
tary units. Gen. Icazo reported that
all elements of the army, totaling
about 10000. except part of the
carabinero and the federal guard,
were loyal to the government


President Quintanilla announced
at noon that conditions were peace
full throughout Bolivia.


Crowds Cheer Quintanilla.


Crowds gathered outside Govern
ment House and cheered Quintanilla
ana PenaranQa.


Penaranda was the only govern
ment-recognized candidate in the
recent election and polled more than
70 per cent of the votes. Others
were split between Jose Antonio Arce
and Gen. Bernardino Bilbao Rioja.


The government declared the elec-
ton was intended to restore consti-
tutional government to Bolivia.
Quintanilla established the present
regime last August % after Dictator
President German Busch had died
of bullet wound said to have been
self inflicted.


Busch had suspended portions of
the constitution; Quintanilla re-
stored some parts and ordered the
election to complete the process.
